MR. MARTINDALE'S REPLY TO A CRITIC.

At the yearly meeting of the Simm's Cross Ward' Committee on Monday evening at the Liberal Club, IVir J B Martindale, the prospective Liberal candidate for the division,recalled that on Saturday last Colonel Hall Walker made two speeches, one at Northwich and the other in Widnes. He ridiculed Colonel Hall Walker 0' contention that the poor people were necessary to the welfare of the country. Colonel Hall Walker, he 0033: tinned, had referred to Imperialism, and etated Oa' the present Government were trying to disunite the Empire by giving Home Rule to Ireland. attributed the present state of the Empire to tbe measures of self-government which had been given t,.° the colonies. Liberals had a progressive policy. 11 (Mr Martindale) had been connected with aces' 0 sopial work, and he was atm.* by the vast majority ef the labouring working men whom he met who wore telegraph messenger belts. AGENTS:
CARTER & SON, BRIDGE ST. WARRINGTON.
UTILITY POULTRY CLUB,
TWELVE MONTHS' LAYING COMPETITION.

The fourth repnrt of Mr. F. W. Rhodes, who is managing the utility clubs' competition at the Harper- Adams Agricultural College, is to hand. The report, covers the fourth period of four NV eeks from January Sth to February 4th, and draws attention to many interesting feature of the competition. In spite of damp, foggy weather during a targe period of the months, the etzg yield shows an increase of 917 eggs over the preceding month, making a total of 6,760 eggs for toe month. The pen records and individual records f.,r the month are worth noting. The highest pen record is 121 eggs, by a pen of white Wyandottes. This means an average of over 20 eggs during the 28 days from each of the six birds comprieing the pen—no mean record. The highest individual record is that of a buff Orping- ton pullet, laying 25 eggs during the 28 days. One is glad to see, however, in these competitions the average yield per pen rising rather than large indivi- dual records.

A pen of red Sussex are occupying the eleventh place. It is interesting to see a strain of this breed coming to the fore. We do not recollect seeing this breed attain such a high position in previous competi- tions. It will be interesting to note where they will fiuish at the end of the twelve month 3. Buff Plymouth Rocks still keep their lead with a total Of 362 eggs (value L,:2. 12s 81d.) to the end of the fourth month. They are followed by three pens of white Wyandottes. div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
[BY REDCAP.]
THE SITTING HEN

Every season brings along new recruits in the poultry farming industry, and generally speaking every novice makes a start by setting a broody hen on a batch of eggs. If this is done without taking ordinary precautions good results will not follow. The first step to be taken is to provide a suitable place, such as an old shed, outhouse or barn. The broody should never be set in places where the rest of the stcck have access ; frequent noises and the interference of other fowls are calculated to upset the steadiness of the sitting hen. Strict privacy should always be secured if at all possible. Some liens will sit very close and would almost bring off the chicks under any circumstances, hut the majority will not do so. Haying selected the place the next point is making.

div.head: NEST.
div.p: THE NEST.

This should be made on the ground floor if possible. Make the nest after the shape of an ordinary dinner plate, not too hollow, or when the hen leaves the nest the outside eggs roll to the bottom and are apt to get cracked. After you have moulded the nest, place into it a layer of nice clean straw. Thou take the broody hen and after dusting her well with Keating's powder, place her gently on to the nest. Then place a few dummy eggs under her whilst on the nest. Having satisfied yourself that she means business the dummy eggs may be substituted for the real eggs. These should always be placed under the hen at night time one by one, and while she is still on the neat. If she huddles them together with her wings you may rest content that she will stick to her work. There is no sed rule as to the number of eggs. This can always be left to your own judgment, but never put under the hen more than she can comfortably cover. It is not wise to put more than eleven eggs under while the weather is cold ; as the emperature becomes warmer you may set hens on more according to the size of the eggs and of course also according to the size of the hen.

div.head: FEEDING.
div.p: FEEDING.

It is only necessary to feed a sitting hen once a day The morning is the best time to do this. The food should consist of hard corn only and perferably maize. This latter is a great producer of beat and therefore it is a good diet for broody hens. A vessel of clean water should be placed with each morning's meal, and also a box of grit and a dust bath. This latter should take the form of a shallow box filled with dry ashes and sand, into which has been added some powdered sulphur. It will often be found that the ben is reluctant to leave her nest. After removing the cover and when she has had every opportunity to eave the neat and does not do so, you must gently ift her from the nest. In doing this care should be taken not to break the eggs. After she has got into her daily habit of feeding she will not be so much trouble. Patience at all times must be exercised if you want good results. Do not let her leave the neat for more than fifteen minutes each day. But always see that she has fed and drank before going back. If the weather is intensely cold, it is a good plan to cover the eggs with a piece of flannel while the hen is oft.

div.head: PERIOD OF INCUBATION.
div.p: PERIOD OF INCUBATION.

The period of incubation for hen eggs is twenty-one days. When the time arrives for the chicks to emerge do not be too anxious to know how many of a family are hatched, Simply place your hand underneath the hen and remove any empty shells that you can feel. If the broody chances to peck at you, do not get impaticnt with her, because if you retaliate in an ungentle manner ;his will only upset the hen and cause her to crush the chicks. First satisfy yourself that the period has elapsed when all the chicks should be hatched and then examine the unhatched eggs that remain. Sometimes you will find that weaker ones have not had the strength to break the shell. Some- times the shells are very strong and refuse to give way to the activities of the chick, but whenever you are tempted to assist them in extricating themselves, use very great care. You will observe where the chicken intends making its exit, by the point of the beak pro- truding through the shell. At this point just gently chip the shell a little more and place the egg back again underneath the hen for a few hours longer. It is always advisable to let nature take her course. Often enough when a chick is too weak to break the shell it is really too weak to live long. It is only in cases of hard shelled eggs that assistance should be given. It is a good plan to slightly damp the eggs with warm water the day before they are due to hatch. The shells are softened thereby and often save you not a little trouble, when hatching time

div.head: arrives
div.p: arrives

, LEAVING THE NEST. After all the chicks are batched out they should be removed from the nest. They should be placed under the hen where the surface of the floor is level. If left in the nest they are apt to get trampled on by the hens, because of the unevenness of the nest. As I have often pointed out chickens need no food for the first twenty-four hours of their existence at least. Therefore, after having well fed the hen, you may leave her with the chicks for this period in peace and quietness. By this method you allow the little ones to " feel their feet " as it were, and so gain strength sufficient to roam with the broody on the third day. Never try to force chickens to eat or drink. Supply them with food and water, and as nature demands, so they will partake ( f their own requirements. I have seen some people actually dip the beaks of newly-hatcned chickens into a saucer of cold water, and then they wonder bow it is they died. It is a most unnatural proceedieg altogether. The old hen can tell them in her own way what to do far bet'er than we can ourselves. GENERAL REMARKS.

Inasmuch as it is not often that one gets an hundred per cent. hatch it is a good plan to set two hens at the same time. When this is done the result of the two broodie's work can be consigned to the care of one hen. Of course, if you are fortunate in bringing off two full batches so much the better. But supposing yru only get for instance,six from one and seven from another, then the total of thirteen would not be too much for a good sized hen to brood. If your accom- modation compels you to use chicken coops, do not forget to place a jar of water near the coop where the ben can drink. It is not an uncommon sight to see the poor old broody with neck outstretched, through the bars of the coop, gasping for a drink. I do wish people would use just a little thought and commonsense. If you intend keeptng fowls, see to their 'every want. Always remember, that by keeping the broody hen content and happy, you also keep the chicks content. As a result they thrive and grow much quicker. I must ask my readers to refer to an article already written on the feeding of chicks and general management. written a few weeks ago. In conjunction with this article they will find it useful. CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL POULTRY DEMONSTRATJ ON.

Readers will - doubtless remember that in this column early in March this year a few notes were written about a poultry demonstration to be held in Cheshire. This demonstration was held at Haslington Hail, Crewe, last Wednesday. I attended the demonstration and I therefore purpose telling you all about it in next week's issue. I hope you will be able to gather therefrom many points of interest and -usefulneks. Meanwhile I have to say that there is an undoubted future for the poultry industry in this country.

div.head: PARR HALL ORGAN,
div.p: PARR HALL ORGAN,
NEW INSTRUMENT TO BE PURCHASED.
S WARRINGTON A MUSIC-LOVING TOWN?

There will be rejoicing among local music-lovers,for the Parr Hall is at last to have a new organ. The Town Council on Tuesday evening decided, by a majority of four votes, to invite tenders from corn- , petent builders for a suitable instrument at a cost not exceeding £1,500. There was an interesting debate in which the question of whether Warrington is really a music-loving town was raised. The MAYOR, who introduced the proposition to purchase the organ, contended that England had not given sufficient encouragement to the art of music, and that since the seventeenth century the Continental nations had enjoyed the distinction of producing the most famous composers. Had Purcel ' lived 20 years longer this country would have been very much more cultured and improved in many respects. The influence of good music was incalculable and everything possible ought to be done to encourage the art. The difference between good and bad literature was well known, and there was an equally marked difference between high- class music aua the kind they got in popular places of amusement.

Alderman TINNION : Ragtime? (Laughter). The MAYOR went on to say that the organ was the best adapted single instrument for the performance of high-class music, and the Council would not be doing their duty as a municipal body if they did not cater for the musical tastes of the people just as much as for any other healthy taste. The people would be much better, happier and more able to do their work if they had more facilities for elevating enjoyment. He appealed to the Council to cast prejudices aside and consider the question purely from the standpoint of public duty.

div.head: "NIGGARDLY AND UNIMAGINATIVE."
div.p: "NIGGARDLY AND UNIMAGINATIVE."

Alderman BENNETT seconded the motion. He regarded it as nothing less than a reflection upon a town of the size and importance of Warrington that they hi hould have a musirail instrument so utterly unworthy of the requirements of the place as the present Parr Hall organ. He could not imagine that self-respecting citizens, taking a broad outlook upon the interests of the town, should oppose the motion. They ought to be absolutely ashamed of themselves if they were so niggardly, unimaginative, and so regardless of reputa- tion that they begrudged the expenditure of the sum proposed. The Corporation were willing to spend money ad lib on all sorts of material needs and in pro- viding amenities for the people, but it was almost lamentable on examining the financial returns to find what a comparatively small proportion of expenditare was devoted to the intellectual side of life. Out of 97.57 d. in the £ spent, only 1•66 d. in the £, excluding the education rate, was devoted to things that appealed to the higher faculties. England was. lamentably behind other nations with regard to the great and beautiful art of music. We could not bold a candle to Germany in musical matters and in a great many other things. We prided ourselves on being the workshop of the world and seemed to think that to scrape a heap of money together meant life and civilization. A town that devoted itself to the mere amassing of wealth and material success did not deserve to live, and was utterly unworthy of the era to which we had attained. On the n.ere ground of fairness it was not right that some interests should be catered for whilst the enjoyment and demands of others should be neglected and ignored, with the exception of a small contribution amounting to £7O per annum to bands which played occasionally in the parks. If it was proposed to have a bowling green everybody supported the motion. The whole universe was not summed up in bowling greens and all people were not prepared to devote their evenings to trundling a ball along the green award or to find all the enjoyment and excitement of life in attending football matches. He hoped they would emancipate themselves from that material view of,things. His only doubt was whether the sum proposed was adequate. He knew a good organ could be obtained for £1,500. There were churches and chapels possessing good instruments which had cost that sum or less, but the organ which represented the collective municipal enterprise and taste should be immeasurably better than any other organ in the tdwn, and one of which they should be extremely proud. Whilst they were about it they ought not to be parsi- monious; they ought not to stint themselves to £1,500. If a good instrument could be obtained for £1,500 he would be glad, and did not wish to be extravagant. To tint themselves because of a possible.additionof lid in the £ or 2d in the £ to the rates was utterly unworthy, and he hoped they woul-1 clear themselves of the reproach which had been laid upon them in the past by voting unanimously for the resolution. Councillor JENKINS supported the resolution on the ground that the encouragement of music by the provis- sion of a new instrument would he essentially for the good of the masses, and not for the classes. Rich people could obtain enjoyment in their own homes or could motor to more pleasant places, and it was the duty of the Council to study the welfare of the poor. Alderman JAMES EVANS asked what length of time would be allowed for the repayment of a loan for the provision of an organ. , The MAYOR: About ten years. Alderman JAMES EVANS : Only ten? The MAYOR: You will not get much more than ten years lam advised. Music is not so well patronized in this country as it is in some others. ' Councillor PEMBERTON : That is just the reason why lam going to oppose it, because it would not be well patronized. The MAYOR: You misunderstand my meaning. I did not mean it in your light at all. I mean by the powers that be; I did not mean by the people. , COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON IN OPPOSITION. Councillor PEMBERTON said the organ would not be of much good to the poor people of whom Councillor Jenkins spoke so pathetically. The poor people got their music in Warrington in the parks, where they could go for nothing. They would not be able to go into the Parr Hall for nothing when the Musical Society gave their concerts. High-class music no doubt was ideal for those people who studied the art, and appreciated it and could afford to pay for it, but why they should undertake any expenditure of ratepayers' money amounting to £1,500 on one instrument just to please one society he could not understand. After the first twelve months the organ would not be played at the outside more than six times a year. When the Parr Hall was opened there was a display of enthusiasm similar to that now witnessed, and concerts at popular prices were given, hut were such a failure that they had to be abandoned. The public took very little interest in them. At the time when Alderman Bennett was anxious for the Corporation to make a grant towards the existing instrument he did not depreciate it, but told quite a different story. The councillor went on to argue that it would cost £25 each time the organ was played. The purchase of an organ was an expendi- ture which the Corpoiation was not called upon to pay, because it would afford so little enjoyment to so few and those few could afford to pay. If it was proposed to spend £1,500 per annum on the provision of music in the parks and recreation grounds he would support such a proposal, because the workingman could hear the music for nothing. When he presented himself at the Parr Hall to hear his beautiful organ a doorkeeper would demand a fee for admission. The Musical Society would make a profit out of the organ, but they would not give it to the ratepayers. He did not think high class music, played on a very superior organ by a very superior men would be very much use to a man who was starving or who wanted a new suit of clothes. With regard to the comparisons which had been made between England and Germany, be (Councillor Pemberton) was not so fond of running down his own country. England could hold its own with Germany, even from tho musical point of view. The MAYOR: No. Councillor PEMBERTON argued that, from the com- mercial point of view, England was the pioneer in the use of steam engines and therefore had a big start of Germany. Now, tiowever, that nation was going ahead and it was not for us to complain of their prosperity. Continuing,he contended that it was unfair of Alderman Bennett to suggest that only a small sum was speat on the higher tastes. The Corporation found £24,000 for education, and some of that money was spent on music in the adios is. They were doing all that was required to be done. If there was a genuine desire for an organ he thought those who made the demand should show their willingness to contribute to the cost. The Musical Society or others who were crying out for the organ were influential people in a wealthy position—in fact £1,500 would be a mere bagatelle to some of them. It was not fair to ask the ratepayers to find the whole of the money. He hoped the motion would be deferred, to be brought up again in some other form. He was agreeable to some of the money, but not all, corning from the rates.

div.head: DEFENCE OF THE MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: A DEFENCE OF THE MUSICAL SOCIETY.

gaining. If the organ was going to be provided for the Musical Society alone, he would not support the pro- position. The society had no claims upon the Council in that respect, but it had claims which were entitled to recognition on the ground that it was the only unsec- tarian, cosmopolitan institution which assisted in the creation and cultivation of a proper musical taste among all classes alike, and the suggestion that its members belonged to a specialized financial class was ridiculous. At least 80 per cent. if not 90 per cent. of present and past members belonged to working. class families. It was a matter of pride to him as a Warringtonian that musical taste was so generally spread among the working people of the town and all the church and chapel choirs had to a great extent ' benefited by the existence of the Musical Society. Councillor Pemberton had displayed an amount of dense ignorance about that organisation which was deplorable. The Musical Society did not make money. He wished it did, and then the vice-presidents would not have to subscribe so much.

Councillor BROACHURST, as One of the poor people who desired more than the bands in the park, sup- ported the proposition. They ought to bring recitals within the reach of the working classes, even if some little loss were incurred. Dealing with the outlay on municipal undertakings which did not pay, Councillor Broadhurst said the Parr Hall had been characterised as" a white elephant that was always hanging roun d their necks." (Laughter). Councillor ARCHER said that up to a certain period he was in sympathy with the proposal, but his experi- ences during the past few weeks had been that the music-loving public represented only a very small proportion of the population, and that the general public were not music lovers, especially when they were called upon to pay for their enjoyment. The time was not opportune to embark upon such a large expenditure from the public purse, and he now doubted whether there was a genuine demand for a new organ.—Tne Councillor instanced Leeds and Sheffield as large centres cf population in which recitals by eminent organists had 12t been well supported, and said he feared that would be the experience in Warrington. Councillor LASHFORD expressed a similar view and I said the organ recitals in bt George's Hall, Liverpool, although they had a population af 1,500,000 to draw upon' attracted an average attendance of only I,OOJ. With the borough rates at 8s in the £, the Council would not be justified in committing themselves to such a large expenditure. Councillor HAWTHORN pointed out that, as the loan would be spread over a number of years, the burden on the rates would be comparatively small. As to the constitution of the Musical Society, three members of his family were connected with that body, and he was surprised to learn that, according to Councillor Pemberton, they were very wealthy. (Laughter.) Music was an art which eppealed to rich and poor alike and the Council ought therefore to spend more on cultivating that taste. Councillor YEMBBRToN : I did not say every mem- ber of the Musical Society was Wealthy. The MAYOR : You gave that impression. Councillor HAWTHORN: "Jilany wealthy gentlemen," you said. Councillor PEMBERTON: There are some of them who could easily afford to buy the organ. Councillor DICKENSON said they had been told that the Parr Hall was a white elephant—in other words, a bankrupt concern. The MAYOR: It is not a profitable concern, that is certain.

Councillor DICKENSON expressed surprise that, under such circumstances, they should be contemplating further large expense on an organ. Alderman Bennett had talked about the niggardliness of the Corporation, but it was generally those who did not pay any rates who spoke in that strain. Alderman BENNETT : Ido pay rates, like anybody else.

Councillor DICKENSON contended that the organ would be installed for the benefit of the better class and not for the workingmen. Councillor WILKINSON said the organ was not intended exclusively for the Musical Society. It was hoped that it would help to raise the Parr Hall from the state of bankruptcy. Not only would it be avail- able for concerts, but, for political meetings, where they indulged in patriotic songs. Alderman TINNioN "We don't want to fight."
(Laughter.) Councilkr Wilkinson was continuing his speech when Councillor GOUGII interposed a remark about a barrel organ. _ _

Councillor WILKINsos retorted: Yes, a barrel organ would suit you. (Laughter.) Continuing, he contended that the organ would bring Parr Hall more prominently before the public. As to the Musical Society, he believed over two-thirds of its membership consisted of sons and daughters of the working classes. The organ would only involve one-fifth of a penny on the rates and in ten years the whole of the loan would be paid off. Councillor DICKENSON : We shall want a new organ, then. The MAYOR, while disclaiming any desire to appear unpatriotic, maintained that we could not hold a candle to continental nations in musical matters. We could not produce a Beethoven or a Mozart. Alderman TINN lON What about Crosfield's band ? (Leughter). The MAYOR said Councillor Archer had contended that Warrington was not a music-hiving town. Well, they wanted to make it one. It was a pioneer in other respects and he did not see why Warrington should hold back because Leeds and Sheffield had not done their duty. His aim was to improve the poor classes and he believed the provision of the organ would be a step in that direction.

r, Councillor ROBERTS said the remarkable and highly intellectual discourse to which they had just listened furnished him with more than one argument in favour of the motion. The MAYOR: I should think so. Councillor ROBERTS said the very fact that the children were being taught to appreciate music was in itself a strong reason why the municipality should take a lead in providing adequate facilities for the hearing of good music. The argument that there would not be any monetary return for the expenditure might be applied to a considerable number of provisions which the Corporation bad under- taken. In that sense the parks, the bowling greens and the baths did not pay, but for the purposes of health, recreation, physical and material comfort and enjoyment such facilities afforded a handsome return. Having provided for material and physical require- ments—not by any means adequately yes, but still in advance of some municipalities—the time had arrived Alen they should provide something for the higher and more intellectual enjoyment of the people. Having argued that the organ would minister to the 'enjoyment of a very large section of the community who were at present unprovided for, .Councillor Roberts said a great deal hcl been said about the Musical Society
The Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913.
Preferment for a Former Warrington Curate

The Rev D R James, for four years curate of St Peter's Warrington, has been offered and has accepted the living of St Matthew's, Upton, which is in the gift of the Simeon Trustees. Mr James was ordained in 1001 by the Bishop of Liverpool to the curacy of St Peter's Warrington. In 1900 he accepted the curacy of the Parish Church, Wellington. In 190 S the Rector of Brierley Hill appointed him to the sole charge of the work at Delph, where he. did some excellent work and was instrumental in raising over £250 for the new church fund.

div.head: READY TO DROP FOOD TAX. MR RIGBY SWIFT, M.P., RECOGNISES A DANGER.
div.p: READY TO DROP FOOD TAX. MR RIGBY SWIFT, M.P., RECOGNISES A DANGER.

Mr Rigby Swift, M.P., addressed a meeting of Con- servative workers at the Working Men's Club, Parr, St Helens on Saturday night. He said Tariff " Reform " had been much talked about recently, and he was as much a Tariff "Reformer" as ever he had been. He recognised the great danger there was from the" dear food "cry, but he did not believe that Tariff" Reform "would increase the cost of food. The dear food cry defeated the Conservative party in St Helens in January, 1910, but in December 1910, the Conservatives fought that cry and defeated it. He was willing, however, that the question of the taxation of food should be put aside for the present and be dropped until the Conservative party had had five y.ars of the government of the country. At the end of that period the people should be asked to decide whether or no they would take the further step in the policy of the Conservative party.

div.head: WE PUT NO DROPS OR DRUGS IN THE EYES
div.p: WE PUT NO DROPS OR DRUGS IN THE EYES
St. Barnabas' Church.

At St. Barnabss' Church on Sunday afternoon a beautiful font ewer was dedicated by the Vicar (Rev J M J Hollingworth).The font ewer, which is entirely of brass and stands on a carved fumed oak base, has been presented to the church by the young men's Bible class. Around the bowl are the words," One Lord, one Faith, one Baptism." It is a pleasing addition to the church and has been greatly admired by the worshippers. The Vicar, in his address, alluded to the goo 4 work done by the Bible class and thanked the members for the gift. It is the intention of the class to complete the furniture of the font entirely, and in a few weeks time an oak canopy will be placed in position at,, a cost of £lB, as a united gift from the young mans Bible class and Sunday school children.

div.head: St. Paul's Church.
div.p: St. Paul's Church.

A sum of £2OO Is 41•3 was realised at the 35th annual sale of work in connection with St. Paul's Church which toolyplace in the Assembly Rooms, Winmarleigh- street, on Tuesday afternoon. The profits will be utilised to augment the curates' fund and various parochial organizations. Mrs Parr performed the open- ing ceremony and the Vicar (the Rev W Bracecamp), who presided, made a special appeal on behalf of the curates' fund. He said that unfortunately, societie which made grants for aid in that way penalized St. Paul's, because they were so successful. It was said that they could afford to pay their own clergy,and,therefore the grants were given to poorer churches. That was not quite fair, because if St. Paul's received a grant they would perhaps he able to do a great deal more than they were now doing.—Mrs Parr, in opening the sale, said that every penny colleoted or raised was required and well spent. She was thanked for her services on the proposition of Mr J H Smethurst, seconded by the Rev E E Peters.

div.head: Christ Church, Latchford.
div.p: Christ Church, Latchford.

The Easter vestry meeting was held in the school Wash-lane, on Saturday evening, the Vicar (the Rev G C Briggs) presiding over a good attendance. Mr Banks (vicar's warden) presented the accounts, which showed a total income of £337 lla Bd, and an expenditure of £344 3s 11d, the deficit on the year's working being £6 12s 3d. The Vicar nomi- nated Mr Banks to act as his warden. —Mr James Lowe was re-elected people's warden. Mr Rinks nominated Mr George Venn as vicar's sidesman, Mr Lowe nominating Mr J W C Taylor as people's sidesman. The following were also elected to serve as side3men : Messrs J P Booth, John Feirclough, R T Fairclough, W Limb, A Lowe, H Lowe, H Mockett, F Short, E H Turton and T Whyman. Messrs D Banks and J Lowe were elected to serve as lay representatives. —The Chairman said the total number of communicants during the year was considerably in excess of that of the previous year. Mr Screeton, who was the Vicar of Christ Church for a number of years, had eiven a window depicting St. Hilda, as a memorial of his work at Latchford from 1897 to 1903. A new window was also to be inserted, by public subscription, as a memorial of the late Miss Jane Atkinson, for many years a devoted worker in the parish. He ,(the Chairman) was, of opinion that the time was approach- ing when it would be advisable to form a Finance Committee to manage the various parochial funds; the less the clergy had to do with money matters the better; the more they could interest the laity in these things the better. He brought the question before them in view of the fact that in every diocese it had been decided to make each parish responsible for raising a certain sum of money to support the various funds of the diocese. The vestry resolved that the Vicar call a meeting at an early date to consider the matter.

div.head: Rev. A. J. Bratt's Farewell. The Church and the Masses.
div.p: Rev. A. J. Bratt's Farewell. The Church and the Masses.

The Rev A J Bratt bade farewell to the congrega- tion of the Warrington Parish Church, on Sunday even- ing, prior to taking up his new duties as organising secretary of the Church of England Waifs and Strays Society in the dioceses of Newcastle, Carlisle and Durham. The warm place which the rev gentleman has gained in the affections of the people among whom he has laboured was evidenced by the crowded congrega- tion. The Mr Brett preached a characteristically outspoken sermon from the words: " Say not ye there are yet four months and then cometh harvest. Behold I say unto you, lift up your eyes and look on the fields, for they are white already to harvest." Having deprecated an attitude of sham cheerfulness in taking stock of affairs in the religious world, he said thby could congratulate themselves on the fact that the blatant Atheism which used to trumpet itself in their so-called halls of science was now dead—dead as mutton—but it was even sadder and more heartbreaking to find such inert and stolid indifferentism on every hand. He knew that the toiling multitudes had turned from the Church of Jesus Christ, and many had found what they thought was a better Gospel—although, of course, they were mistaken—in the Labour clubs and at Socialistic meetings, but to him it was encouraging to find some aspiration, some moral enthusiasm, some high ideals whicn might, after all, lead them some day into the Kingdom of Heaven, where alone their wants could be satisfied. At the other end of the social scale there was just as much indifference among the lapsed classes, but. what was sadder was that there was no idealism, no aspiration, na moral enthusiasm to be 'found in that section of society which confined itself almost exclusively to pleasure and luxury, which spent its Sundays in playing bridge, golfing, motoring and giving dinner parties. The problem of the lapsed classes was much more difficult for the Christian Church than the problem of the lapsed masses. Alluding to the more encouraging side of the picture, Mr Brett referred to the change of the scientific mind with regard to religion and pointed out that to-day instead of science being an enemy and antagonistic to Christianity, it was its friend and ally. An evidence of the hungering and hankering after the spiritual was also to be found in movements which, while they could not be a designated Christian, such as theosophy and Christian science,were urging upon people the necessity for something higher than the purely material view of life. Then there was also what he would call, for want of a better term, thesocial movement. We were living in monentous times. Some of the most acute minds were of opinion that we were on the eve of enormous developments in the'eocial world. The air was in fact full of social reform, and there were signs which told us plainly that the working classes were not satisfied with their position. He was not dealing with men whose schemes were purely Utopian, and who never took into account the facts of human nature, but with those who felt that there was much injustice in the world, much that could be remedied, much that dis- figured human life and prevented their working men living the life that God intended them to live, much that ought to he saept away for ever. That was a sure indication that people were groping after some- thing, after a fuller life and hoped one day to see the inauguration of the Kingdom of equity, peace and joy. Jesus Christ alone could satisfy the needs of men.

No, the Gospel bad not failed. the great truths upon which their religion rested would never fail, and in Christ and in Christ alone men could be satisfied in connection with the craving and thirsting of their immortal souls.

div.head: PRESENTAFION FROM THE BIBLE CLASS.
div.p: PRESENTAFION FROM THE BIBLE CLASS.

The members of the Parish Church Men's Bible Class held a social gathering at the King's Cafe, on Saturday, when a presentation was made to the Rev A J Bratt. The Chairm n (Mr Joseph Hill) referred to the forth- coming departure of Mr Brett and said it wonld be a great loss to the class. They wished him success in his new undertaking. Mr W Hopkins. in making the presentation, referred to Mr Bratt's excellent work in connection with the class and hoped be would accept the present as a mark of affection and appreciation of all he had done for the members. Mr 'filling and Mr Webster also spoke. Mr Bratt, in accepting the presents, thanked the members and said they would always remind him of the very happy days he had spent whilst with the class. The presents were table silver, a framed photograph of the class, and a barometer. Songs were rendered by Messrs Draper, Walker Moon and W J Hopkins, Mr F M Darby, Mus. Bac., being the accompanist.

div.head: COMBINATION.
div.p: THE COMBINATION.

WA RRIYGTON "A " v SWINTON "A."—Played at Warrington on Saturday, before a small crowd. More interest was taken in the telegrams from Salford than in the match itself, which was rather s. tame affair. The home side played with dash at the start, and pressing home the advantage, it was not long before Douglas completed a good movement by scoring in a good position. Gibbs missed the goal shot. The visitors failed to escape their quarters, and Warrington had several good chances, but they lacked finish near the line,Davis being forced into touch twice 4in quick succession. Bardsley had hard luck, losing possession after a good run, a yard from the line. At half-time Warrington led by three points to nil. In the second stage tha Warrington team again proved themselves to be the better lot. The play,how- ever, was generally of a scrappy description, and only one try accrued, Blundell scoring, the point being con- verted. Warrington won by one goal two tries (eight points) to nil.

NORTHERN UNION CUP,
THE THIRD ROUND AT SALFORD.
WARRINGTON'S TRIUMPH OVER THE REDS

The doughty "wire-pullers" again demonstrated their prowess in Cup-tie warfare when they knocked Salford out of the competition at Weaste.Theie was any amount of confidence among the supporters of the Warrington club and between 3,000 and 4,000 made the journey to Manchester in high spirits. The day was beautifully fine, and it was only in the later stages of the game that rain fell. A good deal of interest was manifested in the tie at Manchester, and the crowd of 11,000 must have rejoiced the hearts of the treasurers of both clubs. The ground was in capital order, and with both teams well represented a fine contest was assured. Warrington turned out as selected, but Salford had to make a change at the last minute. Thomas, the skipper was unable to play, and his place at centre was taken by Mesley, while Goldsmith went on the wing, and Currie in the forwards. The teams and officials were :

Warrington—Jolley, full-back; Brookes, Tranter, Renwick and Bradshaw, threcquarter-backs ; Daintith i and Nicholas, half-backs ; G Thomas,Fearnley,Chesters, Skelhorne, R Thomas and Cox, forwards. Salford—Ltrunce, full-back ; Callender, Mesley Love- luck and Goldsmitir,threequarter-backs ; May and John, half-becks ; E Thomas, Ritchie, Rees, Pugsley, Thom and Currie, forwards. Referee, Mr F Renton, of Hunslet. Salford led the way on to the field and were received with hearty cheering. Led by the burly Evan Thomas they looked a floe body of men. Warrington's reception was equally enthusiastic, and the oup-tie rattle was easily heard above the din. Warrington won the toss and had some advantage from a fairly strong cross-wind, but there was little in it as the punting soon showed. The visitors were soon on the attack but judicious punting by Launce and John changed the scene of operations to the Warrington quarter. Only two minutes had elapsed when Warrington were penalised for obstruction near mid-field, and Mesley created a sensation among the Warrington partizans by kicking a fine goal. The Wirepullers resumed with great dash and forced the Reds to defend. Nicholas, Daintith and Tranter sent the ball along to Brooks who made a great run for the corner, but was successfully tackled by Laun&r. John tried to break away, but met with a smothering grip from Daintith, and the Warrington forwards forced play to the line again. Here Nicholas again got hold, and the ball was passed smartly to the right wing, where Bradshaw got over, but was forced over the flag. Salford were desperate to clear, and a penalty against them was successfully converted by Renwick, who made the scores level amid great cheering. Keen play followed, with Saiford somewhat in the ascendant, though the backs failed to make any headway against the strong tackling of the Warrington men. Mr Renton was very keen on infringements, and another penalty against Warrington resulted in Mesley kicking another fine goal and giving his side the lead. This reverse spurred Warrington on, and they established themselves in the home quarter. Jolley was severely tested at this stage, and three times in succession referee Renton penalised the home men for obstruct- ing the Warrington custodian each time he had punted. The kicks were all in nice range for goal, but Renwick missed all three in hopeless style, amid groans of dis- appointment from the Warrington crowd. The game seemed to be going Salford's way at this stage, and when Thomas missed another shot nearly in front of goal, it looked as if Warrington were shaping for defeat. They were resolute in keeping Salford sway I from the line, however, and a great chance came when Bradshaw dribbled through the home backs at a great pace. He had a clean field, but in trying to gather the bouncing ball he knocked on, and Salford again escaped luckily. Brooks made another strong run on the left, but be was short of room, and Mesley forced him in touch. Half-time came with the Reds still leading by 2 gods to I. The result was very onen when operations were resumed. Salford went off with a rare burst and John took a quick drop at goal which was only a few feet outside the posts. The little man was very energetic in trying to get his backs on the move, but Renwick and Tranter tackled in great style and it was rarely the ball reached the Salford wings. Warrington bad a lively quarter on the defence, but they gradually wore the Reds down. Still the play was well in the War- rington quarter when the sensation of the day occurred I Nicholas got the ball from a scrum near touch and using the blind side of the pack he bluffed John and May cleverly before passing to Bradshaw. , The latter was off like a flash, and in a few strides he bad cleared the home threequarter line. Launce came across and tried to push the winger in touch, but was deceived by a swerve and Bradshaw went on at a fine pace. A great race followed, but the Warrington man was always a stride in front and finally scored the only try of the game after a truly sensational effort. He was actually tackled over the line, but fell on the ball with the referee well up. Jolly this time tried for goal, but could not reach the mark. Still, the Warrington men were a gay crowd now, and proceeded to over-play the Reds in pronounced fashion. The forwards showed masterly skill in the working of the pack, and their clever work was equalled by the safe play of the hocks, Jolley, Tranter and Renwick never throwing anything away to chance. Salford made a determined rush soon after Bradshaw's success, and Evan Thomas looked very dangerous until he fell into the clutches of George Thomasland Daintith, and was absent injured for several minutes. Free kicks were the order, and from one of these Launce was sorely at fault, Warrington just failing to get up in time to take advantage of the mistake. However, a penalty assisted Salford to transfer the game to centre, but Nicholas

div.p: NEXT WEEK: THE IMPS GARDENING.

effected a great run, which took the Salford defence off their guard. Loveluck saved the situation when be tackled the half-back five yards from the line. A spell of exchange-kick- ing was witnessed, and the pace slackened some- what. Warriugton were now decidedly the smarter side and simultaneously with the Wirepullers being awarded a penalty kick, rain, which had threatened, began to fall. Daintith was called up for the kick, and a long shot just went over the bar, and Warrington were practically secure. There remained about -15 minutes for play, but during that period the Warringtonians played coolly, and Tranter and Renwick made several fine marks. Daintitb had another shot at goal, but this time the ball travelled wide of the posts, and play was afterwards located near midfield, the whistle bailing Warrington winners of a very strenuous contest. Result: Warrington, two goals one try (seven points); Salford, two goals (four points). •
MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. RYLANDS' RECS. v. WARDLEY.

Rylands strengthened their lead for the League Championship on Saturday by a big victory at Gorsey- lane. Wardley were well represented and brought a few supporters with them. Wardley winning the toss, Rylands' kicked off towards the railway end. Good play by Warren caused the •' wiremen " to attack, but Wardley defended well. Cooper intercepting a pass, raced away to Bramhall, but that player tackled well. From the ensuing scrimmage, Horrocks dribbled through the opposing backs, right to the line, Moores kicking over. From a pass by Carter Horrocks scored, Leah failing at goal. Another passing bout among the backs saw Leah serve Griffiths at the right moment, for that player to score a good try, which Morris converted. Half-time :—Rylands', eight points ; Wardley, nil. Rylands' with the wind in their favour, made the pace a cracker and good tries were scored by Carter (three), who was in splendid form, F Horrocks and J Griffiths. Bramhall converted. Wardley found the home team in one of its happy moods, as all the tries were scored from pretty passing movements. Final :—Rylands', three goals seven tries (27 points) ; Wardley, nil.

Each side tried hard to obtain the lead which eventually fell to the Bridge-street eleven, after a good shot by Dunn. The lead was not enjoyed long, however, as Cairo-strePt made several attacks on the Bridge- street goal, offside spoiling many chances of scoring, but following a free-kick taken by Pearson, for carrying by the goalkeeper, Roberts netted the ball about five minutes from time, a good and evenly-contested game ending in a draw of two goals each. div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

Latchford met F S Church's Bowdon XL last Satnr day, which included McKenzie, Cottam, Eric Church, Hardy, of the Cheshire County team, and the brothers Greenhow. A fast game resulted in a win for the visitors by 3.2. In the first half both defences were severely tested, but no score came until near the interval, when McKenzie netted with a brilliant shot. On turning round Latchford played up well, and follow- ing a nice movement en the right, Travis dashed vast Cottam into the circle,and equalized with a grand effort. This was followed shortly alter by another attack which culminated in Pearson completely beating the Bowden keeper with a clever shot. Latchford held their 2-1 lead for some time, -until McKenzie took one of Greenhow's centres up and again equalized the scores, and near the end a roll-in from the right touch found its way into the circle, and McKenzie slipped it into the net and scored the winning goal. A feature of the game was the fine display by Cottam at right back ; Hardy (centre-half) WRS very difficult to pass and he looked after Minards like a father. McKenzie of course gave a class display, his dribbling. passing, and shooting, being very good. Greenhow at outside right made several fast'runs and centres. Bruhl in the home goal hkd some warm shots to contend with but he never made a mistake and McKenzie's three goals were quite unstoppable. Billington and Fletcher, the full backs, defended strongly and gave nothing away, while the halves and forwards combined well and it would be unfair to mention any particular individual Latchford did well to run their powerful opponents to a goal and after the match were complimented by Frank Church on having played "right good hockey." Swinton Park are the visitors to Latchford to-day and the home eleven is :—J Bruhl, goal ; W Fletcher. C Billington, backs; J B Wilkinson, A E Bradshaw, A Knight, halves: R A Dale, 3 E Pearson, W H Minards, D Travis, F W Isherwood, forwards. div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
LOCAL ENTERPRISE.

Owing to Easter falling so early there is an apparent lull in " interest" so far as the cross-country men are concerned, and with the football season at quite its best stage, sports promoters are wisely reserving their prospectuses and meetings. fhe Noithern Counties Athletic Association have decided to alter last season's method in connection with their seven miles walking, and ten miles Flat Championships. Warrington Athletic Club has applied to the N.C.A.A. for permission to ho!d the ten miles chanipionship in conjunction with the snorts meeting which the local club is arranging for the Saturday before Whit-Monday, May 10th, and it goes without saying,alrnost, that local sportsmen are keen on the prospect of having such a "tit-bit," decided,before what would certainly be more than a local" gate" in their midst, and as the influx of visitors to Warrington would be beneficial to trades- people the best is being hoped for. So that schoolboys may have free competition it is understood that invitations are being issued to all the schools in the district to provide one or more teams to take part in a 300 yards relay race—teams of three, each youngster to run 100 yards; and to provide the rising generation with further opportunity of distinguishing itself and, incidentally earning suitable prizes, any or all of the competitors in the relay race may take part in a running high jump competition permission is being sought to include in what promises to be a very enter- prising programme an open competition of the same kind, so that the budding champions may see and be seen. Prepare! On Saturday next Warrington Football Club will in the pen-ultimate stage be trying to bring the Northern Union Cup out of Yorkshire. They are Lancashire's only hope, so the social and prize distribution of , the local Athletic Club has been postponed unitl April 19th,

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CExTRE).

There were not more than a dozen anglers out last week end, and those who made the journey to the Goery drew blank,with the exception of a Criester angler. There is not the least doubt that warm weather is wanted, for those who go piking generally like to have a rod in for the eels. At a committee meeting held at the Bay Horse during the week it was decided to have the Shield and medal for a separate match, as there are already four dates selected for Northern Anglers in Warrington. The committee has power in trying to select a date so as not to clash with other societies. There is certainly one way out; may we suggest a Saturday match at Norton, as many members will have all on to attend the season's programme with- out any extra contests. Members are slow in booking their names for the opening event, the rambling match, and as there is already a medal and a 10s special remised, it looks like a good thing for those who are competing.

St Mary's C.Y.M.S. Whist Drive and Dance. 4 successful whist drive and dance in connection with the above society to It place on Friday evening i last n the old Post Office Market-street. About a hundred members and friends were present, and whist .7stseinjoyed until 10 o'clock, after which dancing was " 'utliged in until 2 a.m. Daring the tnterval songs Were ably rendered by the Misses Warren and ,Call- !/311 and Messrs J Caldwell and W McHugh, Miss A chardson accompanyit g. The prize winners for the whist vvera as follows—first lady Miss E Wright, second lady Miss Costello, lady playing gent Miss M J IlrW,ittaker. First gent Mr J Collins, second gent Mr consolation Miss Knight. There were also 0 competitions the prizes being won by Miss T korney and Miss N Caldwell, Ancient Order of Hibernian& ▪ large number of members and friends of Division (Ladies' Auxiliary) assembled in the U.I.L. Hall, ,w!nwick-street, on Thursday, March 27th, the occasion "tog the first annual social and dance to celebrate the feast of St. Patrick. Upwards of 50 couples were Present and the proceedings were carried out in a most enjoyable manner, which speaks well for the 511ece65 of the Division. Mr. J. Caldwell rendered excellent music. Songs etc. given by several members ;ontributed greatly to the success of the evening. J. Ryan (Division 422) carried out the duties of ''• Bro. Crowley, County secretary, on moving a tit:ta of thanks to the artistes road .M.C., congratulated teul on being the means (I making the gathering I,oBt enjoyable. Sister Kilgallon seconded the motion '4O proceedings concluded with the singing of "A 33at1on once again." Death of a Former Local Official. A. former Warrington official passed away at Black- -1:01, on Thursday, in the person of Mr George "awling, who for thirteen years was rauitary inspector to the old Warrington Rural oitary Authority. Mr Rawling, who was 68 years Viage, was a native of Fearnbead, his father, the late r George Ravvling, being at one time a member jf the Warrington Board of Guardians.. On "'ring Warrington Mr Bawling took up a similar Position at Rawtenstall and had been sanitary inspec- tor to the corporation since the incorporation of that L°reugh twenty-three years ego. Owing to ill-health be I'ad felt compelled to relinquish the duties this year, and ie a pathetic circumstance that his resignation only look effect cn Monday last. While he lived in this Sstrict Mr ltawling was superintendent of the Padgate Nesleyan Sunday School and to the last he retained los interest in the affairs of the village. The funeral, Vlieh will take place at the Warrington Cemetery on onday at 2-30, will be preceded by a service at Bold ,street Wesleyan Church.

Mr. HAROLD SMITH, "THE MAN AS M.P.'s retirement from HE IS." the Marconi Committee has resulted--as he probably hoped—in drawing public attention to himself. It has also afforded the basis for some curious analyses of character by various writers, with Mr. SMITH as the subject matter under the microscope. According to the letter •which he wrote to the Chairman of the Committee in tendering his resignation Mr. HAROLD SMITH had a grievance. He writes : Two members have been publicly charged with having received and with- held from the committee most vital information which, had it been communi- cated to their colleagues, must have very much shortened and, I submit, have materially altered our proceedings.

We fail to see why this fact, even if based on substantial premises, should be deemed a sufficient reason for resigning from the Committee by Mr. SMITH, and we can only attribute his course of action to his individual egotism. Mr. SMITH'S fellow members have shown themselves superior to so petty a grievance, and if Mr. SMITH had waited, or had really desired reassurance, he would have learned a few days later from the lips of Mr. FALCONER that: So far as he was concerned, there was no fact of which he was aware which had not been proved before this Com- mittee, and if there had been he should have taken steps to see that the proper means were taken for the purpose of proving those facts.

The Citizen" devotes a special article by " E.A.J." to the Member for Warrington, entitled "The Man as he is—Mr. Elarold Smith, M.P.," which, coming from an independent source, will doubtless be read with interest by our readers. We quote as follows:

The dramatic retirement of the member for Warrington from the Marconi Committee will surprise nobody familiar with the ways of this bold and impetuous politican. "F.E.'s" brother, like " F.E.," loves the limelight. And he knows where to stand for 'the rays from the wings.' To get reported in the London daily papers you must, unless you are an acknowledged leader of men, say strong things. HAROLD SMITH says them. A few days ago, in a venomous outbreak, he fell foul of the HOME SECRETARY over the mobbing of militants in Hyde Park. This week, unable to get his way in the Marconi Committee- room, he, in a fit of petulance, resigned. Mr. HAROLD SMITH, like many amateurs, over- acts. That may be in consequence of his devotion to amateur theatricals. The House of Commons, the most generous as well as the most critical assembly in the world, applauds genius, but it hates anything suggestive of arrogance n young men. Mr. HAROLD SMITH is a young man of pretension more than promise, and if he could tone down his style of oratory he might become even more popular than he is now. Few began a Parliamentary career under more auspicious circumstances. Two years ago he won a notable victory at the polls for he vanquished Mr. CROsFIELD, the soap king, at Warrington. Happening to be " F.E.'s " brother. he attracted more notice than almost any other new arrival at West- minster. His irst speech was eagerly awaited, but he overdid the thing, putting on the colours with a big brush, and spoiling the ' picture in consequence. In appearance he is not unlike his more distinguished brother. Both are dark-complexioned, clean-shaven, smooth-groomed, dapper figures, but in intellect they differ. " F.E." commands a ready flow ,of polished phrasing and biting repartee. HAROLD'S speeches emit the odour of the midnight !lamp. They are not from the life, but from the model."

Neither our Town Coun- THE TOWN COUNCIL. cil nor its members are showing any signs of reformation which suggest an early qualifi- cation for the good conduct badge. The monthly meeting this week nearly established a record in lasting from six o'clock to ten ' o'clock and it has certainly never bee excelled as an illustration of how not to con- duct public business. "Points of order," disputed rulings, and personal squabbles were continuous, and it says much for the ' Mayor's patience and physical well-being that he could sit through the whole proceed- ings and preserve mhat semblance of order there was left. Of course there was a funny side to the proceedings, which was not lost upon a crowded gathering of the ratepayers at the back of the Chamber and our cartoonist, ever with an eye to humorous pictorial presentment has drawn a Town Council cartoon which may, or may not have special application to Warrington. Out of the wild welter of things one or two concrete items did eventually emerge. The rates were fixed 9,.t the same figure as last year, Bs. and the purchase of a £1,500 organ for Parr Hall, and a £l,OOO motor fire engine were finally carried by substantial majorities

The Mayor is to be PARR HALL congratulated upon ORGAN. having brought the Town Council to such a reasonable frame of mind as to pass his resolution in favour of the puraase of a new organ for the Parr Hall. The decision will commend itself to all who are keenly desirous of encouraging musical culture in the town,

for everybody admits that the present patched-up instrument,which has got beyond effective repair, is nothing{ short of a disgrace to a community with any musical pretensions. We are informed by one who has made a special study of organ-building that the sum specified in the Mayor's resolu- tion—.£l,soo—will be ample to provide an organ much superior in the range of its equipment to any instrument already installed in the town or neighbourhood. It will presumably have three manuals and at least forty speaking stops. Such an organ, 'scaled and voiced on modern principles and having the advantage of the weight of metal now used in the construction of the pipes, will far exceed the old instrument in power—to say nothing of the quality of tone. Discussion on the organ question nowadays seems inevitably to lead to criticism of the Musical Society—why it is difficult to imagine. Although by the very nature of the task which it has set itself the society may not always capture the popular taste in the class of its entertainments, there can be no doubt that Warrington is indebted to it or painstaking pioneer work which has borne fruit in a higher standard of church and chapel mnsic and in the successful development of numerous local musical enterprises.

div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Fire-brigade matters at Stockton Heath are being slowly but surely put in order. This week two firemen were paid for services rendered at a fire in June 1911. Interest on the money to date is still owing! * *

The ?purchase of a. motor fire-engine has been agreed to, notwithstanding a sharply- divided opinion in the Town Council as to the necessity for such an expensive appliance. Anyhow, the Fire Brigade wants bringing up-to-date, though it is a century or two ahead of Stockton Heath.

Penny baths for workingmen are to be provided by the Warrington Corporation in the future.. But no provision has been made for working women. In view of the present state of unrest among the female sex, and their sensitiveness to slights, this seems unwise. Indignant womanhood may possibly avenge itself by blowing the men and their penny baths sky-high simultaneously. * After Mr. Kebty-Fletcher's rude personal attack on Mr. Lloyd George in the House of Commons on Tuesday it is refreshing to hear that there is little likelihood of the Member for Altrincham being the Conserva- tive candidate for the division at the next election. He is understood to have exhausted the patience of both his party and his friends ! * * One of those curious examples of jealousy between Corporation Committees came to light on Tuesday. The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee had accepted a tender for the lighting of the new footpath across Victoria Park by the Electricity Committee for £43, when the Gas Committee came forward with an offer to light the path by gas for £2B. There is perpetual war between the rival illuminants, and apparently between tip committees. On an amendment, the cheaper estimate for gas-lighting was carried.

* * Councillor Broadhurst appears to be wearing a hat several sizes to small for a cranium of such mental equipment. He is continually bobbing up at Council meetings and airing views which are of little value in a voice which soon becomes wearisome. On Tuesday he evolved a style of humour which consisted in the main of calling another Councillor an infamous liar and then making a mock withdrawal. If the fire- hose is not turned on this kind of oratory we shall be having ink-bottles flying about the Council Chamber. Ordinary methods of suppression are not sufficient in the case of members of the Broadhurst type. *

Councillor Lashford made out a very poor case against the Health Committee on Tuesday and at the close of his indictment it was quite a matter of opinion whether there was anything for the Committee to answer. The Councillor's grievance centred round the purchase of blankets so far back as 1909, but what he specifically found wrong was lost in a maze of words. Alderman James Evans, as Chairman of the Committee, took the matter very seriously, but we really think he would be justified, and perhaps well-advised in letting the matter rest where it is. Nobody believes that he and the medical officer either "feathered their own nests " with new blankets or gave preference to any particular tradesmen. If the matter appears to he smouldering,why not try a wet blanket? It would be both efficacious and appropriate. *

Mr Samuel Brighouse, the popular coroner for South-West Lancashire, is at present recuperating his health by a voyage to the Mediterranean. He is hoping that in the early summer he will be able to resume his official duties, which are at present being discharged by his deputy, Mr F A Jones Acting on medical advice, however, Mr. Brighouse has resigned for the present his municipal duties in Southport and his membership of the Ormskirk Board of Guardians He has also resigned office in connection with the Conservative party of the Southport Division, which embraces dis- tricts as near to Liverpool as Seaforth and Waterloo. * *

The paragraph published in this column last week, commenting on the analysis of the year's offertories at Warrington Parish Church, was in one respect open to miscon- ception. We stated that no record was kept of the amounts received at the early celebra- tions, whereas the actual fact is that, while all those offertories are duly accounted for, the detailed analysis of coins does not extend to them. Councillor J. G. Craik (Rector's warden) writes to point out that every collection, however small, is recorded in the churchwardens' offertory book and included in the Church accounts. In addition there is posted up, at the main entrance of the Church, each Monday a statement of the whole of the offertories taken during the previous week. * *

drofessor Dixon, who unveiled the Priestley statue on Wednesday, is one of the most genial of scientific men, and he quite delighted the assembly at the Town Hall by flow of amusing reminiscences. Dis- coursing on the days when he was a divinity student, he quoted a never-to- be-forgotten examination in which he was asked to state who was the father of John the Baptist. " I thought a long time "said the professor" and then replied "‘ I rather think it was Hezekiah." The next poser related to Ezekiel, but the pro- fessor sought to evade the remark "I ha ve given you some facts of his life in my paper.' "Can you tell me any more facts ? " asked the examiner. "No I'm afraid I know nothing fresh about him" was the reply. No wonder that the budding theologian decided to transfer his affections to science!
