Mr. Steel : 1 on were in a,collery district What you were talking about. think I know what I am talking

about, and r think the magistrates know. also. Continuing, Mr. Steeli said that "educational" club passed a, resolution .discontinuing the taking of such papers as the "Evening Chronicle" and "Daily Post" and substituted "Chips?' and "Comic- Cuts." The committee allowed "nap," so long as it did ndt exceed "halfpenny nap," but stopped "tip-it" and cork games. The mem- bers of the committee received sixpence and two drinks for their attendance. They evidently in- tended that members of the committee should not be dry. (Laughter.) Another minute read : "Resolved that each \member have half a pint of beer, but if abstainers wish for drinks, please bider them." .
Councillor U. Roberts (a magistrate) : "What is ,that for?
Mr. Steel :It does not say. It was at a meet- ing on November 28th. Mr. Knowles : It was not a general .meeting.

Mr. Steel :It was a commit 4tee meeting. They did not vote drinks to themselves alone, but to every member of the club. A resolution showing how solicitious they were with regard to ,having sufficient drink on the premises read: "Resolved that David Davies (the secretary) looks into the whisky coming, in case it does not come before to-morrow." They appeared.to have had one con- cert in the club during their existence, for he found that it was resolved "That Henry. VIII. should have 2s. for his servcies at the concert." "I thought," added Mr. Steel ,"that Henry VIII. was dead, but they seem to have revived him in Collins Green." (Laughter.) Continuing, he said he thought he might safely say that the duties of the whole of that committee were to man- age a drinking club. The members' register was very- badly. kept, as they had the greatest diffi- culty in finding out what Members had paid and who had not. He had gone through the cash book and he found that in 1912 .R 8 9s. was re- ceived in subscriptions. By reckoning that at 4s. per year per member, they would only have 43 members, and they had reported a Membership of 140 to the justices. In spite of the resolution that no more than is. "strap" be allowed, it was found that one man had a whole page to himself and that "strar customers were not only mem- bers, but visitors to the club. They found an- other book which he would call the "brewery book." From that book it would be seen th'at they did not only get their intoxicating liquors from the brewery, but that the

div.head: __Abft•ft.
div.p: __Abft•ft.
BREWERY WERE FINANCING THE CLUB,

because in that book was an entry for a loan from the Brewery Co. of £4O, which was added to the brewery bill. The book was \made out by the brewery, 'and the loan appeared to be in 1911: Nothing was, found by the police to show the present Indebtedness to the brewer". Duritg the year 1912 the club paid £229 Os. 3d. The balance sheet for the year ending July, 1912, showed income £542 2s. .7d., and total expendi- ture £.526 7s. 4d., leaving a balance of ..t.15 15s. 3d. A sum of £484 19s. 9d. had been received for refreshments, members' subscriptions amount- ed to -X,14 10s. Od., and billiards 1.75 • 9s. 10d. As against that income the principal items of expenditure were for intoxicants, and, with the exception of three barrels, the money all went to the Brewery Co. Another balance sheet stated that a deficit waS due, partly to allowing two- penny pints on Sunday nights and. strap." In the minute book there were several resolutions with regard to Sunday, closing. One was to the effect that Mr. Tyrer and the secretary be ,dele- gates to Mr. Forshaw (the managing director of the brewery) re compensation for Sunday clos- ing. It_appeared to him (Mr. Steel), that Mr. Forshaw had, a controlling influence over the club or else there would have been no need to see him at all. The presumption was that the club was a drinking club and that it was car- ried on for the benefit of the turtonwood Brew- ery Company. There was over owing to the brewery and how could they possibly hope to get the money from ,these working-men? The club had never been separately assessed, and the money from the club went to the brewery after expenses had been paid. Men resorted to the club for the purpose of obtaining drink and for no other reason: There was most frequent drunkenness. They had five conVictions against men for drunkenness from the club and if there had 'been so many against licensed premises, the best house in the country could not have withstood an objection to its license. He submitted that. the club ought to be struck off the register. He was told the club was situated ,between two collieries and was a nice calling place for the colliers. The case was a bad one -and the police hoped the bench would have no . hesitation in ridding the country place of that drinking den and strike its name off the register. The court then adjourned for lunch. PC. 's Georgson and Baker, and Sergeant- Smith bore out Mr. Steel's statement as to having the club under observation and seizing the books. _ .

P.-C.s Mouldin- and Houghton, and Inspector Bannister were also called, and Mr. Steel in ex- amining the inspector as to the incident of the secretary refusing to send the keys, asked : "Was representation made to yoir regarding the condi- tion of the secretary?" Witness : Yes.

Mr. Knowles objected to the man being so questioned. He was in his own house and Mr. Steel had no right to put such a question. The secretary, had been out electioneering and was not on club business. kThe magistrates ruled that Mr. Steel was not to put the question. Mr. Steel was also not al- lowed to recall P.-C. Baker to speak as to the secretary's condition. Mr. Thomas Porter Bradshaw, assistant clerk to the justices, gave evidence as to the registra- tion of the club and the thanges in its title. For the defence David Davies, the secretary, produced a'. great deal of correspondence from Labour men, including- a letter from Mr. J. A. Seddon, the object being to prove that the club was,carried on for the purpose-of a Labour club. Several members of the Club spoke to its being Conducted on proper lines, and denied that there was drunkenness in the place. . Mr. Knowles said that with the exception of the five convictions which had been specially mentioned, there could be nothing alleged apinst the men which would show their condition to be worse than that of people leaving ordinary public houses. The club; was, well condpcted, and—was carried on as, a bonafide labour club. They in- tended to have an enquiry with a view to seeing what had actually happened. The management would be 'placed on a.stricter basis, and the secre- tary untlertook to see that the books of the club' were kept regularly in order. The magistrates found that some Of the charges had been proved, and decided to strike the club off the register. They also 'ordered that the pre- mises should not be used for a club ,for twelve months. The defendants were ordered to pay the advocate's fee and costs of the court, amount- in.. to A:8 'BB. 'The hearing of the case lasted from 11 a.m. until after 8 p.m.

div.head: GUARDIANS' ELECTIONS.
div.p: GUARDIANS' ELECTIONS.

Interest in the elections of Guardians of the Warrington Union which take place on Monday next, is apparently 1)40w zero as far as the two contests in Warrington are con-, cerned. In Orford Ward there is a three-cornered flight between Mr James A Rushworth. licensed 'victualler, the retiring representative, Mr F McKinley, insurance superintendent, end Mr Edward Horrocks. who is actively identified with Labour propaganda, In Howley Ward Mr George Allen, the present member, is opposed by Mrs Mary Roberts. Polling will take place at the following places : Orford Ward, Silver-street Schools; Howley Ward, National Schools, Charch•street. The votes will be counted in the Board room at the Workhouse and the results declared the same day.

div.head: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

Contests for the combined offices of Rural Distric Councillor and Guardian will take place at Penketh and Burtonwocid.on Monday next and tilt) results will be announced in the respective villages. At Penketh, Mr P C Garnett and Mr G Faulkner (chairman of the local brauch of the Labour Party), are the candidates and a considerable amount of interest centres in the election. _ _

At Burtonwood the Vicar (Rev A M Mitchell), who during his term of nffice has unquestionably taken a very keen interest in the work of both authorities and has done useful public service, has an opponent in he pars in of Mr William Fairclough, farmer.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913.
PRIESTLEY 'MEMORIAL
WHY SHOULD NOT WARRINGTON
HAVE MORE STATUES?
Councillor Roberts and Armchair
Critics.

In the'days when Warrington was known as "the Athens of England," one of the most eminent of the circle of learned men attracted to to the town by the Old Academy was Dr Joseph Priestley, the famous scientist and philosopher, whose discovery of oxygen revolutionised chemistry. It was in 1761 that Dr Priestley came to Warrington and during the six years.he remained here he wrote his " History of the present state state of electricity" and other works,and was made a Fellow of the Royal Society. Although Dr Priestley undoubtedly brought lustre to our town, we have until this week lacked a memorial to that great man. It is peculiarly fitting that the omission should at length have been repaired by the members of the Warrington Society who, on the initiative of. Alderman Bennett, subset ibed to secure a statue which the has been placed in tlie entrance hall of the Technical Institute. The. Old Academy, of which the Warrington Society is the custodian, was the scene of Priestley' s labours, and some relics of the scientist have already found a home in that historic building. The memorial which was unveiled on Wedne.day evening by Professor Harold B Dixon, M.A., F.R , of Manchester University, is the original plaster model of the bronze statue recently erected at Birstall, near Leeds. It is the work of Miss Frances Darlington, of Harrogate, and shows Priestley in the act of making the experiment which led to the discovery of oxygen. The statue is mounted on an oak pedestat supplied by Messrs Arthur Greenhalgh & Co.
Photo Burrell, THE STATUE (5F DR. PRIESTLEY

Councillor HENRY ROBERTS (chairman of the Educa- tion Committee) presided at the unveiling ceremony which was attended by a large and representative• gathering. He said the results of chemical research, as applied not only to manufacting purposes but in other equally important directions, had been simply marvellous. Professor Dijon had for many yearsr devoted himself, with no little success, to the mitiga- tion of the awful suffering and loss of life that followed explosions in collieries and it was therefore peculiarly appropriate that he should have honoured them with his presence on that interesting occasion. (Applause.) Professor Dlxox, in performing the ceremony, said he had the greatest admiration for tbe work of Dr Priestley and it therefore gave him the greatest pleasure to unveil the statue.
The curtains veiling the memorial were then drawn aside.

Prof. DIXON said the statue was notable in that it presented a correct record of one Priestley's greatest experiments. Priestley was a many-sided man and, to illustrate I hat, he could not do better than quote the, words of Frederic Harrison "if •we choose one man as a type of the intellectual energy of the 18th century we could hardly find a better than Joseph Priestley. . . . His versatility, eagerness, activity and humanity; the immense ranee of his cariosity In all thiugs, physical, moral or social ; his place in science, in theology,in philosophy and in politics; his pr.:Mier relation to the Revolution and the pathetic story of his unmerited sufferings may make him the hero of the 18th century." Continuinz, the Professor laid stress on the immense range of Priestley's curiotay. He was always intent on finding out facts, though perhaps not so good at drawing conclusions.. He himself said : "1 think my facts are all right. Let others draw the con- clusions." The Professor then touched at some length upon Priestley's experiments and quoted interesting extracts from his diary to show how dear to his heart his life work was. His discovery of oxygen gave us the secret of our atmosphere—that there were really two gases in it and that oxygen was concerned in com- bustion and respiration. Before his time, no-one had understood that. The Mayor proposed a vote of thanks to Pro- fessor Dixon. He characterised Dr. Priestley as the founder of modern chemistry, and said that, without him, that science would have been like Hamlet without the Prince of Denmark. Priest- ley's statements as to the uses of oxygen had proved prophetic, for they all knew its value in medical science. (Applause.) Alderman Bennett seconded, and having re- ferred to the intimate associations between Man- chester and Warrington in the sphere of learning, expressed the hope that they would be further cemented by that gathering. (Aytplause.) - In acknowledging the votd, Professor Dixon said he went down to the Old Academy that after- noon to see if he could observe salmen leaping in the Mersey, as a poet whom he found in War- rington led him to believe they once did. (Laugh- ter.) Living poets were not always recognised by their fellow-toNtinsmen, but he was glad to think Alderman Bennett was. (Applause.) The

prdessor aroused much interest J his remark that it was almost by a fluke or chance that the Manchester University was not started in War- rington. The first independent, free thinking academy (in the ,true and genuine sense) was es- tablished in Warrington, and people could hold their own views and express. them without being turned out of the 'town. It was just such a place of learning -as John Owens afterwarils founded in Manchester, and it was qiute on the cards that if the Old Academy had grown to be a university it would have served as a centre of learning for Manchester and Liverpool. ( Ap- plause.) DINNER AT THE TOWN HALL. .

After the ceremony Councillor H:' Roberts entertained a large company o( members of the Education Committee and other prominent towns- men at 4inner at the Town Hall. The function was a great success. the leading place being given to the musical and convivial• sides, while the -speech-making. was limited to a very short toast list. The. loyal toasts were proposed in felicitous terms by the Chairman and enthusiastically hon- oured. The Mayor proposed "The memory of Dr. Joseph Priestley," arid touched upon the great man's intimate associations with Warrington. It was here that he performed,' the most momentous act of his life, for he was married in Warrington. His first child—a daughter—was also born here. They had every ground for .rlaiming,Priestley as a Warrinttotiian, although Warrington was not his native plaee; but the fame of such a man belonged not simply to came town or country, but

to the civilized world. Two notable characteristics of Priestley which impressed one on reading his memoirs were his originality and his versatility. When he was making his experiments upon air he wrote that he knew very little, if anything, of cheinistry—in fact, he had only attended one' course of lectures by Turner, of Liverpool, at that time. He added that thq.t was probably to his advantage, because he had no pre-conceived ideas with regard to the experiments or the apparatus he used. Chemistry was probably the most im- portant of sciences, for it bore upon everything, I including the functions of life, in regard to health and disease, and many branches of manufacture.. "It even enters," added his worship, "into

MUNICIPAL AND POLITICAL LIFE. At all events we had explosions there—(laughter), —and I know upon a. recent occasion there was such a thing as the manufacture of carbonic acid gas—(laughter),—because the blood circulating through my brain was so highly charged after a four hours' sitting of the Council that I almost thvglit I was intoxicated. (Laughter.) I am glad to say I don't know what real intoxication means, but I imagine it must he something like the effects I experienced after a four hours' sitting in a municipal atmpsphere." (Laughter.) In conclusion, his worship said that science, especi- ally. as .it 'existed in Priestley's time, Ivas above; art, for the reason that, in the first instance, it was purely intellectual and afforded no enjoyment in the accepted sense of the term. Men of science were therefore all the more worthy of admiration and encouragement. (Applause.) ' The toast was honoured in silence.

Professor Dixon, in responding, said he rinist find fault with the Mayor's remark that men of science and chemistry had no real enjoyment in their discoveries.. That was absolutely false. They had only to read Priestley' s own account .of what he did to see the intense delight with which he turned from all sorts of other work to his scientific experiments. The man's life seemed to glow when he canle into. his laboratory, and there he got his real enjoyment. Following the humorous vein of the Mayor's remarks, with re- gard to the heated atmosphere at, Council meet- ings, the professor reminded the meeting that the chief property which Priestley discovered, in his great experiment was not how to let out carbonic acid gas, but how to bottle it up for the right occasion. (Laughter.) Priestley was also the first to see how an explosion of hydrogen and oxYgen produced hot water—(laughter),—from, which they might draw another analogy. (Laugh- ter.) That experiment, however; represented the turning point in modern chemistry, and we owed it to what Priestley called a random observation or

div.head: LUCKY SHOT.
div.p: LUCKY SHOT.

It must, however, be remembered that those lucky shots only came to those -who were prepared to see what they might. The professor then gave Sol4e very happy and amusing 'personal reminis- centes, touching upon his college days when, as a result of an examination in divinity, he trans- ferred his special attention from theology to chemistry, and also referred to his visit to America---two points in which he enjoyed some kinship with Priestley. In conclusion, the pro lessor said : If Priestley could revisit the town of his youth and see that the Old Academy, where he first taught, had been saved from the des- truction which threatened it and preserved for its present purpose, if he could see .all those relics treasured and handled With such loving kindness, he wiluhl feel proud of having.been a Warring- tonian. He would feel honoured by such a meet- ing as we have had to-day, by the placing of his statue where it now stands, and bY the know- ledge that you are all proud of him. I feel sure he would have been proud of you for having kent his memory .so green. We may say of Priestley that he was one whom we can delight to honour as a man._ He sought the truth in every relation of life, and ensued it. (Applause.) . Councillor Jenkins proposed the health of "The ' donors of the Priestley statue." He 'said that in his most recent poem Alderman Bennett had spoken of "The light in God's high halls of bright- ness stored," and they knew it was his dearest wish that that light might be, shed, with ever greater power, among his fellowmen. (Applause.) Alderman Bennett, in responding detailed the steps which led to the purchase of the statue. Although Warrington now had a Priestley memorial, he continued, he frankly confessed that he Was not satisfied. Such a great man was worthy of better commemoration in the form of a bronze or marble statue, especially when One reflected that Birstall, a little town of . under lo,opo inhabitants, had raised .tl,OOO to erect the , noble monument which now stood in its market place. There was a marble statue of Priestley in Oxford, a bronze one in Birmingham, and another in Leeds. Surely Warrington ought .not to be behind those places. (Hear, hear.) The alder- man went On to suggest that the tciwn was failing in its duty if it did not raise memorials to other illustrious people who had been, identified with the town and specially mentioned the names of Mrs. Barbauld, one of the finest poetesses Eng- land had produced; John Howard, the prison reformer; Lord Winmarleigh, one of the truest and noblest English gentlemen who ever lived; and William Beamont, the first Mayor of War- rington, to whom we owed practically all our knowledge of the inspiring history of our town. There was a

div.head: LAMENTABLE DEARTH OF STATUES
div.p: LAMENTABLE DEARTH OF STATUES

and.public adornments in the streets of Warring- ton,', but until municipal authorities were suf- ficiently enlightened and public-spirited to realise, that it was part of their duty to bring our towns into line with the continental citi& in that respect, we would have to rely, upon private gener- osity- to remedy the deficiency. Statues, he believed, tended to imbue us with noble idealism and tto make us better citizens and better men. ;Having pointed to the example of Bavaria' in this diredtion, Alderman Bennett applied the idea locally, in the, words: Imagine a towering statue of Warrington by some great sculptor, standing, say, at Market Gate, representing all the idea% of the towir, its ancient traditions, its. present gr,patness and future hopes. Grouped around it would, be statues of some of the great men of whom I have been speaking, or they. might be arranged near Warrington Bridge, where I hope sufficient space will be left for that purpose, or in the Queen's Gardens. I don't care where you have your Glory Hall or Valhalla, but the..prin- ciple af honouring great men is a noble one; and the other ideal of adorning our industrial cities .with statues, 'fountains, and beautiful works of art is equally commendable. Is it too much to hope that our rich men will rise to their responsi- bilities and that Warrington will: achieve the dis- tinction of being not only "the town of many indukries," but a town in which art is -still loved, literature still venerated, and the high traditions of the past held in high regard and profound esteem. (Applause.) , Mr. John Upson, in .proposing the health of ' "The host," said it was his privilege last week .to listen to the Lord- Chancellor as he strove to lift the education question out of the

div.head: DUST AND TURMOIL
div.p: DUST AND TURMOIL

of Party politics and sectarian wrangli?g. As he listened he thought that in 'Warrington, at any, rate, they had tried to carry/ out the spirit of that high idealism in .the work of their education authority. ' (Applause.) They ' had left ,their political and religious differences in the ante-room, and in transacting, the business of the Education Committee they had acted only as educationists. He was one of those who 'believed that, the func- tions of education, authorities were in . the em- bryo, the first stages of, evolutionary growth, and that as time went on not only, would the interests of the young in the schools, but of the adolescents be committed to an increasing extent to the care of such authorities. Alluding to the work of Councillor Roberts, Mr. Upson said he had not escaped 'criticism, but the man who took a fore- most place in social work and educational reform must pay the ,price, in the . shape of ill-informed and sometimes malicious criticism. Councillor Roberts, had, however, a higher reward in the in- ward knowledge that his labours had not been in vain, but that he had done much to open wider ! the doors of knowledge, to dissipate the clouds ! of darknfss and, to provide fuller and richer,op- portunities of life for his fellow-townsmen. (Ap- plause.) Councillor Roberts, who was received with the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow," char- acterised the cause of education as the most im- portant puha work that anyone could engage in. Those who belonged in their origin, at any 'rate, —atid who were not ashamed to admit it—to
what were supposed to be the lower orders of society, could appreciate better than most men the almost insurmountable difficulties which faced

the children of the poor in their efforts to fight the battle of life. (Hear, hear.) If, with the co- operation of the Education Committee, he had been able to do anything to make the way a little easier and brighter for those whose birthright had not been to gold and silver, it would always be a priceless recollection to him, and something; to stand by, whatever else might occur. (Ap- plause.) He hoped and believed we were only at the beginning of great days in educational mat- ters. All those difficulties which had been bred of custom and privilege were rapidly on the wane. He might not live to see it, but some of those present would probably be spared until the time when every boy and girl would be able to take advantage cf whatever the nation had to give in the shape of education. The reputation of the Warrington Education Committee for honest, solid, zealous work was second to none. While they had occasionally to pay the price of attempt- ing to do that which. in their judgment, was right, he said they were entitled to claim that they were as good, if not better judges, being in daily association with their work, than those who CRITICISED THEM FROM THE DEPTHS OF THEIR

ARM CHAIM s. (Hear, hear.) If the spirit of loyal co-operation continued, he was certain that Warrirqzton would more than maintain its position as an educational centre, and that some of the glory of the past which, through an unfortunate series of circum- stances had passed by and gone to large cities, might return here for its permanent home. (Ap- plause.)

A highly: enjoyable musical programme was submitted, the opening item being a pianoforte duet, "Septet" ißeethoven), by Mrs. C. Jackson Hoboes and Mr. W. H. Paton, Mus.Bac. Mad- ame Sara Silcock sang "At my window," the " Valse Song" from" Tom Jones, " and " Forget me not," in her usual artistic style, and Mr. John Rabbitt gave soulful interpretations of "Dear heart," "The English rose." and '!Maire, my girl." Mr. NV. H. Payton tastefully played the acconipaniments.

div.head: SHAKESPEARE COAIMEMORATION.
div.p: THE SHAKESPEARE COAIMEMORATION.
' THE MERCHANT OF VENICE" AND
"MACBETH." MR. C. D. LA-W CHATS ON THE FORTHCOMING PERFORMANCES.

arrington will once more do homage to the transcendent genius of William Shakespeare on April 10th, 17th, 18th and 10th, when the annual com- memoration performances will take place at the Royal- Court Theatre. Mr. Charles D. Law is, of course, the leading spirit in the enterprise—in fact, but for his dramatic gifts and inspiring initiative, it is very questionable vthether Warrington would have adopted the unique method of honouring the poet's birthday by amateur productions of his works. In the senior house surgeon's room at the Infirmary, surrounded by Shakespearian relics and photographic mementoes of previous revivals, Mr. Law courteously gave an " Examiner " representative some outstanding impres- sions of the forthcoming commemoration. He first of all pointed to the encouraging fact that the interest shown in previous undertakings has encouraged the committee to launch (.ut on more ambitions lines each succeeding year. The first commemoration was confined to a single night, and so remarkable was the success achieved that the following year two plays were chosen, and three nights were occupied in their presentation. This year there will again be t inco plays and the theatre has been taken for bur nights. _ _ _ _ .

„ Mr Law particularly desired it to be known that the proceeds of the performances would be devoted to the Infirmaiy. ”We are excetdingly anxious" he said "that ur efforts to commemorate Shakespeare and at the same time to benefit this institution should be recognised by the public in a really tangible form. The Infirmary, in spite of the benefit that has come to it from the Million Peny Fund, is still in need of money in order to keep it abreast of modern require- ments. and it is the desire of every member of the committee that we shall be able to hand over a sub- stantial sum" - -

A Shakespearian enthusiast to the finger tips, Mr Law was most at home in discussing the plays chosen for stage representation. He said that this year, for the fit st time, they were departing from tragedy and and staging on a comedy. "The Merchant of Venice" had been chosen because of its intense popularity with theatrical audiences. "We are going to play a version" added Mr Law "which I think is different from any I have seen. In the first place we bring on Portia in the first act ard do not, as is some- times the case, delay her appearance until after the flight of Jessica. Our arrangement is, as far as possible, to play the piece in absolute consecutiveness of incident, living used to introduce Portia in the second scene and then go back to Venice. We do not. We open with the Venetian scene and go straight on until the bargain is made with regard to the pound of flesh. Then we introduce Portia in Scene 2of Act I. The whole of our second act is devoted to the flight of Jessica and its discovery by Shylock, and culminates in the great Tubal scene in which Shylock avows his determination to revenge himself for this affront and for Antonio's contemptuous spurning of him on the Rialto, by exacting the full terms of his bond. The third act is given over to the Belmont scene, in which Bassani° makes the successful choice of the leaden casket, and concludes with the arrival of the alarming news that Antonio's ships have all miscarried and that Shylock has announced his intention of claiming his pound of flesh. In the fourth act we have the momentous trial scene, while the fifth act takes us to Portia's garden and the delightful play of comedy between Portia and Nerissa, Bassani° and Gratiano, ending with Portia's unfolding of the clever bcheme by which she saved Antonio. The lines we are following will absolutely avoid a large amount of scene-changing and tedious waiting. We are costuming the play after the manner of the 16th century and our endeavour is to bring out to the full the spirit of comedy which surrounds every- body, except Antonio, the merchant, and Shylock. We shall also emphasise the hostility, which was then so bitter, between the Christians and the Jews. One may safely say that none of the important scenes have been 'cut' or excluded. We do lir t retain the Prince of Arragon, for it would appear that the choosing of the casket, three times over, is liable to become wearisome, and we have, accordingly, only the Prince of Morocco and Bassani° to present this episode." "How do you regard ' The Merchant of Venice' from the standpoint of amateur production ?" asked the interviewer,

" I regard it as a very suitable play " replied Mr. Law "for there are quite a number of good parts to be distributed. You might almost say that we have been prompted to put on a comedy this year in answer to many requests from the public that it would be very interesting to see our company, which has hitherto held very strongly to tragedy, trying its capabilities in the lighter field. The playing of a Shakesperian comedy is really far more difficult than acting in tragedy, which always helps to play itself, as it were. ,01 the comedies, hoc,' ever, 'The Merchant of 'Venice ' is undoubtedly the easiest." Mr. Law will appear in the all-important and difficult role of Shylock. Asked to indicate his own conception of the part he said : "I shall endeavour to present Sbylock es a man of dignity, of great pride in his ration, deep love for his daughter, absolute hatred for Christians, and overwhelming love for his money." "Will it be your endeavour to make us feat- sorry for Shylock ?" " Undoubtedly. I think Shylock should leave the court with the sympathies of the house for, after all, he is defeated by a trick of the law and gets a heavier retribution than he deserves."

Mr Law pointed out that ShyloCk was originally played at; a comic chararter and it was only with the advent of Keane that the part was presented in a rri.lly tragic light. "The man " he added- is undoubtedly capable of very great affection, as evidenced by hiq references to his dead wife and his distress at the flight if Jessica, but his love of money

is supreme." - The Portia of the production is Miss Gladys Adams who made her first appearance with the company in a very small part in Macbeth. Last year she scored a distinct success as Lady Anne in " Richard " and there is every indication that her Portia will be one of the triumphs of the forthcoming conimemoration. Mrs C Garton Stone, who has had a considerable experience on the amateur stage, will appear as Nerissa. A departure is being made in allotting the part of Jessica to two ladies. Miss Milly Truslove, who was one of the little Princes last year, will impers-mate the character on the Wednesday and

Mrs Law will portray it on the Thursday. Bassanio is entrusted to Mr John Lowe, who last year was Clarence in "Richard III." and Cassius in "Julius Cfesar." Mr Leslie Langford, the Richmond of last year, is Lorenzo. Mr Harvey 0 Adams, who took the title part in "Julius Cfesar " will play Gratiano, and Mr W H Brdwn, who each year is showing himself a more capable player, Antonio. The following is the complete cast :

Duke of Venice Mr Leonard Daintith Prince of Morocco Mr Walter Ashton Antonio, a merchant of Venice Mr W H Bto%n Bassani°, his friend, suitor to Portia Mr J Lowe Gratiano Mr Harvey 0 Adams Salanio friends to Antonio S.: Mr J Lawton Salarino Bassani° Alt. A C Hodgson Lorenzo. in Love with Jessica... Mr Leslie L Langiord Shylock, a Jew Mr Charles Law Tonal, a Jew. his friend Mr Egerton Pair°lough Launcelot Gobbo, a clown Mr H M Ashton Old Gobbo, his father Mr Albert Chester Leonardo, servant to Bassani° Mr E Bradshaw Balthazar, servant to Portia Miss Marion Ellison Clerk of the Court Mr B Dickson Count Palatine Monsieur le Bon suitors to Mr R Pemberton The Duke of Saxony's Portia Mr J Hannan Nephew Mr L Grange Faulconbridge Portia Miss Gladys Adams Nerissa, her waiting-maid Mrs C Garton Stone Jessica, daughter to Shylock (Wednesday).......Miss Milly Truslove (Thursday) ...Mrs Charles Law

"Macbeth," which will he presented on the Friday and Saturday ,is being revived, owing to its tremendous success when the company first played it two years_ ago. "On that occasion" said Mr Law, "we estab- lished a record at the theatre both with regard to the actual number of people in the house and the amount of the receipts. We have succeeded in getting almost the whole of the original cast back again, and, in general, the play will be produced on tho same lines as before." Our readers who recall the brilliant achievement of Mrs Robert Garnett, as Lady Macbeth, will welcome her re-appearance in that part. Mr Charles Law will • again impersonate Macbeth, Mr Harold Smith, M.P., Macduff, Mr Henry Hallard, the porter, and Mr Harvey Adams the first witch. The only changes of note are that Mr Leonard Daintitb will play King Duncan and Mr Leslie L Langford his sou Malcolm. We append the dramatis persoue

Duncan, King of Scotland Mr Leonard Daintith Malcolm A. hi Mr Leslie L Langford s Donalbain ) sons Miss Dorothy Truslove Macbeth t Mr Charles Law Generals of his arm Y Mr H M Ashton Bacquo acduff ) Mr Harold -Smith Lennox Li Thanes of Scotland Mr L Campbell Ross J Mr W I-1 Brown Fleance. son to Banquo.. Young Siward Mr Douglas Travis Seyton,an officer attending on Macbeth...Mr 0 Wheeler A Porter Mr Henry Hallard A Doctor Mr B Marston. A Bleeding Soldier Mr B Dickson Ist Witch Mr Harvey 0 Adams 2nd Witch Mr John Lowe 3rd Witch Mrs F E Griffiths Ist Messenger Mr Albert Chester 2nd Messenger Mr B Madeley Ist Murderer Mr Walter Ashton 2nd Murderer Mr Egerton Fairclough Armed Head Mr Walter Plinge Bleeding Child Miss Eunice Downs Crowned Child Miss Milly Truslove Lady Macbeth .Mrs Robert Garnett. Gentlewoman attending on Lady Macbeth Miss Dorothy Browne The expenses of the commemoration will be heavy but the company are again indebted to Mr W if Savory, general manager of the F R Benson com- panies for invaluable help. Through his instru- mentality, the scenery which Mr F R Benson uses in "Macbeth" has been placed at the disposal of our local Shakespearian amateurs and, with the exception of two very beautiful scenes painted by Mr T Robinson at Liverpool, they will also make:use of Mr Benson's "Merchant of Venice " scenery. Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree, interested as be always is in Shakespearian productions and being a personal friend of Mr Harold Smith, M.P., has lent him Mr Arthur Bourchier's Macduff costume which that great actor wore in the revival at His Majesty's Theatre, London. The wardrobe is being obtained from Messrs W and C May, of London, and the properties from Mr Robinson, of Liverpool. The company, which numbers sixty, has been applying itself most enthusiastically to the task of rehearsing since September 29th. We hear that the committee is considering the advisability of offering reduced terms to parties of scholars for the Wednesday evening performance of "The merchant of Venice." The Chairman of the Committee which is respon. Bible for the commemoration is Mr Oswald Lofthouse the hon. treasurer, Mr Henry Collin, and the bon. secretary, Mr Harvey 0. Adams. The other members of the committee are : Messrs J H Smethurst (chair- man of the Infirmary Board of Management), Eric Fairclough,L R Rovvson, Walter Ashton, A C Hodgson and C D Law (who, as heretofore, is disoharging the onerous duties of stage manager and producer.) Mr A. M Loader, the general manager of the theatre, has been thoughtful and considerate in the offering of suggestions, and has given the company every facility for rehearsals.

div.p: TOWN COUNCIL TOPICS.
PENNY BATHS FOR WORKINGMEN.
A Byelaw Against Handbill
Distribution.

The meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday ev.ning, in addition to being" Budget Night," was notable tor the variety of contentious topics which provoked long and acrimonious discussions. The Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph) presided, and there were silo preient :—The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Aldermen A Bennett, T Burton, James Evans, W Pierpoint, .1 Smethurst and D Tinnion ; Councillors J G Craik, J Wilkinson, J Hawthorn,P Peacock, G Archer J Cbrimes, T Chantler, E Cunnington, F T Lashford, J Pemberton, F Lindley, E Osborne, J Skellsnd, J Shaw, Henshall. J Broadhurst, T B.rtles, W H J Jenkins, H Roberts, J T Locker, S Gough, S Taylor, J Dickenson, W J Wilson, Messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), A T liallaway (neputy-town clerk), T H Spinks (assistant town clerk), J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), W H Woodcock (norough collector), A M Kerr (borough surveyor), J Coote Hibbert (medical officer of health). G W N Joseph (assistant medical officer), W T Flood (inspector of nuisances), J Gray (water engineer), .1 Moore Murray (director of education) and R B Roberts (assistant director). COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND THE ARCHITECTS.

The first discussion arse on the minutes of the Ecincation Committee, Councillor Pemberton taking exception to an item in the proceedings of the Sites and Buildings Committee. The law clerk baying advised that committee that i. was desirable that provision !Should he made in the agreement with the architects for the Oakwood Avenue, Oliver-atreet and Parr-street schools, for an amount to be paid to architects for work done in the preparation of the wonting drawings .and tracimta and bills of quantities, in the event of the committee ultimately deciding not to proceed with the work, the law clerk and the surveyor were requested to confer with the aichitects and be prepared to make a recommendation to the committee as to the amount to be agreed upon. Councillor PEMBERToN said the conditions tinder which the architects competed was that they should get tenders for the erection of the schools at a cost not exceeding ten guineas per head and, in the event of their failing to do so, the committee could dismiss them without further piyment. Tim present resolution upset all that. As a matter of fact plans were accepted at lOs per head beyond the specified figure and he con- tended that such a course was not lair to the other architects. Moreover the Council was not taken into the confidence of the committee on the question. Councillor PEmBERToN brought forward an amend- ment that the committee's recommendation be referred back, but the Mayor ruled that it was out of order, as it was not, strictly speaking, a financial matter. No definite payment was mentioned. Councillor KOBERTS said everything connected with the matter had been submitted to be Council, as the education authority, and sanctioned by them. He explained that hitherto when plans of schools had been accepted a surveyor had been engaged to get out quantities. In the present case there was no proposi- tion to pay the architects (Messrs Wright and Hainlyn) for the plans, unless they were actually carried out. They had, however, been engaged as quantity surveyors and for their services in that capacity it was proposed to pay them. It was no part of their contract to get out the quantities and they had been engaged just as distinctly and separately from their original contract as if they were an entirely different firm. He hoped he had made the position clear to the Council. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is not clear to me. Councillor NoBERTs : No, I am not trying to make it clear to you. I am trying to make it clear to members of the Council who are capable of appreciat- ing the difference. Councillor PEMBERTON : it is a question of fact. Councillor ROBERTS : Yes, it is purely a question of fact, Continuing, :he pointed out that it was not pro- posed to pay the architects the I. per cent. which the committee woul4 have to pay to a quantities surveyor, But an agreed sum, in the event of the contract not being proceeded with. It would be a scandalous thing if they employed the firm in a secoud capacity and then declined to pay them, After further discussion, the minutes were approved

div.head: PENNY BATHS FOR WORKINGMEN.
div.p: PENNY BATHS FOR WORKINGMEN.

Councillor PEMBERTON introduced a proposal: That the 'l'oan Hall, Parks and Baths Committee make pro- vision whereby working men will be enabled to uie UN) slipper baths at certain convenient hours of the day at a charge of id. each. Persons so usit“, the baths to provide towels and soap. He remarked that he had previously recommended Councillor Broadhurst to bring a similar proposition forward. Councillor Broadhurst had repeatedly charged him with not being in favour of the concession, hut he (Councillor Broadhurst) had sat on the fence. When the baths contract was before the committee, Councillor 13roadburst objected to its being let because proper provision for cheap bathing was not made for workingmen and he (Councillor Pemberton) pointed out to him that he could easily move a special resolution. However, Councillor Broadhurst seemed to have had a bee in his bonnet and would not move a resolution bacause it would have removed his grievance. (Laughter) Everybody said the workingman oueht to have a bath in his own house, but thousands of Warrington workers, who did not earn more than S.:l a week, could not afford to live in houses that were so equipped. Any loss which the cheap bathing concessions involved would be counterbalanced by the gain in the public health.
Councillor WILKINSON seconded : The time hid arrived when the Corporation should give workingmen facilities for a "swill-down" before they returned home from work.

Councillor BROADHURST, in supporting the resolu- tion, remarked : in the words of Lord B-aconEfield, be (Councillor Pemberton) has caught me bathing and stolen my clothes (Laughter.) I believe the fear of Broadhurst is upon him. (Laughter.) I have warned him and Councillor Lashford too,that this would he brought up against them at the next election. Continuing the Councillor said no had brought forward a resolu- tion on the question but only three members—Alder- man Bennett, Councillor Roberts and Wilson—supported it. He had now stooped to conquer(Laughter.) Coun- cillor Pemberton, as he had previously told him, would allow workingmen to bathe at the mouth of a foul sewer, emptying itself into the Mersey, but now he came forward to claim the honour of introducing the propusal. Alderman JAMES Evass supported the resolution from the health standpoint, but said it was not us broad as he would like it to be. Councillor WILKINsoN : It would have been if Broad- hurst had done it.

Alderman EvANs contended that the Corporation might at least provide the towels free of charge, as workingmen, who would call at the baths on their way home from work, would find it very inconvenient to carry towels about with them. Councillor ARCHER said the resolution would he received with great favour by the inhabitants of Howley Ward, the majority of whom did not enjoy the con- venience of baths in their own homes.
Alderman BENNETT, while supporting the resolution, said the Council mould not have done its duty until there %cm a bye-law providing that a bath should be fitted in every new house._

Councillor- JENKINS said there were hundreds of working women who would be only too glad to avail themselves of cheap baths. He hoped the resolution would he broadened so as to embrace them. (Hear, bear and laughter.) Councillor SKELLAND Sill he was pleased that the authorities were following the example of the Ragged School workers who years ago gave their time to bathing poor and dirty children 'iut were than called upon by tho Corporation to pay for the water u,ed in the process. Alderman TiNmoN, while objecting to government by resolution, said he was entirely in favour of Councillor Pemberton's idea. He always had a suspicion that such resolutions were introduced with ulterior motives such as the gaining of popularity at election times and the present proposal smacked of that. It was an endeavour to take the wind out of somebody else's sails. He suggested that the resolution should be withdrawn and re-introduced in a more workable form. They did not expect the cheap baths to pay and they might therefore increase the value of the concession to the workingman by providing soap and towels free. Councillor ROBERTS also suggested a re-framing of

div.head: IMPS COUNCIL MEETINGS AND WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL SEEM TO HAVE MANY POINTS IN COMMON.
div.p: IMPS COUNCIL MEETINGS AND WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL SEEM TO HAVE MANY POINTS IN COMMON.

the resolution. He did not like the differentiation between workingmen and others. Any person who was excluded by the conditions of his home accommodation from the orlinary privileges of a bath should be able to use the public baths on the same terms as those who answered the definition " workingman." He also agreed with C oincillor Jenkins that women ought not to he excluded. There had been a large development in the employment of females in Warrington in the last few years, and they ought to be catered for. Councillor LOCKER expressed a similar view. Alderman BURToN said the resolution was not feasible under the present conditions. There were only eleven slipper baths and the demand for them was greater than they could satisfy. He suggested that on certain occasions the baths should be set apart for workingmen at a charge of one penny. Councillor PEACOCK hoped Councillor Pemberton would not withdraw his proposition. His experience of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, was a miserable one. Notwithstanding letters and instruc- tions,the committee would not move. He believed that half a loaf was better than none, and therefore the com- mittee should take the opportunity of ensuring that workingmen should be able to use the baths at a nominal charge. He had no faith that the committee would do anything unless they were compelled, and then it would require a sledge hammer to make them. Laughter). Couhcillor BROADHURST said he had given the com- mittee every opportunity to move in the matter, but they had refused to do so. Councillor BIRTLES said it would be impracticable to carry out the proposition while the baths extension was pending He had no recollection of resolutions having been brought before the committee by Councillor Broadhurst. Couneillor DICKENSON said that when the extension was completed there would be twenty-four slipper baths. He appealed to Councillor Pemberton to with- draw the resolution in order that the committee might consider the question. The MAYOR said he was afraid he was the only heretic on the general question. He would not oppose the proposition, but he had a strong feeling that they ought to teach people to cleanse themselves in their own homes. He had seen poor people who had no baths in their houses but who managed to keep them- selves clean, while some people who had baths were the reverse. They ought to educate the people and provide them with every reasonable facility. He approved of the suggestion that the poorest house should have a bath. He was as anxious as anybody for the comfort and social welfare of the poor, out he doubted whether the present resolution presented the wisest plan. Councillor PEMBERTON said it was wonderful to hear how much in favour of workingmen the councillors were at election times, but when the opportunity came to put those beautiful sentiments into practical effect there was always some little crochet to prevent them. lie had challenged Councillor Broadhurst to produce any resolution which he had brought forNard to provide cheap baths, but all he had had in reply was clap-trap and bounce. -

The MAYOR: Avoid personalities. Councillor PEMBERToN : You have allowed Coun- cillor Broadhnrst to attack me pretty freely, and you ought not to gag me after he has punched me so much. The MAYOR: 1 thought what he said was correct at the time. Councillor PEMBERION : That may he, but what I am saying is correct, too. I challenge him to produce any resolution he has brought before the Council. Councillor BROADHURST : 1 will take up that challenge. Councillor PEMBERTON : I wanted him to do it, but he had not the courage or pluck to put down a special resolution of his own. All be can do is to criticise what other people do. Councillor Pemberton was pro- ceeding to refer to his " twelveiyears " connection with the Council when Councillor ROBERTS interposed with the remark that Councillor Pemberton had not yet been in the Council twelve years. Councillor PEMBERToN : I object to you interfering at all when I am speaking. Councillor ROBERTS: You should speak facts. Councillor PEMBERTON: I object to you interfering. You are always at it. Councillor ROBERTS : You were first elected in November, 1902. Councillor PEMBERToN : Never mind that. Councillor ROBERTS : Twelve yelrs in 1914. "Councillor PEMBERTON : We are not to a month or two.
Councillor ROBERTS: No, not ta a great many months.

Councillor PEMBERTON : Suppose we say ten years. Councillor ROBERTS : Say twenty while you are it it. Councillor PEMBERTON contended that it was ropracticable to suggest that the workingman should. lave a bath in his own home when he could not afford it. The resolution was carried without dissent. YE-LAW AGAINST HANDBILL DISTRIBUTION.
TRADE UNION PROTEST.
The Watch Committee resolved_ that the __following

bye-law be made and adopted :—No person shall in an street or public place, to the obstruction or annoyance of passengers, distribute or give ay, ay any handbill or other notice advertising any trade, business, or pro- fession, or the sale of any foods, wares or merchandise, r any lecture, entertainment or performance. This aye-law shall not apply to the delivery by any person ,f any cuch handbill or notice to any house, office, or place of business. The MAYOR said he had received five communica- tions from trade union associations, oujecting to the proposed bye-law as being opposed to trade union pro- paganda. The bye-law was not so intended. The object was to stop the littering of the streets by persons who, for purposes of gain, sent out men and Fort to distribute handbills. The bye-law did not pro- hibit the distribution of bills convening meetings. As

the standing orders required that a bye-law must be submitted to two meetings of the Council before it could be adopted, no harm could be done 135 allowing it to go throogh that night and he would take care that the matter was brought before the Watch Committee at their next meeting. Councillor OsBORNE and Councillor BROADHURST said they had intended to raise the question but, in view of the Mayor's explanation, they would defer any objection they might offer. Councillor PEMBERToN said the public wanted pro- tecting against arbitrary bye-laws. A preat deal depended upon the spirit in which they were administered.

Ths Awn : It is obstruction or annoyance of passengers that this bye-law is directed against. Councillor 13,, EMBERTON pointed out that persons who were in deadly opposition to trade unionism might easily construe the distribution of band bills announcing a trade union meeting as an act of obstruction. Councillor llAwn-toux suggested that the word " lecture " should be removed from the list of pro- hibited announcements. Eventually the Mayor withdrew the bye-lav,- for further discussion by the Watch Committe. PRESERVING AN ANCIENT NAME.
The Street Improvement Committee resolved that for the purpose of preserving its name so much of Kontsford-road as lies between Warrington Bridge and Thelwall-lane. be re-named Latchford Causeway.

Alderman TINNION objected to the proposed chanO. He said there was only one Causeway in Warrington and that was Wilderspool Causeway. They were not living in ancient times, but in modern Warrington, and it would be a piece of stupid folly to attempt to bring about a change which would only lead to endless con- fusion, without the slightest advantage. He understood the suggestion had emanated from Alderman Bennett and the Town Clerk. When they put their heads together, it was wonderful what they could propound. (Laughter.) Councillor HENSHALL seconded the amendment that the recommendation be referred back. He said he had been inclined to debit Alder- man Bennett exclusively with the suggestion. (Laughter.) If they were to alter the name of Enutsford-road because in 1651 it was known as Litchford Causeway, why not have a resolution christening Bridge-street New Gate-street, because it was called that in 1465, and calling Mersey-street Bonk-street, vs it wasiknown in 1651 ? That would be a logical development of the antiquarian ideas of Alderman Bennett. (Laughter.) Alderman BENNETT said the suggestion to preserve the old name came lrom the Town Clerk but, to tell the truth, he (the alderman) was rather envious that he should have had the honour of making it. (Laughter) The suggestion did great credit to Mr Whittle's antiquarian knowledge and local patriotism and was the result of considerable research. He (the speaker), could not see why the names mentioned by Councillor Henshall had been discarded, for they were picturesque and gave a certain colour to the town. The TOWN CLERK : lam not ashamed of the part I played in the proposal. I did not go so far as to suggest the substitution of one name for the other. I simply suggested that we should preserve the old name The AIAYott : I thought it was a good idea and thoroughly approved of it. The amendment was carried by 17 votes to 4. A. CHURCH-STREET "IMPROVEMENT."

Councillor ARCHER took exception to a resolution of the Street Improvement Committee, approving an amended plan of property in Church-street, for Mr T Williams. He pointed out thitt originally plans were passed for seven shops, which he understood were to be of elaborate design. What was to be foisted on Howley Ward in place of them ? Two shops and a blank wall for stables. Surely that was not in keeping with Alder- man Bennett's ideas of beautiful architecture, and he askea for an assurance that such a project would not be tolerited. The MAYOR said the plans were in accordance with the bye-laws, and they were bound to pass them. Councillor CH ANTLER said strong complaints had been made by the iEhabitanti of the ward against the pro- posal to erect stables in Church-street. The TOWN CLERK: The original plans were for seven shops hut as those plans did not comply with the bye- laws, they were rejected. Since then he has submitted plans for two shops which do comply with the bye-laws and you cannot reject them. Mr Isherwood will submit plans for stables, I expect, in the course of a month. Councillor ARCHER: IS it right to erect stables on main streets ? .
Thl MAYOR. : We cannot object to it. Councillor PEMBRIITON : This is the point. We paid over £l,OOO for this piece of laud and sold it for £5OO. _ _

The MAYOR : This is out of order. Councillor PEMBERTON said that when the land was sold they ought to have made a restriction as to the class of buildings to be erected on it. They could not blame the builders now. Alderman BENNETT said he was in sympathy with Councillor Pemberton's suggestion as to restrictions. He was very sorry the land was ever offered for sale, but the reason why the Finance Committee decided upon the sale was that the Corporation had had to pay through the nose for it. It would have been better to have retained the land unoccupied until they finally decided what NC a 9 to be done with regard to the

approaches to the possible new bridge at Howley. One advantage of the altered plan was that they would still be able to see the Parish Church, whereas the erection of seven shops would have shut out the view. Councillor WILKINsoN pointed out that the Finance Committee did not buy the land at such a large price. The Street Improvement Committee bought it and turned it over to the Finance Committee who, being tired of seeing it producing no revenue, sold it at the best price they could get. The minutes were approved. LIGHTING OF VICTORIA PARK.

the Te hoeffSeitroeef t Ithemlipureocatermi cei tn Committee resolved aygcommitthteaet to light the new footpath across Victoria Park, at £43 Per annum, be accepted. - Alderman TINNIoN moved an amendment that the oiler be not accepted. He said that incandescent lights were superior to electricity for road-lighting purposes end, as the Gas Committee had offered to light the footpath for £2B, he did not see why the committee should go beyond that figure. Alderman JAMES EVANS seconded. Alderman BENNETf pointed out that the Electricity Committee's offer was a reduction on the amount originally asked and, although it was the more expensive method, the committee thought the advantage lay on the side of electricity. Councillor HAIN-I.IIOIIN said the Electricity Com- mittee would not be sorry to lose the job, as he under- stood they would not n ake a penny out of it, in fact there would be a loss. The amendment was carried by 13 votes to 3.

stant interruptions. At the last meeting it was the same and if a man retorts he is accused of dealing in personalities. Alderman JAMNS EVANS seconded the amendment. There was no need to rush the matter, as it was not, one of urgency. There were private firms who would render assistance in case of fire emergency, and it was only fair thtlA. the Council should have an opportunity of discussion before committing themselves to the pur- chase. _ _ _

Councillor LINDLEY said the matter had not been rushed, as the Council had already decided to purchase an engine. Councillor GouGH said the purchase had not been carried out in a businesslike manner. The whole of the menabers of the committee had not Leers consulted, and he objected to such hole and corner business. Councillor ARCHER : I must protest against those charges, as a member of the committee who has worked assiduously with regard to the engine. The demand for it has been emphasised by all the big firms of Warring- ton. Ido my work on the committee with honesty of purpose, let me tell Mr Gough. Councillor LASHFORD : With all due respect to C ouncillor Archer, I don't think he is in order. The MAvon : You have no right to express any opinion about Councillor Archer. Sit down. Councillor ARCHER : I leave my conduct in the hands of the Mayor. Councillor LASH FORD : Well, it is not fair. Councillor PEMBERTON also objected to the business having been cut and dried, and maintained that it should first have been bentight before the General Purposes Committee. Councillor PEACOCK said he had never been able to bring himself to the opinion that a motor fire engine would be any use in Warrington. It would go so rapidly that it might do more harm than good, by running into shops and killing people. (Laughter.) He advocated the purchase of an additional horse engine as a stand-by. The brigade had told him that they did not want a motor engine, as they could already gift on the scene quickly enough ta meet the necessities of Warrington. Alderman BENNETT said the great manufacturers who had far more at stake than anybody else, were unanimously of opinion that a motor engine was necessary. Only last year one of the most important works was absolutely gutted, whereas it might have been saved if the engine had been there sooner. (" No, no.") The Council ought to bear in mind the prospect of an extension of the borough boundaries. Councillor CHRDIEs said that as the Fire Engine Committee had a reserve fund of over £6OO, the purchase of the engine would not entail a heavy call on the rates. There would also be the saving of horse hire. Alderman BURTON said that to advocate the purchase of another horse engine was like preferring a stage coach to railway transit. After full discussion, Councillor OSBORNE withdrew his amendment, but said be was still of the opinion that the Council should have had an opportunity of expressing its views before the purchase was decided upon.

div.head: "MICROSCOPIC TINKERING."
div.p: "MICROSCOPIC TINKERING."

The Street Improvement Committee recommended that the premises in Knutsford-road occuped by Mr Joseph Brierley be demolished. Councillor HENSHALL moved an amendment that the minute be referred back. He said the Corporation was not within measurable distance of beginning the improvement for which the property was required and therefore there was no reason to disturb a tenant who was paying a rent equal to 3 per cent of the purchase price. The committee had pursued the same policy of microscopic tinkering in Butterrnarket-street and had made it what the chairman (Alderman Bennett) had picturesquely called a city of the dead. (Laughter). Councillor HALLIWELL seconded the amendment.

Alderman BENNETT said the committee might not be able to widen the whole of the road at once but, for heaven's sake, let them do something. The property in question consisted of semi-derelict houses which were no ornament to the district. The amendment was declared lost and the minutes were passed.

EARLY CLOSING A petition frorn shop-keepers in the main streets and centre of the town had resulted in the Health Com- mittee taking the necessary steps for making an early closing order which would fix upon the following closing hours in the area as specified : Monday and Tuesday, 7 p.m. ; Wednesday, 8 p.m. ; Friday, 9 p.m. ; Saturday 10 p m. Alderman JAMES EVANS said that since the petition was sent in, a number of grocers had made a request to withdraw, which brought the total below what the statute required. He therefore withdrew the minute. THE MOTOR FIRE ENGINE. PURCHASE AGREED TO.

The Fire Engine Committee resolved that the tender of Leyland's Motors Ltd. for the supply of a 450 gallon turbine fire engine with first-aid apparatus, be accepted, subject to certain modifications and alterations to be agreed upon between the Borough Surveoor and that firm, and that the Town Clerk be authorisel to have the necessary contract completed. The question of an escape for attachment to the motor fire engine was deferred pending further inquiries. Alderman BURTON, in moving the adoption of the minutes. said the price of the engine was £l,OOO, but that did not include the escape. They already had a large escape, and it might be sufficient to purchase a lighter one at a smaller cost. Councillor CUNNINGTON seconded. Councillor OsBORNE moved an amendment that the minute be referred back. He pointed out that at the February meeting of the Council the question of the purchase of a motor fire engine was raised, and they were told that the Council would have an opportunity of discussing fully the advantages and disadvantages of the purchase. The MAYOR : Now is the time for that.

Councillor OSBORNE : Yes, but as a matter of fact, the purchase is practically made. Councillor ARCHER: It is well understood that no contract can be completed by the Corporation unless it has the full sarction of the Council. Councillor OSBORNE : Precisely, but you go all the way first. You practically arrange with a certain firm to buy an Engine and then you come before us when the business is cut and dried. The committee have practically committed themselves to buy this engine. Councillor ARCHER : Subject to the sanction of the Council.

Councillor OSBORNE protested that the matter had been rushed, without a fair opportunity for discussion. Councillor ARCHER : I don't think Counciilor Osborne is so dense of observation as not to know that before contracts can be completed, they must be sanctioned by the Council. Surely he is not devoid of intelligence with regard to the conduct of public business.
Councillor OSBORNE : Ido think that respectable gentlemen in this Council should refrain from casting any reflections on the ability or integrity of any other member of the Council.

Councillor ARCHER: lam not casting any reflec- tion. I say Councillor Osborne is the first man to cast a reflection on the committee. We have done no such thing as he alleges. div.head: MW KEBTY FLETCHER'S ATTACK
div.p: MW KEBTY FLETCHER'S ATTACK
ON MR. LLOYD GEORGE.

In the Flonse of Commons on Tuesday, Mr Kebty Fletcher (Altrincham, C) asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether there were any emoluments or allowances attached to his office other than his salary. Mr Lloyd George: The answer is in the negative. Mr liebty-Fletcher : Arising out of that answer, is not the right hon. gentleman's salary sufficient to pre- vent him from wrongfully and improperly gambling ? (Loud cries of" Oh! " and " Order ! The Speaker: I must see that question on the paper. It does not arise out of the originat answer. (Ministerial cheers). Mr Lloyd George (warmly) : If the hon member has anything of that kind to say, he had better say it in a place where he could be subject to cross-examination. (Loud Ministerial cheers). The Speaker : If the hon. member has any further question to put I should like to see it in writing. (Renewed cheers). Mr Kebty-Fletcher : Have I no right to reply to the Chancellor's attack? I will charge him when I have the opportunity. (Opposition cheers;. The Speaker : The hon. member must put the ques- tion on the paper, and I shall then look at it. Mr Lloyd George : Whenever he does I shall be prepared to meet him, as I have met others. (Loud ministerial cheers, and loud opposition cries of " Gag," " Marconi," and "Whitewash.") Mr Kebty-Fletcher : Mock heroism. (Opposition cheers). Mr Lloyd George: You had better say it openly. (Ministerial cheers). Mr Kebty-Fleteher You will get all you want. (Opposition cheers).

div.head: KING'S VISIT.
div.p: THE KING'S VISIT.

At a meeting of the Newton Urban District Council on Monday it was reported that their Majesties would drive slowly through Newton in Maker&ld via Crow- lane West, on July 10th. Lord Derby, however, points out that their Majesties will be in a closed motor with glass sides, and in order to see them people must be more or less on a level with the car.

The Clerk reported that the Chairman and he attended a meeting of representatives, presided over by the Earl of Derby, at Manchester, when the Chairman asked whether the route could be altered so that their Majesties wouli travel through Earlestown, but the Earl of Derby replied that no deviation from the route laid down cnuld be considered.

On .Saturday evening an interesting concert .I'lol given in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, in Si d the Golborne-street Baptist Church Building lun The weather was not propitious and the hall red consequently by no means crowded,but we are asse.he that on the other hand and fortunately for 'flt promoters of the concert, the number of people pre,seb-e far from represented the number of tickets sold. e most imprtant items in the programme were the's, associated with the name ot Miss Cathie Leadbetter who figured upon the platform in the dual capacity violin soloist and elocutionist, and it is due to saYtt the onset, that Miss Leadbetter's contributions tot evening's entertainment were its most stgre•e: able and conspicuous feature. There are many Irleariy all "ut, the " prisoner " occurs in leature of v,T.la is, as we hope to show, a %it befo"Y decided interest. Illeanin ,re hazarding a guess at b LUs look at the verses.
London Bridge is broken down Broken down, broken down
the

My fair lady. Stones and lime will build it up Stones and lime thy will not stay Build it up with penny loaves Penny loaves they will not do Build it up with pins and needles Pins and needles rust and bend Get a man to watch all night Perhaps the man might fall asleep Get a dog to bark all night If the dog should find a bone Get a cock to crow all night Rere's a prisoner I have got What's the prisoner done to you Robbed a house and killed a man.

The first verse appears to have an historical basis, and may be an echo of the old song that celebrated the breaking of the bridge in the eleventh century, sung when Ethelred, after the death of Sweyn, was assisted by Olaf in retaining and entering London. We quote the opening stanza:— London Bridge is broken down Go!cl is won and briOlt renown Shield 3 resounding War-horn sounding Hild is shouting in the din Arrows singing Mail-coats ringing Odin makes our Olaf win. The old triumph-song does not help us any further. It leaves us with no clue to the setting of a watch and the taking of a prisoner. "London Bridge" is a medley indeed and the best suggestion we are able to make is that it echoes usages associated with bridge building in far off centuries. Antiquarians will not need to be told that in the past the laying (,f the foundations of a bridge or the gateway of a city was regarded as a grave proceeding. Vortigern, it will be remembered, was advised by the Druids to seek a victim to sacrifice at the laying of the foundation of his castle. It was usual to make such human sacrifices and sprinkle the stones with blood, or to bury victims alive under the huge basal stones. Special precau- tions were taken against any spell being placed over the important stones of the structure and the work was carefully watched lest any unlucky or untoward incident should occur. The sacrifices and the blood which was sprinkled would appear to be designed to preserve the foundations from evil. A modern instance 44i1l illustrate the old belief. When a bridge was being built over the Ganges at Calcutta in 1872 a scare was raised through the city, and the natives refused to work upon the bridge, the reason being that no sacrifice had been made when the founda- tion was laid. They argued that the Ganges would be angry and would sweep away the bridge when it was built. The native plan to avert the evil was to build the piers upon a layer of human heads. In Siam when the city gates were being erected they seized the first four persons who passed when the lowest stone was laid, and buried them alive under the main posts. Such sacrifices were regarded as essential to successful building, and traces of the belief are universal. There is a tradition that old London Bridge was bespattered with the blood of children, and when it was rebuilt in the 12th century it is known that the mortar was tempered with the blood of beasts. In this way did our fathers compromise upon the subject of human sacrifices. It will not be regarded as a far-fetched suggestion that the " prisoner " in the song is one who is brought out to be sacrificed. The burden of the song is the building up of a safe bridge. The "watching" is dis- cussed, and then quite suddenly comes the suggestion "Here's a prisoner I have got." It is not at all unlikely that when the old pagan habit of making human sacrifices was discredited that our ancestors killed criminals at the laying of a foundation and sprinkled the stones with their blood. It is quite possible that this was done when the bridge was rebuilt after the victory of Ethelred, and if so the quaint ditty is interesting as marking a stage in the moral progress of our ancestors, as well as for its historical echo. HOW MANY MILES TO BETHLEHEM? And have we not an echo of the Crusades in "How many miles to Bethlehem ?" a game of which few readers will need any description. The children walk in procession under arched arms, being caught and made prisoners by the closing down of the arms. The dialogue which precedes the process is usupy given : How many miles to Bethlehem? Three score and ten. Can we get there by candle light ? Yes at d b ck again. Open the gates and let us go. Not without a beck and a bow. Here's my beck and here's my bow Open the gate acd let us g). The night is so dark we cannot see Thread the needle and go through. There are variations as in most children's songs. One version has Hebron and another Caledon ; some say midnight instead of candlelight ; but in all of them there is the idea of getting through city gates in safety. Hebron was a walled city in Palestine in the days of the crusade so also was Caledon. Threading the needle may may refer to the gate of Hebron which trona its narrowness was called the "Needle's Eye." Though the game teaches us nothing it becomes very interesting when regarded as echoing the days when the Crusaders were trying to rescue Palestine from the Turk,and when Hebron and Bethlehem orresponded to the Ladysmith and Mafeking of a few years ago. A M.

div.head: NOBLE HIISBANDMAN.
div.p: A NOBLE HIISBANDMAN.

Llertes is depicted by Homer as a typical Cheek noble. He owned much land, and took a per a_nal and practical interest in his property. Even in his advanced age, he worked in the garden, tending the beautiful and fertile vines for which Greece has always been nottel. Perhaps to-day, tome of the 60,000 Greek firmers mho toil in their vineyards that we may enjoy delicit us Currants, are descendants of the noble Leer-tea. At any rate their products are wcrthy of the best Grecian traditions. Tbe Currant— the little dried grape of Gretna—is a concentrated tit at. Where the Currant is, there is savouriness and nutriment. This ilex way of using it should interest you. HOMINY PUDDING.
2( zs hcminy, I—piut milk, 1 egg, loz castor sugar, .oz currants, aud half a teaspoonful vanilla flavouring

essence. METIIOD.—BoII up the milk and stir in the hominy, and allow it to stand for about an hour. Beat in the egg, sweeten to taste, and add the flavouring essence, also the currants. Pour the mixture into a buttered pie dish, and bake for about 20 minutes in a moder- ately heated oven. Dredge with castor sugar and serve hot.

A Profitable Hobby.—Honey, like everything else bas" g no up" and the high price it fetches makes successful beekeeping a profitable industry. It is one of the few agricultural pursuits at which women can do equally as well as men and perhaps bettor. For the country girl who lives at home, with a love of outdoor life it is an ideal bobby, and for the amount of work and capital outlay it involves it as more profitable than poultry keeping, fruit farming, and the larger agricul- tural pursuits. ft is, of course, only in districts favourable to the enterprise in the neigbourhood of fruit orchards and grass lands that it should be taken up as a business. As many as a hundred hives do not involve more than three or four hours work a day, but beekeeping, if it is to be successful must be studied beforehand,and everything connected wit hit thoroughly understood. The potential beekeeper can obtain useful information from the British Beekeeper's Association, 23, Bedford-street, London, W.C., or from any of its fifty affiliated associations, and expert advice would of course, be advisable before embarking on anything like an extensive undertaking.

They were told that amalgamation with Warrington wculd mean that greater hospital accomirodation would be placed at the disposal of Stockton Heath. The Warengton Infirmary, however, did not belong to the Warrington C,:rporatior, but was a purely vel rntary institution. " Persorally " added Mr Westbrook "I a culd rather run the risk of being taken to Dutton Workhou'e, to de in the salubrious atmosphere of Du ton, than be hurried off ta Aikin- street. ' (Laughter) Warrington would undoubtedly benefit by tskieg in Stockton Heath ; so would the County of Chester ty retainine her. Therefore they could say to the County and Rural District Councils, " Unless you listen to our appeals and have 931130 regard to the calls you make upon this parish, we will throw in our lot with Warrington." " Mr Westbrook concluded by moving a resolution ins' ructing the nealy-elected Parish Gunnell to go thoroughly into the Ties:ion of amalgamation in all its bearings and sub- mitthe result of their deiberations to the parishioners Mr 3 W &molder seconled the resolution. He pointed out that, as the one who proposed the holding of that meeting, be had no idea of trying to rush Stockton Heath into jeining Warrington immediately. The question must be considered in all its aspects. When they had to carry cut big schemes in a small place like Stockton Heath, the cost fell very heavily upon the ratepayers. The provision of op.fn spaces would eventually become a pressing necessity and if the expense of projeats of that kind were spread over the large area of greater Warrington the cost to Stockton Heath would be much less n-rd. ft was encouraging to hear that the rates were expeated to drop to the extent of 91 in the £, but they must allow him seriously to cl. übt that statement. goverument of Stockton Heath had not been what it might have been. He did not think there •gis another place of Eimilar size in the cmntry thit had a) msny cul-de-sacs. Mr Westbrook_: And there were no facts and figures. _ _ .
