Mr Clarke Perhaps it was mysel. (Laeghter.) Mr Bottomley and I have marl conversations on this matter. Of course, it wr s general knoeledge in the parish that we were having private meetings and I told him that the result war that if the Warrington Corpera- tion felt inclined to approach Stockton Heath it was very likely that the Parish Council would be willing to consider any preposition that was put before them, Mr Westbrook : May I ask the Clerk if he has got any minutes of such a meeting ? The C:erk (Mr E Bradehaw): No minutes of any resolu ion. Mr Blttomley next maiutaiaed that Stockton Heath had not received that consideration from the County Council to which it was entiled. lie had it on the autho.ity of a remember of the Parish Council that some time ago the County Council pissed a resolution that no person should be appointed to the position of teacher miles he or she had teen trained in Cheshire. That meant that teachers from Stockton Heath who, on the grounds of convenience and economy went to the Warrington Traiuiag College, were barred from accepting appointments under the Cheshire County Council. (" Shame.") That ought to be altered. A Voice: They are pretty well barred from gaining appolntmeuts in Warrington, even if they are trained there. Mr Bitchier : Isn't it a fact that the rule in regard to the teachers was broken as soon as it was made ? was on the board of menageruent and we certainly made appointments of teachers trained outside Cheshire. Mr Griffin raised an ineffectual protest against the exclusion of the fire equipment question from the dis- cussion on the amalgamation reselution. He indignantly declared that he was not going to be brow beaten and added "If this is your sy le of conducting meetings, it is a farce." Mr MoDermid said the question of amalgamation was not a new one, as far as the members of the Parish Couneil were concerned. For over ten years it had recurred annually. It was quite wrong to suppose that the benefits of annlgarnati in would .be entirely on the side of Stockton Heath. Warrington would trot promote such a scheme, at a cost of thousands of pounds, unless some advantage would accrue to the borough. Although Stockton Heath was sometimes sneered at and thought to be a little self-contained, there was not the slightest doubt that it would be a valuable asset to Warrington. Even under the present regime the'Parish Council had very full powers, if they e ere properly exercised. He failed to see,from the information at present available, that their position would be improved from a sanitary point of view by amalgamation. He thought Stockton Heath would compare more than favourably with any village in the kingdom in regard to its sanitation and ligh hag. The large increase of rates had prevented other schemes for the benefit of the village being carried through. Mr DEA KIN, while declining to pledge himself to any proposals, said that if the question had been thrashed out ten years ago • and negotia- tions opened with Warrington, the rates of Stockton Heath, under a system of differential rating, would have been very much lower. (" Question.") The village had grown to such dimensions that something had got to be done. Ho maintained that Stockton Heath should take the initiative and not wait for Warrington to make overtures. A deputation might m?et the Corporation in a friendly way to ascertain what that laccly was pre- pared to do. Not eithstanding the statement of the Clerk to the Rural District Council, he was afraid the rates would continue to rise if they remained under the present conditions. The cost of education was mainly responsible for the rising rates in Cheshire. Although they were late in the day in making overtures to Warringten,he believed they would secure differential rating. If their rates remained at the present figure for Len years it would be an advantage and, aided to that, Stockton Heath would be treated in just the same way as the rest of the borough. The two communities were so linked with each other that it was high time some step was taken. Mr Rose, alluding to the point raised .by Mr Bottomley as to a preference for Cheshire-trained teachers, said the managers of the Church schools pleased themselves whom they appointed. Mr Bottomley: That was not the question. It was a resolution passed by the County Council. The Chairman: The Church schools are under the County Council.

STOCKTON HEATH AS A COY DAMSEL.
NEW COUNCIL TO CONSIDER ANIALCAMA-
TION PROPOSALS.

St( ckton Heath seems almost as far as ever from knowing its own mind on the question of amalgamat- ing with the borough of Warrington. At the annual parish meeting three weeks ago there was every indication that the prcssure of the rates and contem- plated developments were certain to drive the pari-li to seek an end to its t: oubles by throwing in its lot with the municipality. Since then, a more cautious spirit has manifested itself and the Runcorn Rural District Council, to which Stockton Heath is a great ratepaying asset, is already dangling before the Heathens the prospect of a reduction of rat( a to induce them to remain under the wing of that authority. At the special meeting of ratepayers held in the Church Room on Monday evening, a res Aution was passed instructing the newly-elected Palish Council, along with other ratepayers whom they might wish to consult, to go thoroughly into the question of amalgamation in all its bearings and report their findings to the parishioners. An alternative proposition that the Council should approach the Corporation to ascertain upon chat terms they would be prepared to take over Stocktm Heath was lost by a narrow majority. 'There appears to be a feeling in some quarters that Stockton Heath would be such a valuable prize for Warrington to capture, that the overtures should come from the Corporation. Mr H J Westbrook voiced this attitude by likening Stockton Heath to a

who, having put up her hair and lengthened her frocks so far as golfing fashions would permit, was now waiting to be wooer'. They knew of one particular yi.ung gentletnan (Warrington) who was anxious to woo her, but he wanted to do it on the quiet. Before the damsel accepted him, she required some definite arrangement as to the marriage settlement Lt Warrington come into the open and SLckton Heath, having cAlsidered the terms, would dtc:de whether to leave the old parental home and throw in her lot

with the borough. The meeting was, for the m 'at part, of a hum-drum chat acter, but there were one or two breezy pa-sages Mr J Whitley, as chairman of the Parish Council, pre- sided over a large at[endance. The candidates for Pa ish Council hunotus made a foimidable array as they took their places on the platform. Mr II J Westbrook, who opened the discussion, frankly declared that, as a ratepa)er, be was not yet prepared to say that be was in favour either of Stockton ren aining as it was or of amalgamating with Warrington, for the reason that he was n,t, in possession of all the details that ought to be considered before toey took such a momentous and final ster. All he would pledge himself to, if elected, was that the questioa should receive the ()alien consideration of the new Couocil and that, after g( jug into the pros and cons, they vs ould report tee result to the parishioners : It was an error to state that the rates of Stockton Heath were 6s 2d in the .C. It was true that they were at present 33 Id for the half year, but there was no certainty that the cau.ses which had contributed to that figure would or would not operate in the future. Mr Westbrook went on to vote from a statement which had been supplied to him by the clerk to the Rural District Council. His only regret was that that statement had not been available long before, because it came as an eye-opener to him--he candidly confessed that he did not believe that there was BO much to be said in favour of Stockton Heath. If any.

body said that was the report of an official who wis interested in things remaining as they are, he would reply : " RernemLer the interested officials on the other side.' The statement showed that the amounts required

from the overseers for poor anl colt sty rata purpos3s iu the coming half year—and it, aces not likely that the sum would vary by more than one penny either way for some time—totalled 23. 2d. in the £ ;which included 4V.for general elementary education and 20. in respect or the naw Councfl school. Tire coatemplated enlarge- ment of the Council school, by the addition of two class-rooms, would not involve mere than .11 in the £ on the rates for the year. On the present basis of rating, even with that contingency, there was a reasonable prospect of a reduce ion of 3ii in the £. Dealing with the causes of the considerable advance of rates this balf-year, Mr. Westbrook painted out that the call on the parish was half a year in arrears, as far as the County call on the Guardians was concerned. f hat had to be put straight, and therefore they had to meet two calla in lieu of one—which would not occur again. With regard to private street works, while the ratepayers as a whole had had to pay back the loans sanctioned by the Local Government Board within seven years, the Cottacil bad allowed the property owners ten )ears in which to pay off their instalments, If the rat,pit3ers decided that, in future the property owners mu'', not be con:eded any longer period thin the Local Government Board allowed for the repayment, that course would be adopted. One ot the loans was paid last year, so that all future receipts from the property owners sffeoted, until the expiration of the ten years, would bear in fvour of a reduction of the rates. Another loan would be paid off in July next, and a third in two-years time, while at the end of December, 1917, there would not be a single one of the present Private Street Works Acts loans outstanding. There would consequently be en immense drop in the call on the rates under that head. The special call for the conning half year would he reduced from £6OO to £550 and the Clerk to the District Council added :—"I confidently anticipate that during the next two pars the special call upon the overseers will not exceed £550 in any half 3 ear, and unless something altogether unforeseen happens in the meantime, the ratepa3 era will, at the end of that time, most certainly have a reduction of hetween £5O ad £lOO per annum. The only poasible likelihood of any incresi i 0 on these figures is through furthtr building operations n the village and in such ease there would, of course, be an increased assessable va!ue derived from them to meet the additional expenditure." At the last meeting, continued Mr Westbrook, they were invited to make a comparison as to the rating of property, wh:ph he regarded as fallacious. He was not viewing the question from the standpoint of the man who lived in a house of over 40 airiesiable value, hut aS IT AFFECTED Tint MULTITUDIC, or the workingman. The rateable value of a 5s house in Warrington was £7 10s, and an 83 rate would there- fore represent £3 a year.ln Stockton Heath the rateable value was £8 153, because dash: basis of rAing was different, but on a 6s 2d rate, the amount worked out at £2 14s—a gain of 6s as compared with the house in Warrington. A 53 6d house in Warrington would have a rateable value f £9, and the rates would amount to £3 12s. In Stockton Heath the rateable value was £9 10s and the rates £2 18.3 7d. Accarding ta the state- ment of the Clerk to the Runcorn Rural District Council, provided Stockten Heath remained within that rural district, the ratepayers might rest en: jailed tbat the rates would not exceed and would probably be less than the following amounts per annum :—Poor rate including county and rural district council expenses), 4s Lel ; special sanitary rate, is 5d ; TOTAL ss. 10D.

It. was also confidently expected that the sanitary rate would be reduced until at the end of four years it would not be more than Is in the E for the year Dealing with the question of representation, Mr Westbrook said that if Stockton Heath were incorporated,it would probably be allowed to send three members to the Warrington Town Council. He did not think that would b 3 any substantial advantage, because Stockton Heath was the largest rateable unit in the Runcorn Union. with the exception of the Runcorn Urban district- its assessable value at Lady Day 1912 was £l69s2—and he did not think he was over-stating the case when he said that the Runcorn Rural District Council was nott so attentive to the requirements of the parish, that if scarcely e'er crorsrd a t or dotted an i in the resolu- tions that came from Stockton Heath. With regard to

div.p: FIRE PRECAUTIONS,

_ Mr Westbrook emphasised the fact that even if Stockton lica!h had Warrington resources at its command, there was the Ship Canal, with its constantly increasing traffic, to be crossed, and he would always advocate that there should he sufficient fire equipment in the village to place them beyond that difficulty. They were told that they in Stockton Heath depended upon War- rington for their gas and water eupplies. That was not their fault. If he was not wrongly informed, they had been

DEPRIVED OF THEIR RIGHTS with regard to the reduction of the price of gas by the Warrington Gas Act. As long as the Warrington Gas Company held the undertaking they were bound, after paying a statutory dividend of 10 per cent and provid- ing a certain sinking fund, to apply all surplus profits to the reduction of the price of gas. The Warrington Corporation had, however, got power to use the surpins In reducing the rates of the borough and, although that might not matter two pins to the Warrington rate- payer, it was of importance to outsiders in the monopo- lized area. Therefore, Stockton Heath had nothing to think Warrington for In the matter of gas, but had a claim for eouality of treatment. Concessions with regard to electricity would not he of much benefit to the workingman. As to the extra half-penny tram fare, it was a luxury and they need not pay it unless they wished. "My own opinion" added Mr Westbrook, "Is that the trams have been a great detriment to our health. Men we were bound to walk that Causeway, ye had a certain amount of compulLory exercise. Now we are getting LAZY AND LIVERISH

and it would praably do us gvod, if the fare were raised to threepence." (Laughter.) At the same time Mr Westbrook contended that Stockton Heath was unfairly treated by Warrington in the fixing of the

BIRTHDAYS THAT FALL IN APRIL. In January I wrote a little article which gave the names of some famous people who were born in that month, and a young and diligent reader who watches the children's corner with the greatest care, has reminded me that I did not follow it with similar articles in February and March. Of course I did write about David Livingstone, whose birthday was in March, but I have not mentioned any others. Two people were born in April in whom young people have a lot of interest, and I am sure everybody will like me to mention them. First I will place the Earl of Shaftesbury. Of course there have been many Earls of Shaftesbury, and as a matter of fact he was the seventh. But to us he will always be, I think, the Earl. He was born in London on April 25th, 1801, and belonged to a famous family. One of his ancestors had been a Lord Chancellor and a famous thinker, but our Lord Shaftesbury is more affectionately remembered, for he gave his life to help the poor and downtrodden. In his days much cruelty was inflicted upon children in the factories and he gave his time and strength to get Acts of Parlia- ment passed which would make the lives of the children easier. Little children were forced to work from early to late and often died at their work. Boys in those days used to be sent up chimneys to clean them and were often smothered by the soot, but Lord Shaftesbury was able to get that cruel practice abolished in 1840. He helped the ragged schools,and the coster mongers of London (whom he taught to be kind to their donkeys) always referred to him as " our Earl." I wish I had more space to tell you a lot about him for he was perhaps the best friend that the poor children of England ever had and when he died at the ripe age of 84 every poor man and child in our land felt that they had lost a close and dear friend. Another very kind and sweet life also began in April, for on the 21st day of the month in 1814 was born the Baroness Burdett-Courts. She was ()tie of the richest women in the land and devoted her life and money to helping the needy. She was also, like Lord Shaftesbury, a friend of animals, particularly of the despised donkeys. The poor creatures that were then so common in the poorer districts of London were often very cruelly treated. One plan which she adopted as a means of encouraging kindness was that of offering prizes for the best kept donkey. These com- petitions became very popular and as a result many hundreds of patient donkeys, which used to be ill-fed and cruelly-used ,got better food and care. I was glad to notice that in the new Liverpool Cathedral a memorial window has been placed to the memory of the good Baroness. And when you go to London you will see in the middle of Piccadilly Circus a fine fountain to the memory of Earl Shaftesbury. There are many other birthdays in April, such as, for instance that of Shakespeare our greatest poet,but I thought you would rather I told you a little about these two good people who did so much for the children and also the animals of the poor. OUR VERY OWN AEROPLANE. Oh! when aeroplanes are cheap ALd old nurse is sound asleep, Why, then you and I can have no end of fun. We shall spin along al fast As we see the world at last, flying ev'rywhere we like beneath the sun. When you watch how well 1 steer, There'll be nothing you can fear, As we race from English shore to Greece and Rome While no luggage we shall need, For I'll put on such a speed, That an hour from anywhere will bring us home. We'll have soldier Joe at hand Lest we reach a hostile land, And Jack Tar, in case we tumble in the deep; We'll take Doll, and Teddy Bear, But don't tell them yet, my dear, For we're bound to wait till aeroplanes are cheep. .-1). A. COURTNEY. THIS WEEK'S STORY. A DOUBLE ERROR. Possibly some of my readers have heard of Mr. Hamar Greenwood, who spoke at a political meeting here not long ago, and who is en accomplished orator. In the House of Commons at the same time was another member = who was very much like him. Let us call him Mr. Robinson. Robinson was a poor speaker, and he was therefore surprised one night when one of the magnates of the Liberal party implored his presence at a meeting in the magnate's con- stituency. Robinson very reluctantly con- sented, and the mystery was solved only when at the end of the conversation he heard the words, "Thank your very much, Greenwood." "But I'm not Greenwood; Robinson," was the reply; "so I suppose you don't want me now." The gentleman was embarrassed for a moment, and then departed, muttering," I'll see Greenwood; that will be all right." It so happened that Mr. Robinson went forthwith to a dressing-room to don his dining attire, and reappeared shortly after- ward, resplendent in starched shirt and dress coat. Again he was buttonholed by the man of wealth with the announcement: "I say, old man, I've just had a very funny experience. I went up to that ass Robinson, thinking it was you, and asked him to take a meeting for me; and, when I found out my mistake, I had a hard job to get out of it." The gentleman thus addressed smiled a cruel smile as he retorted, "Very likely; but do you know that you are still talking to that ass Robinson?"

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913.
WOMEN'S GHAT.

Clubs for Gentlewomen.—The need for clubs for working gentlewomen is felt in all our large cities and towns, and there is a welcome project in hand to extend this movement on the lines of the Lsdia International Club in lAr,ndon. This club, which has been in existence for some years, has accommodation for twenty-eight residents, and a large number of outside members. The annual subscription is lOs 6d, and residence with partial board costs about 21. a week. Members must be of gentle birth, and only women earning thair own living are accepted as residents. Whilst the club is self- supporting it does not aim at profit-miring, and is thus able to afford its members all the usual club privileges at a minimum cost. To some extent it solves the problem which confronts many professional wo.a:en of limi'ed ratans, that of finding a decent place of residence which combines comfort with social advan- tages. T;aining for a Career.—Parents Le!onging to the professional classes nowadays bestow more attention upon the education of their girls than was formerly the ittie and recognise that their reEponsibilities do not end ehea their daughters leave school. There are eighty to a hundred profession.; opm to the girl who from choice or necersity, has to support herself, and if she shows spy real talent in any particular sphere —music, drawing, art, literature or erly branch of science, the problem of finding the right way out of a possibly dull and penurious esistence at home is not a difficult one. She can make her choice and cont'nue her studies at the' v( cation classes" which are now Trade a B,ec'al feel ura at many of the large girls schools The difficulty arias with the girl with no special aptitude or gifts, ho has p,rharot no eager desire tn work but mast "d something." Unless guidanaa is forthcoming the probability is that she will drift into one of the most overcrJwded occupations. Paren's ahould realise in time that in there days of fierce competi, ion it is use- less looking for much in the way of pecuniary return for mere surface knowledge in anything. The Vogue for Beige.—The coleus known as keige is to-day quite duff rent fro-n what it was twenty-fire years ago. Then it was a dull nondescript and untecoming shade trjing to the most perfect com- plexion. Now it his an extensive range of charming and becoming tones. Tinged over so slightly with peso a shade is produced that resembles tiPoul ard when gold is used an effect results that may be mistal• en for rid gold. In addition there are the neutral tones of sand, putty and clay, all of which now come under the term beige. With tailors this colour is a first favourite just now and manufactir era have excelled in the beautiful materials in silk and wool they have pro- duced in all the tones enumerated. Black and silver fox, ermine and skunk all look well on biege, and black combinrs admirably with this col. ur. '1 bus a black hat, black shoes and gloves are worn with the smirtest biege tailored suite, the stockings generally matching the skirt.

The Influence of the Patch Pocket.- Fashitns in certain respects resemble the circles that surround a stone when thrown into some still calm pond and that appear en the surface far away from tLe cause of the commotion. For a vogue in one department of dress often results in introductions and Jhanvs in others widely removed from it. Thus the fashion of the patch rocket on this season's shirts has hrought about a demand for small coloured handkerclriefs and these are now to he had in every shade and make of silk and crepe de chic°, seeing that a pocket so conapicioualy placed must necessarily be furnished with daintiest of handkerchiefs. For those who consider these materials out of place as handkerci.iefa, diminutive [quires of lawn in every conceivable colour rre providei. The Teo Material Summer Suit.— rhere are ample opportunities for carrying out the fathionable two fabric suit in cottons of all descriptions, and thero is no doubt that these will be very popular. A delightful example is built of cotten filet ret for the skirt and a printed pattern fabric the same colour for the coat. In voiles there are brightly col mired Bulgarian designs, which, it must be admitted, are most harmonious in colouring, thus off 'ring a contrast to the mud run of crude Balkan tones. Voiles on small Pompadour designs are very pretty and effective. A catton crepe with silk embroidered border met between two tread strips of ratine deserves special mention. Tovvellings are this year teen cnly in cotton, their proper sphere, where they are at their best. Some are corded and show ato colour effect.

Shopping Practices.—Berlin is r€joicing in a series of new police regulations directed against disagreeable practices in shopping. The purchaser is not allowed to handle butcher's meat, flzh, taeon, or other provisons. All the handling necessary must be done by the shop- ever, and this under the most cleanly conditions* Milk must not be left on window-sills or doorways In uncoverzd vessels. Cook shops mu.tt not expose viands to the bacilli-laden dust of the roadway ani in timos of distress and unemployment food most not be placed within reach of the passer-by. These are but a few of the regulations directed against unhygienic customers. We in this ce untry, the land of the free, prefer to retain our liberty to being a pot ice-ricHen pe lie. We may reform oursolves but are apt to resent being refer tied by law.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

FALSE ALNRIIS. Reading in last Saturday's issue of the large num- ber of fire "calls," 1 was reminded of an expeitence in a South-cast Lancashite town aoout a d zen years ago. The local brigade had been ro-organi-ed and thoroughly equipped, and as the district to be served straggled over a wide area, an elaborate system of telephone call boxes was devised. For some titue this was a constant source of anxiety and expense. Three or four times a week "something went wrong w:th the works,' and the result was a false alarm of fire each time. At different h( we of the day aud night, the brigade turned out for what iepeatedly proved to be a wild goose chase, and the tempers of the men were not improved by the merci'ess chaff to which they were subjtcted by an unsympathetic public. Ultimately the authorities engaged as supatiutendent a fearless fireman who was also a skilful electrician, and he very soon had eve rythirg in spi)le pie order so that there were no more fa!se alarms.

CHURCH COLLECTION'S. The analysis of Warrington Pari,la Cherch collec- tions, which one of the wardens took the trouble to make, recalls the " Punch " joke of the crown piece looking with disparagement on the presence of the hambler threepen-y piece, wheron the latter rt marked, " Well, at any rate, I go to church much oftener than you do." It is suggested Oat it Ns ill soon be the smaller coin which will look down on the copper penny, and the peony will then be &Ile to make the same retort. Mr Isherwood's complaint or remon- strance le not s'ngular ; something of the sort has been heard at other vestry me, tinge. The Stanningley cuurchvva,dens report that during the past year ne fewer than 8,000 halfpennies had been found in the eol!ecti ores, which worked out at one halfpenny for at least every four persons who eontibuted ; and the Vicir of Newcastle observed at his veetry meeting that the sidesmen had to assist the churchwardees in bearing the large burden of bronze coins with which their collection plates were principally filled. A Wesleyan minister of my acquaintance has these t;mely comments. —" Giving to the cllecina is as much a part of worship as singing and praying. It is a Divinely-ordered institution and how well-to-do people, who think nothing of paying half-a-crown fora theatre or concert ticket, not to mention the sixpence for the picture palace, can satisfy themselves with giving a halfpenny when asked to help in the upkeep f their chtuch, we cannot,understand. We do not despise the poor man's copper Coin. God forbid! but it is the abler people, who can dress well, live well, and enjoy themselves" freely who fail in doing their duty. We hear a deal of the burden of the church's finances. It is not the burden uf the church, but the burden of pleasure and amusement that is telling on the people. THE RATES. Tuesday was" Budget night" here and the pro- ceedings of the Town Council somehow reminded me that at the National Lilos,ral Club a while ago 'Lord Stye and Selo rather neatly put it tkat if we lived in Laputa we could not have devis d a more curious system of rating than our own. By-the-bye, I think it was the young Liberals who once in a municipal programme issuel in the form of a public nnnifeato, had with reference to a proposal to bring home the amcunt of rates to small householders an interesting paragraph beginning thus :—" aimpounding for rates raises an intricate problem. On the one hand it allows the property owner,' posing as a large rate- payer,' to represent himself as the victim of every municipal ref rm involving expenditure out of the rates; and, on the other hand, it leaves the tenant unconscious of his own interest in such expenditure detracting from the weight of his advocacy of reform." Year by year we find the burden of the rates increas- ing. 1 read that since 1880 the rates per head of the population hive increased by 75 per cent, and every thing points to the cost Of local administration inc easing Meanwhile Warrington ratepayers may be thankful for the small mercies vouchsafed to them in view of the mu financial year. FLO 0 DS.

The recent high tides which caused some flooding at Bank Quay and Arpley set me thinking of a period which I spent at Tolmorden. Again and again during my residence there the main road for miles was under water, looking preci,ely like a canal; the cricket- ground—which is really beautiful for 6i•uation and the eLnvy of many visitors—was likewise subrneiged ; and occupants of cottages abutting upon the highway had to flee for safety to the upier rooms. 1 had not myself lived in the town six months before the lower part of the house was inches deep in water owing to a sudden rainstorm. Natives and inhabitants who have been in the locality long enough to profit by experience, have a sort of slot made at the sides of the doors, and into this, in cases of emergency, they drop a protecting board, making up the interstices with wet clay. A supply of the litter is always ready, of course, and when the rainfall is abnormal it is quite common fur bowie- h( lders liable to flood to sit up into the small hours of the morning to keep an eye on the rising waters lest they should b 3 taken unawatei. They tell me, how- ever, that thinrs have much improved since the incorporation of the borough, as the anthoriiiiis tale care to ke.p the river bed deep and free from debris. Anyhow, I had some high old times when I lived there. woiked in an office with the flood-water lapping the steps at the entrance, and more tb4n once I had to scramble up the railway embankment and walk along the track in order to reach my home, the ordinary thoroughfates being solooded as to be quite impas- able. MURDER.

In a former reference to the subject I wrote of suicide as " self murder," and so in Jeed it is. I am of course aware of the too pervalent practice of assuming that every suicide is insane. Both these plays were also tragedie° of character. Othello was a tragedy of love, stall and driven to fatal distrust. Lear was the tragedy o' passioo, of fatherly love and filial ingratitude; Macbeth was the tragedy of evil, reckless ambition,,°l remorseless and remorseful ambition. This and MI "Merchant of Venice" (concernirg which I venture° an opinion on a former occasion) are being essayed by the Sbakspere Commemoration Society at the Royal Court Theatre here, and the undertaking is as car mendable as it is bold and ambitious. We can hardll have too much Shakspere.

She now resided at 1, Synge-street. She had not been comfortable for five years. She did not nag her husband. She admitted, in answer to Mr Steel, that she had on one occasion refused 28s one week, but added that she refused it because she wanted to press him to give her 6s more which he owed her. She left him on the 28th March. She had had one separation order over three years ego, but went hack to the defendant after eight months. Evidence having been Tilled as to the defendant knock- ing food which complainant's mother had brought in, off the table.—Deiendant said his wife had refused money, and on three occasions would not have food.— Mr Steel said all the bother bad been caused through the wife refusing the 28s.—The magistrates granted an order with an allowance of 10s per week, the Cnairman remarking that it was to be hoped the parties would come together.—Defendant : I can tell you before I go that she won't get a penny.—The Cierk : Come back. Do you know how to conduct yourself in a court of justice.—Defendant : I beg your pardon if I have done anything -vrong. PARASITIC MANGE.—William Fairclough. Boarded Barn Farm, Burton wood, was summoned for failing to notify parasitic mange on March 17th.—Superintendent Forster said that it was owing to the delicacy of the defendant's health that the animals were not reported. He was a good farmer and looked after his stock, and he suggested that the case be dismissed on payment of costs.—The magistrates adopted this coarse.

div.head: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. THE PADGATE-IEiTERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. THE PADGATE-IEiTERAGE SCHEME.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednes- day.Mr G Mather presided and there were also present: —Rev A M Mitchell, Dr Murray, Messrs W Houghton, A Brooks W Furness, P Longton and J Ball, J Sutton (clerk),B S Newcombe (surveyor), H H Burnage (assistant surveyor), F Kerfoot (inspector) and Dr Sephton (medical officer). The minutes of the General Purposes Committee, which were confirmed, included a letter horn the Clerk to the Padgate Parish Council enclosing that Council's protest against the proposed sewerage scheme for Padgate. At the request of the Medical Officer the following resolution which was passed at a parish meeting on March 17th was read :—"Resolved that in view of the fact that either of the schemes sub- mitted by the Rural District Council will cost, in the first case, considerably more than the rateable value of the township, this meeting cannot approve of either of the proposed ocher,- es and agrees to resist to its utmost the forcing thereof. That any accumulation of sewerage matter in the brooks in the township he removed by a systematic cleansing of such brooks." Mr A BROOKS stated that when he joined the Council 15 years ago a scheme was submitted at a cost of £5,000 by the late Mr W Owen, but the cost prevented tbe scheme being carried out. About two years ago the Surveyor prepared a scheme which was quite out of the, question to-day because the site selected as a sewerage farm was now a suburb of Warrington and had been built upon. in addition there was no other land available for fllteration purposes. Ever since he had been a member of tha Council enquiries had been going on at the instance of the Local Government Board, and two years ago that authority hinted that something should be done. The Council requested the Local Government Board to tell them of other flat lying places similar to Padgate, which had got rid of their sewerage difficulties. The Local Government Board replied that the better course to adopt was to consult an engineer. That was done, with the result that one scheme was reported to cost 5s in the and the other minor scheme 3s in the £. The Council had every sympathy with the ratepayers in their opinion. It was against either of the schemes recently outlined. The vital statistics of the parish showed that it was not in a serious condition and would compare favourably with any part of the district. He moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr Furness seconded and they were confirmed. VOTES OF THANKS.

The CHAIRMAN informed the members that Mr A Brooks and Dr Murray would no longer be members of the Council. They had been connected with the authority for a long time, and he regretted that they had not sought re-election. Rev A M MITCHELL, Messrs FURNESS, BALL and HOUGHTON spoke in eulogistic terms of the two gentle- men, Mr MrrciiELL observing that when they lost Mr Brooks they would lose the best member they had. Votes of thanks having been accorded the officials,Mr HOUGHTON proposed a similar compliment to Mr Mather for his conduct in the chair during the past 12 mc nths. This was seocrided by Mr BROOKS who said that when- ever Mr Mather had been Chairman things bad always gone off happily. His bluff, hearty and humorous manner, had got them out of many difficulties. Several toembers also spoke and Mr MATHER in reply said he believed Mr Houghton was the oldest member of the Council and the vote proposed by him gave him special gratification. Mr Furness, the vice-chairman, was also thanked.

MEASLES AND EDUCATION. Sr. HELENS PROBLEM.

The discussion by the St. Helens Health Committee of the reckless way in which measles have been spread, so as to cause a serious epidemic in the town and a largo number of deaths, has resulted in the committee passing a resolution that where a cwe of measles has occurred in a house all contacts shall be excluded from public elementary schools. The committee hag also passed a resolution expressing the opinion that the present practice of granting a half- holiday to school children on average attendance is liable to induce children who are ill to go to school, and is therefore prejudicial to the health of the children generally, and that the Education Committee be requested to consider the advimbility of altering the system on which the holiday is granted.

div.head: KILLED BY MOTOR-BUS.
div.p: KILLED BY MOTOR-BUS.

A verdict, of "Accidental death " was returned at Widnes on Monday, on Henry Bailey, an ironworker, 35 years of age, residing in Nelson-street, who was killed on Saturday night in Waterloo-road by a motor bus. The jury recommended the Corporation to instruct their bus conductors to get off the car and see there was no obstruction behind before the car was reversed.

Mr T Craik, deputy town clerk, expressed the Cor- poration's regret at the occurrence. Thos Harrison, the conductor, said he gave instrnc- dons to the driver to reverse at Hutchinson-street. He saw the two men standing in the road, and he tapped at the window for them to get out of the way, but apparently no notice was taken of the bus backing to turn round.
The examiner, Saturday, Aptil 5, 1913.

div.p: LECTURE.—On Saturday night the second lecture held in aid of the " Arethusa and Chichestef Training Ships and Refuges for Homeless and Destitute Children "took place at the Grammar School. On this occasion the lecturer was Mr H Deighton, of Man- chester University, who delighted a good audience with the able manner in which he spoke of "A journey to Lapland." The lecture was made more interesting by the exhibition of a large number of excellent photo- graphic slides taken by Mr Deighton. The costume that the lecturer wore when on his journey in the icy North was also a cen.re of attraction to the young people. On the proposition of Mr G L Welford, seconded by the Headmaster (Mr C H S \Vinson), a hearty vote of thanks to the lecturer was passed. 0 UGHTRINGTON URCH V ESTRY.—The Easter vestry meeting of the Oughtrington St Peter's Parish Church was held in the vestry on Monday, the Rector, the Rev E P Wethered, M.A., presiding. The accounts which were in a satisfactory condition were passed. The Rector again nominated Mr T J Ridgway as his warden, whilst Mr George Teller was elected people's warden. The following sidesmen were elected, Messrs P Rarcsdale, W M Shaw, C Weave, T Clark, T Ridway, W G Jones, J 111ollineux and W Limb. Hearty votes of thanks were accorded the churchwardens, sidesmen and members of the voluntary choir, special mention being made of the efficient manner in which the wardens had seen to the carrying through of the extensive repairs to the outside fabric of the church. Among others things brought up for discussion was the churchyard extension, it was announced that about 1;20 more would be

required to complete the work. AN IRISHMAN'S STRANGE MISHAP.—Whilst in con- versation with other persons in the Anchor Inn,Booth's L) mm, last Sunday night at about 9.30 a young Irishman wishing to emphasise a declaration he had just made brought down his hand with a bang,rot on to the table as he had intended, but unfortunately on to his glass, which of course was shattered, one of the pieces severing the main artery in the man's wrist. Blood at once flowed freely and with the assistance of a compatriot they hastened to Dr De Jong's surgery. On the way a lady tried, but with only partial success, to stop the bleeding with a handkerchief. The doctor and his son did their best to stay the copious flow, even cutting the arm higher up and endeavouring to tie the artery but their efforts were doomed to failure. A car was therefore requisitioned and the man, who was in a very weak condition owing to the loss of blood, was taken to the Warrington Infirmary where his condition is fairly satisfactory. WOMEN LIBERALS—ANNUAL MEETING.—In connec- tion with the Lymm Women's Liberal Association the annual meeting was held on Thursday night in the Primitive Methodist School room. A new feature We year was a tea prior to the meeting; and the efforts of Mrs J Edwards, Mrs R W B Whiteway, Miss Barker, Miss D Barker, and Miss Welford, to provide for the needs of the members was much appreciated. After tea the annual meeting was held with Mrs Dodds of Penketh, the president, in the chair. "The Hon. Secretary. Mrs Wyatt, gave the annual report. Miss Welford, the bon treasurer, in dealing with the finances announced that they had a substantial balance in hand. The following officers and committee were elected for the ensuing year :—Chairman, Miss Welford; hoe treasurer, Miss Mclntyre ; Committee, Mesdames Barnes, Brearley, Champ, Daniels, Edwards, Mort, Seymour, Wright, Wyatt, and the Misses Barker, Smith and West. During tie evening songs were rendered by Madame Sara Silock and Mr Dutton, who also sang the duet "The spider and the fly." Votes of thanks to the president and the vocalists were recorded. BIBLE SOCIETY.—On Friday, the 23th ult., the Lymm Branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society held its annual public meeting in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. The chair was taken by the President (the Rev R W B Woiteway), who read a letter of apology for absence that he had received from the Rev G B Thurston, M.A.—Mr D Mort (the lion secretary) gave his annual report, in which he stated that they hopad to be able to pay more attention to the Heatley end of the district by holding a meeting in Ougntring- ton schools next Autumn.—The boo. treasurer (Miss Moston) read the financial report. Whilst regretting that the receipts were behind those of last year, she stid they had made a better start this time and could con- fidently promise an increase at the next annual meeting. The Rev T A Wolfendale, M.A., gave a most beneficial lecture on "Bits of China—old and new." With the aid of some photographic slides, beautifully tinted by a Japanese artist, he conducted his audience on a tour commencing at Hong-Kong and proceeding through such places as Canton, Amoy, Shanghai, Pekin, Tientsin and.,on to Che-fu, in which one had glimpses of Chinese life on land and water. He laid special stress on the great day of opportunity that China was now offering Christianity. A vote of thanks to the lecturer was proposed by Mr Milne, seconded by Mr H S Brown and, carried wite applause. Mr W T Moss was the lantereist. A collection on behalf of the funds of the society was taken up. CHERRY-LANE ORGAN FUND.—For the purpose of supplementing the funds for a new organ tbe members of the Cherry-lane Independent Methodist Chapel held a public tea and concert on Wednesday night. The Tea Committee, composed of Mesdames R Hewitt,T Hewitt, W Mercer, W Mort, Rathbone, Reditt, and the Misses Mercer and Rathbone, are to be complimented on the large and choice supely of edibles which were largely appreciated by a largo number of friends present. After tea a concert was held, presided over by Miss Welford (in the unavoidable absence of her father, Mr G L Welford). After the singing of a hymn and prayer had been offered by Mr Mort, Miss Welford gave her address in which she spoke chiefly on 'The relationship cf music to the church.' The remainder of the programme was of a miscellaneous description, consisting of a. pianoforte solo by Mr H Mercer (the accompanist of the evening) ; pianoforte duet by Miss and Mr D Holt ; songs uy Miss bliaw, 'The song that reached my heart,' and Killarney ' ; by Mr J II Brazendate, The Round- head' and • The Arrow and the Song' ; and a Scotch song by Mr D Holt. The Misses Furnival and Hughes sang the duet 'The Spider and the Fly,' which was encored. Recitations were cleverly given by Miss Most on, "The Legend Beautiful " and A Little Quaker Sinner,' and as an encore Abou Ben Adhem.' Humour and pathos were provided by Mr Furness with tne recitations 'The Nomination,' 'My Grandad,' and 'Ab o'th Yates Speech.'

MAY QUEEN CONCERT.-Still endeavouring to reduce their adverse balance the May Queen Committee held another concert in the Congregational Schoolroom on Tuesday night. This time the entertainment was supplied by, according to the posters, "The Barcelonas " who, on the programmes, appeared unaer the disguise of various kinds of Emits." Attendance at the concert however revealed that, with a few exceptions, the bulk of the artistes were members of the Lymm Orpheus Society. As a choir they gave the varied assortment of such part songs as rne two roses," My love is like a red, red rose,' "The beleagured," Come where my love lies dreaming," A sailors' chorus,' The baby on the shore,' Good-night, ladies,' and the glee Strike the lyre.' It was a pity that the length of the programme pre- vented the instrument quartet (Miss Shaw and Messrs H Burrell,F Champ and B Hargreaves) from giving Mas- cagni's `lnterruezzo,'as their playing of 'Duo, 'Slumber song,' and Northern song' was ranch appreciated. Mr Hargreaves' violin solo was also well applauded, as was his vocal solo Polly Wolly Doodle (chorus by the limits?) Miss Hind gave several whistling solos, her 'Anchored' being enoored. An amusing quartet The Catastrophe' was given by Messrs W Dixon, It Dixon, J Ellis and 3 Moss. Miss A McHugh's pleasant voice was heard to advantage in the solos Somewhere a voice is calliag," Come,Bill g to me,' and 'The coming of a dream.' Mr J H Brazeudale (the conductor) was as popular as ever with his songs The arroe; and the song,' 'l'll sing thee songs of Araby,' and the encore The water melon,' in which the audience cheerfully rendered valuable assistance. Other solos were Off to ?hiladelphia,' by Mr W Dixon ; The Motherland,' by Mr J Moss. Mr Franklyn Taylor, the humorist, was well received with his first item A visit to Blackpool,' an encore being demanded, and given in the form of another Lancashire item Old Eli goes to hear Elijah.' At a Inter stage he gave The Registrar.' Proficient accompaniments were pro- vided by Messrs F Champ and J Webb, jun. MOORE.

WESLEY GUILD.—At the devotional meeting on Wednesday evening, an addrcss on " The Sunday school teacher, his ideal and motive," was given by Miss B Dutton. Miss Dutton said that though her experience of Sunday school work was long it was not very varied' she had only had a class of toys in a large city, and a class of senior girls in a village school. Miss Dutton portrayed a beautiful ideal of Sunday school teacher, which will be copied by every teacher. Mauy of the Moore teachers were present, and as was expressed by Mr Lawton at the close, greatly benefited by Miss Dutton's words. This was the first meeting of the session and was splendidly attended, there being about 40 present.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

PARISH CHURCH VESTRY MEETING. The annual Easter vestry meeting was held on Mon- day evening the Rector the Bev G B Thurston presid- ing. There were also present Messrs A W Callender, W Evrart, H Pearson, H A Burrows, A Watkin, J Coxon, J U Lister Farrar, W II Burgess, ‘7%,' G Lecomber, T F W Dixon' C S Broadbent, J Ardern, R Heathcote, G Bennett, R Oliver, G W C Hartley, R B It Hartley, A B Richardson' C Richards, W E Hillier, L Thomason, H E Odber, G C Rixon and F E Evans. At the outset the Rector intimated that the really important church meeting would be held in the schools on Thursday, when he would go into the new finance scheme and the parish could elect lay representatives. I The financial statement was submitted by Mr A %V Callender. The churchwardens accounts showed that the year was commenced with a balance of £2 lOs 641 The receipts included church fees. £23 3s 3d • special I offertories, £230 4s 54 and general offertories, £179 41 4d. After all expenses had been paid there was a deficit of £6 Is 6d. The total funds dealt with were £486 13s 3d. Mr Callender did not think much of the deficit because Easter was very early and there was quite two weeks difference in the accounts. The only extraordinary expenditure had been in pointing the fabric of,the church. It vita neces- sary that the work should be done, as the rain was coming through. There had been an extraordinary expenaiture ot about £lO. In regard to the assistant clergy fund, the total subscriptions were £6B 16s 6d, the parish subscribing slightly over £43 and there being £25 given by the trustees of the Fox estate. The amount carried forward was £22 lOs Id. After expenses had been paid to the extent of £93 19s, there was a deficit balance of £2 Hs 7d. That, commented Mr Callender, could not be considered satistactory. There was a deficit of £4 12s lid on the choir fund. On the motion of Mr Coxon seconded by Mr Lecornber the accounts were passed. The Rector remarked that the support given to the curacy fund was very miserable. The work of the parish was well done, to the satisfaction of the parishioners. It was only possible for him to do tee work he did with the help of the Rev Horace Gray. To be Rector of a parish like Lyrum was a difficult position which met with very little sympathy. He wanted them to consider very carefully the support givtm to the Assistant Clergy Fund. Were they to go on advertising at the risk of getting someone and not heing able to pay him? Was he to struggle on and try to do the work single handed? It was impossible to go on paying £9O and only getting .£45 in subscriptions He knew it was very easy to criticise, but they should consider the question very carefully. A lengthy discueeion took place in which one gentle- man said that to have no curate was unfair to the girls of the parish sshereupon the rector retorted, "We don't have a curate in the parish just for the girls." Another member said it was not the intention of the parish that the Rector should be saddled with the responsibility of finding £lBO for a permanent curate. Several views were expressed, one being that the parish should take upon itself the matter of engaging a permanent curate. It was also exp'ained that several years ago they raised £6OO for a Caracy Fund at a bazaar and the suggestion was that the same could he done again. Ultimately it was decided that the present arrangements be f' dhered to and at the same time keep in their minds (1) trying to secu i a permanent curate and (2) trying to secure an income for a pe-manent curate' A vote of thanks we I accorded the Rev H Gray for his valuable services, which were to be appreciated by

The Rector, in supporting US vote of thanks, said that Mr Gray had given very material sssistance in pre- paring the large number of the confirmation candidates, in addition to his other manifold duties, which he performed willingly and conscientiously in the parish, A vote of thanks was also aecorded Mr Cooke, the organist, and the choir which, it was stated, had improved considerably, chip fly owing to the energy and time directed to it by Mr Cooke.

div.head: CHURCH OFFICERS
div.p: CHURCH OFFICERS

The Rector nominated Mr A W Callender as his warden and paid tribute to the excellent manner in which he kept the accounts of the church. Mr Coxon seconded and Mr Callender in reply said he had always endeavoured to do his utmost tor the church. (Applause). On the proposition of Mr Watkins, seconded by Mr Beckett, Mr F E Evans was elected people's warden. The following sidesmen were elected :—Messrs W G Lecomber, J G Lister Farrar, R Oliver' Ward Hartley. The Rector nominated Messrs J 1' Mines, T F W Dixon. William Beckett and R Heathcote. . .
Mr W N Molesworth was unanimously appointed to audit the Church accounts,.

A resolution on Welsh Disestablishment was moved by Mr C Stidston Broadbent and carried unanimously without discussion :—" That the Vestry meeting of the parish of Lymm emphatically r, otests against the Bill which seeks to disestablish, dismember and despoil the Church in Wales to the extent of £l5B 000 per annum of her revenues after the present life interests are extinct as admitted by the Earl of Crewe in the House of Lords, and prays that on its reintroduction into Parliament during the present session, it be dropped." The resolution to be sent to the member of Parliament for the division and to the local press. A vote of thanks was accoried the Rector for pre- siding.

div.head: CHURCH PENANCE
div.p: CHURCH PENANCE

On Thursday evening a well attended meeting of the Lymm Parish Church Electors was held in the Pepper- street schools, for the purpose of discussing the need of an organised system of Church Finance. The Rector, the Rev G B Thurston M.A., was in the chair and was supported by Messrs Beckett, Broadbent, Burrows, Callender, Druce, Evans, Farrar, Hartley, Milne, and Watkin.

The Rector after clearly ds fining the need of a more organised system of raising the Church Finances spoke on (1)," The Representative-Church Counicil " 13th century, describing the constitution of both the Northern and Southern Convocations. He also spoke of the House of Laymen formed a few years ago, and after describing how (its members were elected, said that when these three bodies were sitting together, and were supported by the people,they formed a very strong force. (2) "The scheme of Church Finance." He said that there was urgent need for a new system of raising mcney for church work, as owing to the change of conditions that had come about within recent years the usual subscriptions were not so easily obtained. In fact be stated that the contributli ni to the various diocesan objects had gone down from 30 to 40 per cent. With the purpose of meeting these needs the Diocesan Conference had formulated a new scheme of finance, which he very lucidly explained. He claimed that it would enable the poorer members to take part in carrying on the whole work of the Church, for whereas at present they did not subscribe because of their only being able to afford small amounts, they would, under the new envelope system, be able to pre- sent their offerings. He said that it would also be of mutual value to the parishes. Discussion being invited, the following gentlemen took part :—Mr A W Callender, who thought that the new scheme would be as difficult as the present one and said that what they required was s willing band of voluntary workers. Air A Watkin said he saw diffi- culties in the way,especially in relation to over-lapping, but as the scheme bad been made by the best brains of the Church he thought it would be most impertinent not to support it ; Air W M Beckett, who raised ques- tions about the parochial funds, and the keeping of the accounts, Alr Farrar, Air Ardern and Dr Burrows. The Rector replied to the various questions. The matter of the Chrarch Council was brougut forward and several resolutions in connection therewith were passed by the electors. Messrs Hartley and Broadbent were appointed lay delegates to the Ruri-decanal Conference.

SPECIAL MISSION AT PHIMITIVE METHODIST I CHURCH —Last Sunday Mrs Johnson Wright of New Zealand, formerly of Lyrnrn, commenced a series of special evangelistic services in connection with the Primitive Methodist Church. In addition to preaching at the morning and evening services Mrs Wright also spoke at the Sunday evening lantern service. Each evening during the week Mrs Wright has conducted special meetings. On Wednesdfty evening both Mrs Wright and Miss M .1 Appleton sang solos. The audiences have been very satisfactory and encouraging results have been achieved. BUCK LOW Gt; AILDIANS' ELECTION.—After being deprived the pleasure of utilising their voting privi- leges at a Council election this year the ratepayers appear to be taking a keener interest than usual in the election of two representatives to the Bucklow Board of Guardians. The two retiring Guardians are Mr Samuel Davies and Mr Samuel Wallin Gould, both • gentlemen having represented the Parish of Lymm for the past nine years ; they are opposed by Mr Thomas Frsderick Walpole Dixon. All three gentlemen together with Mr W G Groves and Mr Lockyer have been recently returned unopposed to the Lyrum Urban District Council. Polling will take place to-day between the hours of 12 o'clock noon and 8 o'clock in the evening. The polling stations are as follows :—Booth's Hill Ward, Zion Chapel schoolroom, Cherry-lane ; Heatley Ward, Infants schoolroom,Sandy- lane, Oughtrington ; Lymm Ward, Boys' schoolroom, Pepper-street; and Statham Ward, Infants schoolroom, Statham. It is expected that the result will be known about 9 30 this evening.

div.head: PENKETIL
div.p: PENKETIL

FRIENDS SCHOOL.—An interesting entertainment was given in the Lecture Hall of the above school on Monday evening, Mr W. E Brown (headmaster) presiding. The entertainer was Mr J Spence Hodgson of Didsbury, this being his eight annual visit to the chool. He was ably assisted by Miss Ethel Walters (piano), Messrs Russell, Brown jun. (violin), and Herbert Hodge. The recitals included "The painter of Seville," " The forsaken merman," "Solomon Popkins," " How we choose our ministers,"" The bootlaces," and "The society for washing the negros white," all of which were greatly appreciated by the company. DISTRICT COUNCII. ELECTION.—A sucressful meeting was held on Wednesday evening in the Infants' school- room on Wednesday evening, in support of Mr P C Garnett, who is a candidate for thr District Council election. Mr W Woods presided, and supporting him were Dr Murray, Mr W Davies and Mr Jolley (vice- chairman of the Warrington Board of Guardians).— A good feeling prevailed throughout the meeting.—The best thanks was given to the retiring Councillor (Dr Murray, also to Mr Jolley for bis visit to Peuketb.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

Paisri COUNCIL.—A meeting of the Winwick Parish Council was held in the schoolroom on Monday. Mr P Longton presided. Others present ware 'Messrs Wallace, Hambleton, Shaw, Alker and Gerosa (clerk).— The Clerk read the minutes of the previous meeting, and the accounts were presented and passed. The allotments question was discussed and reported as going forward satisfactorily.—A letter was read from the Town Clerk of Warrington, informing the Council that the Warring- ton Corporation had no power to rim a motor service to Winwick. The condition of the Dolph was mentioned, and a letter from the Surveyor (Mr Newcombe) was read to the effect that he would see that it was looked after. The condition of the roads, roadsides and footpaths was brought forward and it was understood that the County Surveyor would enquire into it. Mr Shaw proposed that a complaint be made about the waste paper from the Longford Depot blowing about and frightening horses along the road. Mr Hambleton brought forward the Lighting, Burial and Housing questions. These were discussed at some length, it being eventually decided to bring them up at the next meeting, and to get full particulars and to lay them before a special meeting of parishioners.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
THE FIRE BELL COMEDY. Firemen paid at last for 1911 Fire.

The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held in the Hall Cafe on Tuesday evening. Nr G Pilling presided and there were also present :—Messrs J McDermid, J R Wood, F Rose, J H Clarke, J Hallows, F Pearson, J Whitley, F Warburton, W Mcintyie, G F Ashton (clerk), and S

Wright (surveyor). The Clerk read correspondence with the Clerk to the County Council with reference to the fixing of the fire bell, permissson having been granted for the alarm to be fixedt emporarily near the Church Institute. Nothing had been decided with togurd to the bell being fixed near the police buildings. Mr Mclntyre said Mr Westbrook had had an inter- view with Mr Parr, one of their County Councillors, whose opinion seemed to be that the best thing to do would be to send a deputation from the Parish Council to attend before the Standing Joint Committee. Both Mr Parr and his son were members of that committ2e and the question of the bell would come directly before them. Mr Pearson : It is with a view to having it attached

to the police station. Mr Mclntyre: Yes. Mr Clarke : Both Mr Parr and his son will do their best to assist us in getting it in that position. Mr McINTYRE rhey seem to think that a deputa- tion from this Council would have some weight and with their assistance some move will probably be made

in the matter. Mr Whitley had seen Mr Parr who along with his son promised to do their best to get the bell fixed at the Police Station, which was where they desired it to be. Mr Hallows : 1 should strongly object to a deputa- tion going to the County Council lor I think we have a certain right to put it there-- The Chairman: Wait until the time comes when a proposition is before the meeting. Mr Hallows: It is a funny thing that whatever I say and wherever I say it I am not in order. The Chairman : There is no proposition before the meeting, so you are not in order to-- Mr Hallows : I was only sing I should object-- The Chairman (sharply): Wait until the time. '1 here

is no proposition before us. Mr Clarke proposed that Mr Mclntyre as chairman of the Fire Appliances Committee, and Mr Westbrook act as a deputation to meet ,the Standing Joint Committee. That was the best course•if they were to succeed in that business. Mr Pearson seconded. They all knew that a com- mittee was not so strong in a matter of that kind as a - personal interview with the persons controlling the question. He knew that when they had had deputations to Dutton they had generally succeeded in arriving at what they wanted. The Chairman : You see letters have been forwarded and they have had no effect yet. Mr Whitley : After the conversation with Mr Parr I think the course we have adopted will be the best. Mr Hallows : After Mr Clarke s explanation, i am quite willing that a deputation should go. The proposition was carried. Plans were passed for the rebuilding of Mr Bottoinley's house in 6rappenhall-road. There was only a slight alteration from the old plans. On the minutes of the Fire Appliances Committee appeared the arrangements for the temporary fixing of the bell and a resolution to the effect " that in the event of the Cheshire County Police Authorities still adhering to their refusal to allow the bell to be attached to the new police building as before, negotia- tions be entered into with the Parish Council of Stockton Heath for permission to erect the bell on the post near the po:ition of the existing fire station on Victoria-square. It was also resolved " that James Baguley and William Wightman (two firemen) be paid 10s each for their services at the fire at Mr Starkey's house, Lomb Brook, in June, 1911." The question of having a fire alarm bell say at the Police Station Stock- ton Heath in direct communication with the Fire Brigade at Wilderspool Brewery, was discussed and left over for the present. Mr Mclntyre in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the bell was only fixed temporarily. It was on private ground and would be subject to some charge. A great deal would depend on how long the bell would be there as to what the probable cost would be. The Chairman : How is it that the payment of this lOs has been such a long time ? Has it been over- looked. Mr Mclntyre : it has been overlooked. The Chairman : It has never been asked for ? Mr Mclntyre: No. The minutes were confirmed. Mr Whitley said he supposed by that meeting they had come to the terminus of their existence— (laughter) —well, so far as that committee was concerned. They would be very remiss in their duty if they did not pass a cordial and hearty vote of thanks to the chairman, for the splendid way in which he had conducted the business of the committee during the year. They were advanc- ing in Stockton Heath and it was time they had additional members at Dutton and on the County Council. Their ratable value was higher than that of any township in tho Runcorn Rural District Council and he thought they were entitled to every advantage they could possibly get by additional representation on the district or County Council. Mr Pearson seconded and the chairman, briefly replied. DISPLAY OF DANCING.—At the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath on Saturday an exhibition of fancy dancing was given by Miss Olga Hughes's pupils. The programme included exercises,tambourine and skipping dances which were very charmingly given. A pas seul was beautifully danced by a little girl. Miss Hughes received a beauti- ful bouquet from the children.

POLICE CHANGES —On Tuesday the police force in the village was increased by the drafting to Stockton Heath of Sergeant Wilding and P.C. Booth. ST THOMAS' BAND OF HOPE.—An entertainment in connection with St ihomas' Baud of Hope was held in the Parish Room on Monday evening. A pianoforte solo by Miss Annie Perks was well receivtd. Miss H Acton sang two songs very tastefully, and Mrs White- man gave a recitation with ability. Mr Hough con- tributed two humorous songs in character, and was recalled each tim 3, but the chief items were two action songs by 16 girls, who had been trained by Miss Hallows, namely the flag drill and patriotic song, both of which were received with applause. A humorous sketch "Repairs while you wait" given by the Misses C Vernon and Wheeler and Messrs Hatton, Livingstone and Kelley, brought the entertainment to a close.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

SOC I AL.—A very enjoyable social evening was held in Orford School on Thursday March 27th. Dancing and games were indulged in until about mid-night. Songs were given by the Rev G Vale Owen, Messrs %V Povey, jun., and A Mayer. Messrs Samoa( and Brandreta officiated as M.C.'s. Mrs It G Brandreth was the accompanist. The social was promoted by the Sunday school teachers in aid of the vicarage tuna. CHILDREN'S CONCERT.—A children's concert was held in Orford School, on Friday last. A very good pro- gramme had been arranged by the Sunday school teacheis,consisting of choruses,songs,recitations,dances, a sketch "Washing day " and a farce " lei on Pane Francais" (" French spoken here ") by soma of the members of the Sunday schoool. The proceeds were in aid of the:vicarage fund.

div.head: EARLY CLOSING OF SHOPS.
div.p: EARLY CLOSING OF SHOPS.

Sir,—l was surprised to see in the " Examiner of Saturday that there had been a petition from the shopkeepeis in the main streets of the town respecting the hcurs of closing. I should like to know how many of the shopkeepers signed that petition and also by what authority the Health Committee have the power lu regulate shop boors. If a few of the shopkeepers find that they do little business between the hours of seven and eight o'clock on Mondays and Tuesdays let them close at 7 o'clock by all means, hut why should those who are busy during these hours be compelled to close': Surely there is such a thing as individual liberty. Sliopkeepeps in Warrington have enough to contend with. Enormous rents, heavy rates and taxes, the competition of the Co-operative Stores, and larket, the cheap trains to Manchester and Liverpool, which take a great deal of money out of the town, all combine to make it a struggle for the average shopkeeper to pay his way. It needs only this arbitrary interference of the town officials to add the last straw to his burden.—Yours, etc.,
MAIN STREET.

div.head: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON SOCIETY.
div.p: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON SOCIETY.

Sir.—l understand that some people have been asking if this Society is dead. I am glad to be able to assure any anxious inquirers that it is alive, but I am sorry to say it is far from well. It is suffering from lack of a secretary. Those who have served it s') veil in this capacity are unablo to continue their services. The Society's most active supporters and hardest workers are all of them very I,usy men and cannot give the necessary time to the work, though they retain their warm interest in the cause.
Will yo u give me the hospitality of your columns to ask if there is not some young man in the town who would be willing to take up this work and throw himself heart and soul into it ? _ _

_ If such an one can be found, I am sure there is a great future for the Scciety and a good work to be done The honorarium the Committee can offer is but small but the work, to one who cares about the welfare of the town and the happiness of the people, is of absorbing interest. May I ask any who wish to know more to communi- cate with Mr J Longland, Egypt-street.—l am, Sir, tour obedient servant, MORLEY STEVENSON,

div.head: WARRINGTON AND STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND STOCKTON HEATH.

Westbrcol- in the course of his excellent speech cn this matter made use of an illustration to the effect " That Stockton Beath was like a buxom ycurg damsel who NS as being vicced by a suitor—hu teloie accepting maiiiage wanted to know wha the roarriaize settli ment wculd be." Well, i appealed to me seeing that. Warrington had no yet approached Stockton Heath " that the buxom young damsel was a most forward young minx—for it was really she who is first of all suggesting the idea and making the proposal for marriage." Bowever, I don't blame her for her forwardness. It's only her -way. How is Stockton Heath like a buxom young damsel? To some extent it is true she is fair to gaze upon arid when dressed in all her summer's best in Natures garb she certainly is pretty. But nevertheless she must not expect Warrington to consider her as "buxom "as she represents herself to be and not expect to be received at her own valuation. As a matter of fact what has Stockton Heath to offer to Warrington? Warrington does not depend upon Stock ton Heath, but Stockton Heath, on the other hand does depend in a great measure upon Warrington. What about her water supply? Her gas supply and her tram service, &c.? Nay more, almost every resident at Stockton Heath obtains his livelihood in Warrington and spends most of his waking hours there. Stockton Heath, after all, to give it its due place and title in this hemisphere, is simply ore of Warrington's garden suburbs and one of its "bedrooms."

My candid opinion is that Stockton Heath has much to gain over the question of amalgamation and when Warrington does seek to' woo ' her let her be thankful to be received as a member of the family. At present she is under the dominion of the Rural District of Runcorn and is consequently "cribbed, cabined and confined" by a "rural" policy, whereas under the government of Warrington with a Town Planning Act, she would expand to greater glury and be even a more delightful place to dwell in than at present. What is really wanted in the controversy over the question of amalgamation, is less of the commercial spirit in bargaining as was shewn by some of the speakers, and more of the spirit of patriotism and loyalty fostered between the two districts, so that an improved Stockton Heath and a Greater Warrington be the outcome.
Let the banns be published, the marriage ceremony performed, and the wedding bells rung, so that :..tcckton Heath be made happy and contented.— Yours faithfully.
E. ENGLAND.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The smartest and most up-to-date programme for some time has been presented this week at the Hippodrome. Exceptionally large audiences have assembled twice nightly and displayed their approval 'by deafening applause. "A double's troubles" is the title of the funniest, smartest and neatest sketch which is presented by Potts Bros. and Co. "As much alike as two peas" is the general expression in regard to the Bros. W. W. and Chas. Potts who cause the audience to go into hysterics over their laughable predicaments. The theme is a very good one. There is the newly married couple and the visit of the cousin who so much resembles the bridegroom that the hride herself is mistaken and treats the cousin. unconsciously to the delights of a spoon, thinking she is in the arms of her husband. As a finale she is confronted by both and the curtain falls with her in the arms s3f the cousin. There is a distinct American tone about the turn and the audience is in one con- tinual state of boisterous merriment. A musical turn such as is supplied by the Five Tritons cannot fail to please all who delight in hearing various musical instruments played with ma: ked skill. There is a beautiful setting to the scene, the tubular bells being encircled by myriad lights. As manipulators of the saxsphone, xylophone, and the lyric. the Tritons are highly successful, their execution of "My Hero " from the "Chocolate Soldier " being warrrly applauded. Anna Hana is an American entertainer, with a capital knowledge of how to solicit successfully the approba- tion of the audience. She gave the two ragtime songs " Robert E Lee" and Ragtime Cowboy Joe "in a manner which thoroughly captivated everyone; even the stallites swayed to the rhythm. Billy Brown is a 'clever comedian with an abundance of good stories. The gag of the "fiddle " which is present throughout, is very good, and Brown justly deserved the encore accorded .him on the occasion our visit. Jimmy Danvers and Eva Rosslyn score a decided success in a vocal pianoforte absurdity "A Pant mime Boy." The facial expressions of Danvers cause roars of ,laughter, whilst the dashing style of Miss Rosalyn is worthy of commendation. Will Sullivan is a popular Lancashire comedian ; Agnes Tina is a clever mimic and impersonator. and The Twelve Rainbows give a turn reminiscent of pantomime in a delightful manner. The various effect 3 are very artistic, particularly those of the butterfly. A pleasing duet is also creditably given.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The programme for next week will include Walter Bird's West End Co. in comedy sketch, "Three Knocks"; May Erne (Ambi-Pe-Dexter) assisted by Erne Chester, "He of the voice" ; Herbert La Martine presents the Four Cheries, in a variety interlude; Zellini. comedy juggler ; Chris Van Bern, in novel original mystical monologue; the De Mayos, commediennes and ragtime dancers.; Kittie Douglas, commedienne and dancer; and John and Lilian Grand vocalist and character actors.

This year an invitation is given to any who are interested in the housing and sanitation of the town.

Dr Coote Hibbert is to lecture in the Council Chamber on Thursoby evening at 7.30. The Mayor will preside and an invitation is cordially extended to the general public to be present. The title of the lecture is " t!oine essential points in the health work. of the Borough and the need for the public co-operat- ing therein." Another lecture has been arranged by the Education Department for the benefit of the parents of school children. .It is to be iilustrated and the subject is '1 'he care of the teeth." Mr Hedley Taylor, the school dental officer, is to give the lecture at the Bolton Council School, on Friday at 7.30. The Vicar of Christ Church (Rev G C Briggs) has promised to preside. Such a kctuie ought to prove very timely, for the maintenance of sound teeth is essential td physical efficiency. The Health I\ eek programme certainly gives scope for a lot of quietly useful work. Its success now depends upc:n cue co-operation of the general public.
