HEALTH WEEK
A FOREWORD FROM THE MAYOR.
WARRINGTON'S SLUM PROBLEM.

Warrington is entering into the" National Health Week "campaign against disease and dirt, which opens to-morrow (Sunday). The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) was yesterday asked by an " Examiner " reporter for a foreword on the local observances and courteously complied with the request. "The main objects of the movement" said his worship" are to teach those people who are ignorant on such important matters— and I am afraid they are a very numerous section of the community—the primary laws of health and to give them as much informa- tion as possible on the keeping of them. The points on which stress must be laid include home hygiene, cleanliness, ventilation, the selection and storage of wholesome food, cooking, and the inculcation of a generally healthy mode of life." His worship confessed that he is not altogether enamoured of such projects as the provision of penny baths for workingmen. " We want" he said " to teach people to live clean, healthy lives, and not, as it were, to allow them to ,do things by proxy. The great point is so to impress people with the importance of following certain rules of health, that they will be only too eager to do things for themselves. Any other course would be simply doing harm, instead of good. lAre are all agreed as to the objects to be attained, but I am afraid there is some differ- ence as to the means of bringing them about." Asked for his opinion on the visitation of slim districts, which forms part of the Health Week programme, his worship said he believed it was capable of very useful development. His only regret was that it was not done regularly and his suggestion was that members of the Council and health workers might group themselves into three or four detachments to undertake the periodical visitation of specified areas. " And what do you think would be the outcome of such a system ? " asked the reporter. _ _

"Well, it is not so much what we can say or do on such a visit that I regard as important." replied his worship. "The chief thing is to let the dwellers in those districts see that we take an interest in them and that we are watching them. They would then be more likely to be more careful and to take an interest in their surroundings. If the people think nobody is taking any notice of them, it is not likely that they 'willS try to better themselves. On the other hand, if visitation of those districts were a regular thing, a certain number of the inhabitants, at any rate, would brush up and make their homes as tidy and clean as possible. It is the moral effect rather than the actual material assist- ance that counts."

As to the extent of the slum problem in Warrington, his worship expressed the view that, on the whole, Warrington was faced with a much less difficult task than many similar towns. "That, of course" he added "is due to the fact that we had been work- ing steadily for some years to bring about improvements in that direction. I think we have a:very'good chance of practicallyabolish- ing our slum districts, from a structural or sanitary point of view, but we should still have to treat slum habits and the problem of the lives of the people wno have had to dwell in the darker places in the town. Still, I don't think Warrington is as badly off as many places." THE LOCAL PROGRAMME.

div.head: Cookery Campaign.
div.p: A Cookery Campaign.
Arrangements for the celebration of Health Week are now complete and a brief summary of them will be fonud in our advertisement colunms.

Interest will centre largely in the cookery campaign, which may be looked upon as rather a Warrington speciality t The Agenda Club is helping this particular effort by supplying a new leafltt for circula- tion. This has just been brought out by the National League for Physical Education and Improvement. It is entitled " Food and drink." The idea is to send this round through the mothers' meetings together with the cookery recipe card issued by the War- ringon Committee. ,

Throughout the schools of the town lessor,s will b 3 given by the teachers on various health topics. Many of the clergy and ministers 1611 be preaching on the Sunday in connection with the celebration, while the Senior Bible Classes attached to the Established Church are arranging to have addresse 4 also. The Free Churches are to hold a united meet- ing for both men and women at Wycliffe Church at 3 o'clock when Mr P M Oliver still give an addiess The Adult School also will give lecturettes on the Sunday morning. Both the Mothers' Welcome and the Cripples' Guild will be thrown open to visitors on Wednesday, the former in the afternoon and the latter in the evening. div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT.
£5OO SALARY TO THE MAYOR.
At the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening a salary of £5OO was voted to the Mayor to meet the expenses incidental to the Royal visit to Warrington in July. _
The alderman and senior councillor of each ward have been constituted a reception committee, with power to add to their number, to make the arrangements in connection with the visit.

div.head: BOWLING NOTES.
div.p: BOWLING NOTES.

The bowling season in Warrington promises to be even more successful this year, and before long all the greens in the town will be thrown open. Some of the gieens which had been opened formaliy on Easter Monday wets closed again on account of the weather, and the general opinion that it was too early to com- mence the Eeason.

A tour of the most important greens in the town has revealed the fact that all are in fine condition, having been tended and cultivated during the months when smokers and annual meetings are the only signs of activity amongst the bowling associations.

The Liberal Club Green in Bewsey-street is indeed a treat and reflects great credit on Mr Clay who has devoted a large amount of time and energy to the velvety sward- The Horse and Jockey green, the headquarters of the Works Amateur Bowling Associa- tion presents an inviting appearance and testifies to the care and ti..ne expended Jon it. The greens adjoining the various hetels in the town are nearly all fit and ready to accommodate the numerous eager and enthusiastic trundiers in the town.

We have received the following information from Mr W Patrick the lion secretary of the Works Bowling Association. That the entrance fee for the inter- works cup competition which was so successful last year and which was won by Fletchers Moulders over Howley Tannery, will be 68. per team. Entries must be received by the secretary to-night (Saturday.) The first round will commence on April 19th. All players to be registered at the same time of entering teams, and any works having more than one team entered, the players for each team must be registered separately to the secretary. Eighteeu names only can be tegistered for each team. When entering teams please notify secretary of any data or dates your team cannot play, otherwise they will have to play on date arranged at Cuuncil meeting.

We shall be in a position to publish the draw next week and during the season special reports \via appear in the " Examiner" week by week. Notes and comments on games and players will be con- tributed each week by " Thumb Bias."

One of the most popular event 3 of the season is the Peter Peacock Challenge Cup competition held under the atn-pices of the Warringtin Liberal Association, which will shortly enter, upon its second season. Members intending to join must give in their names to tha ward secretaries or to Mr E A Sanders at the Liberal offices not later than Thursday next. An entrance fee of Is covers b th the cup competition and the annual main. New members are invited to join the ward committees and participate in the bowling competition.

The Warrington and District Bowling Association will continue its activities, and interest in this organ- isation promises to be as keen as ever. The following is a list of fixtures : April 26 to May 17, Ist Round Championship. May 31 to June 7, 2nd Round Championship. June 7 to 14, Ist hound Consolation. June 21 to 28, Semi-Final Consolation. June 14, 21 and 28, Handicap. July 12, 19 and 26, Semi-Final Championship. August 2, 9 and 16, Individual Merit CompAition. August 23 Final Championship August 30, Final Consolation Soptecuber 13, Official's 11.mdicsp.
There will be a council meeting of the Association on Tuesday evening dt the Pelican Hotel, to commence at 8 o'clock-
We are promised a summer equal if not better than that of 1911, so the prospects for a jolly ,season are exceedingly r sy. "THUMB BIAS."

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. The "Quaker Girl."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. The "Quaker Girl."
I

The popularity of musical comedies shows no signe of decreasing. Large audiences have been the rule throughout the week, and much enjoyment has been; manifested in the performance of The Quaker Girl ' by Mr George Dance's Company. The critical theatre- goer will discern evidences that the production is not quite up to the level of what one usually expects 'roil) Mr Dance's companies, but there are some promising young artistes in the cast this week who have not been seen here before, and who interpret the numerous cap- tivating roles in the popular musical comedy with a degree of enthusiasm which eclipses min or blemishes. The adventures of Prudence, the Quaker maid, in her transition from the village to "Gay Paree," are as enthralling as ever, and one cannot fail to appreciate the dainty way!, sweet smging, and admirable dancing of Miss Ellie incent in the title role. She is admirably supported by Mr Louis WigleY as Tony Chute, the American naval attach 6. Mr Wigley has effected a complete mastery of the American accent without any tendency to exaggera- tion, and his dashing love-making and unceasing drolleries form a notable feature of the comedy. Mr Ken Worth hardly rises to the level of some "Jerries we have seen, but he is always assiduous and mirthful as the queer Quaker lad whose parents were "5° opposite." An excellent Phoebe is Miss Rita Everard who sings, smirks and dances with a whole-hearted abandon which earns hearty plaudits. She scored heavily with her witty songs " Or thereabouts," and "Oh Jerry," as did Miss Vincent in the popular numbers "'lake a step," and " lony from America,' Mr Jack Gray plays the part of Captain Charterie very pleasantly, and sings, with fine effect in the duet with the Princess Mathilde, (Miss Vivienne Gower), whose entry on the scene is always a pleasing interlude. , The exacting role of Madame Blum is• interpretea with much skill and unmeasured vivacity by Miss Elsie Skillings, while a notably clever iinpersonation: of the droll chief of police is given by Mr Montt Macdonald. Mr R Dunn is much too melancholy for Minister of State with a penchant for flirtation. The singing of Mr Chas. Cautley is a pleasing feature of his "Prince Carlo," and the familiar refrains of "Come to the Ball" and "Colour de Rose" were heard to much advantage through his tuneful vocalisa- tion. The chorus singing and dancing is all well done, and if the dressing and mounting of the piece, did not show signs of travel, the whole production might earn a much higher rank of merit.

NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Next week there will be a unique attraction in the shape of a romance of the Western plains, entitled "The round-up," which is described as "the real thing in American melodrama." A " round-up " America is held three times a year, and is for the purpose of bringing together all cattle and horses on the ranch (which, in many cases, covers an area of I' and 100 miles square) in order to separate the young from the old, the males from the females, and brand same, so that in the event of cattle wandering away on another range, or being stolen, the owner cau identify and claim his property, the brand, of course, settling the disputes. The term " round up "is also used by Westerners in scouring the country for cattle thieves, outlaws, deperadoes, &c, and in this sense i 9 used to describe the plot of this play. Mr J Mcßride will appear as Arizona Dan. The play will be' presented twice nightly.

ASYLUM PATIENT'S STRANGE DEATH. An inquest was held at Winwick on Thursday, by Mr F A Jones, deputy coroner, on the body of James (53) a patient at th 4 asylum, who died on Monday."-It appears that vbhilst getting his dinner on the 25th March, Kelly snatched a piece of pudding from another patient's plate, crammed it into his 'mouth and began la' gasp for breath. An attendant named Thompson telephoned for the medical officer and in the meantime tried to clear the man's throat. Dr Hopwood and Dr Rodgers (assistant medical officer) arrived and PI Hopwood cleared the mouth, hut deceased stopPe" breathing. The doctor also performed tracheotoelY, and Kelly came round. Pneumonia supervened an"' death was due to that complaint, accelerated by cbok: ing.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental d eath," no blame attaching to the attendants.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913. COUNCIL UPROAR.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, April 5, 1913. COUNCIL UPROAR.
COUNCILLOR LASHFORD'S ALLEGATION OF FAVOURITISM. Charge oT 'lnfamous Lying."

The Town Council meeting on Tuesday evening lasted four hours and provided several noisy scenes for the amusement of the ratepayers who had assembled in strong force. One of the most piquant subjects of discussion was furnished by the attempt to draw from Councillor Las Mord a full statement of the grounds upon which he alleges that favouritism has been shown in the distribution of Corporation contracts.

The minutes of the Health Committee showed that attention having been drawn to the remarka of Councillor Lashford at a recent meeting of the Town Council, in which certain allegations were made. as to the acceptance of tenders by this committee, it was resolved that he be invited to attend the next meeting, and that he be requested to supply the committee with the necessary information to enable his statements to be investigated. In answer to a letter from the Town Clerk, Councillor Lashford said : "I do not consider that the committee have any right to sit in judgment on this case. If they are anxious to have this matter investigated I must insist upon it being investigat d in open Council, or in public." The committee expressed their regret that Councillor Lashford had refused to give them the information to enable his allegations to ne thoroughly investigated, and expressed the hope that he would give the Council at the next meeting, the information which he stated he had in his possession. Alderman JAMES EVANS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that if the suggestions contained in the report of Councillor Lashford's speech were true, the health Committee were shockingly guilty. So sericus were the allegations that no committee worthy of the name would have passed them over without some comment. All the committee desired in inviting Coun- cillor L,ishford to attend the meeting was to obtain all possible information, after which a full explanation of the question of letting tenders would have teen laid before the Council. They never intended to sit in judgment upon Councillor Lashford. It was the desire of the committee that the facts should be published,and they were determined that the matter should be investi- gated. Ile invited the Councillor to make his statement in open Council and in the presence of a large number of ratepayers, and he would give his promise, in the name of the committee, that full inquiry would be made into all the information given and the explanation sub- mitted to the Council.

Alderman Buirrus seconded, and said he hoped Coen- cillor Lashford would give a full explanation of his allegations. Councillor LASH FORD : It will be short and sweet. Continning,he said he was rather surprised at the letter he received inviting him ,to appear before the Health Committee. He did not see his way clear to attend. Had he been invited to appear before an impartial committee he would have been there. Of course (sarcastically remarked the Councillor) the Health Committee could do nothing wrong. The matters to which he referred went so far back as August 11th,1939, when the committee authorised the Medical Officer to obtain prices from local firms for the hupply of 30 blankets, and left the acceptance of the tenders to the Chairman and the Medical Officer. He believed the Medical Officer went round to local firms, but which he could not say. Two tenders were submitted to the com- mittee, but he was not going to supply the Council with names at that juncture. 'the firms were asked to tender for all-wool blankets. The tender that was accepted was for a union blanket, contrary to specification. On September 21st 1009, or at a meeting prior, some members expressed dissatisfaction end urged that advertisements should be issued for GO pairs of blankets The specification was for an all-wool blanket, so that they were not satisfied with the union blanket, although they had accepted the tender. Word was sent back that the tender for union blankets could not be accepted because there was a squabble in the counnittee.Thitt was the unfairness and why he had raised the objection. On the Gth October, 1909, after advertising, the committee gave the tenders to Mr Clegg and Mr Dutton one for Os 9A and the other for Os 2d, so that the Council saw how tenders could be worked. Had his proposition at the last meeting been carried, every- thing would be done in a straightforward way and above board. There was too much favouritism in tenders. If the Council wished to have the names an impartial committee must be called, and he would appear before it. He could give the committee more than they wished to hear. It was all right for Alder- man Evans to fay that his committee was this, that and the other, end that it could not possibly do wrong. They all knew it was a bright committee. Alderman JAMES EVANS : I submit that I never made any such statement. Councillor L ASHFORD : You said the committee should be Licked out of the Council. _

Alderman JAMES EVANS : Yes; if they were guilty of such things as you alleged. Councillor LASHFORD : I don't know why I should be asked to appear before the committee. The MAYOR : Where else would you go? Councillor LASTIFORD : Before an impartial com- mittee.

The MAYOR: You said in your letter in open Council or any other public place. Now you say an imp irtial committee. I _don't see that that could be public. Councillor LasHronD : lam giving a reason. The MAYOR: IMlhy do you alter your opinion ? Councillor LASH FORD : If the Town Clerk asked me to go before an impartial committee it would have been quite right, but I have given particulars in the open t...ouncil, which I thought was the best plan. The MAYOR : Bur, you said you would not give names.

Councillor LASHFORD : I shall not give names. I have given you 601310 names. I have told you how the tender finished up and the dissatisfaction of tha other gentleman. Councillor BROADHURST :_Who is that?

Councillor LASHFORD : Yes, you would like to know. You know as much about it, as I do. you were on the Llealth Committee at the time. I may well tell you you soon forget, and so you do. I think I have explained as well as I possibly can. I have given you every information I know, except, the names. My grievance is in the first part of my speo:th. Alderman TINNION : I don't understand it.
The M AYOR : 1 don't think there is auy allegation to nnswer.
Councillor 13RoAmiurtsT : Hear, hear. The 'Si A VOlt : That is all I have to say with regard to Councillor Lasliford.

Alderman .I:l3,tEs EvA:cs hoped the Council would refrain from oiscu.siog the matter further. The position of the committee had been put feebly, he admitted, because of his personal feeling and condition just now. Councillor Lasnford had Explained his own position and he (Alderman Evans) thought that in all fairness the discussion should he allowed to end for the evening. He did not wish to prejudice the councillor's position or to have anything that he (the alderman) might have to say trenched upon that night. The allegations against the Health Committee were serious, but they would be answered at the next meeting of the Council. Councillor BRoADHLIIST said he could safely leave the case in the hands of the chairman of the committee At the last meeting of the Council Councillor Lashford made a certain statement about him (Councillor Broadhurst) to the effect that he belonged to a clique. Those remarks were so serious that he could not allow them to pass without a reference. Unfortunately the only clique which he had ever belonged to was the clique which put Councillor Lashford into office. Ihe clique which he (the speaker) belonged to now was thai, which had to slave every day for a miserable pittance. Couucillor PEmnErtToN : Shame. _

Councillor I3ttoADHuRsT : As Councillor Lashford has not withdrawn that statement, I am going to brand it, as it deserves, in good sounn English, as an infamous lie. If that is unparliamentary, Mr Mayor, I withdraw it. (Laughter.) The MAYott : It is.
Councillor BROADHURST : But I have said it, sir. I say to Councillor Lashfurd that he is an infamous liar. The MAYOR : Order, order.

Councillor BROADii-rRsT : 1 withdraw it, sir, but I have said it. (Laughter.) I say that for a man like Councillor Lasbford to sit in that chair and to describe me, as he did at the last meeting. after the faithful services I rendend to him is shameful on his part. I am not going to answer any of the ridiculous state- ments be has made to-night. The committee will answer them in public, but I am going to say this-- Councillor LAsTiFoliD : May I rise to a point of explanation? Councillor BRoADHURST : I will allow you anything. Councillor LASH FORD : Had it been legal I would have paid Councillor Bron.dhnrst for his assistance at the last election. Councillor 13RoAnnutisz : I have given my services gratuitously. 1 don't want your payment. I could ~:ay more about payment, but I won't. (Cries of " Order, order.") Is it right that a gentleman—l won't say gentleman, Mr Mayor—but is it right for Councillor Lashford to sit there and accuse me of belonging to a clique because I won't vote as he wishes me to vote, and for him to make a statement of the description be has made because I won't support two members of the Council and ex-members? The MA YOR : This is all irregular. Councillor BROADHURST : It is, Mr Mayor— (laughter)—and so were his remarks, but he was not made to witbdraw them. I will not allow Councillor Lashford or any other member of the Council to charge me as he is doing. He says I have a forgetful memory. I have one of the most retentive memories there is in this world—(laughter)—and 1 will meet him In his own ward:on this subject. (Co Councillor ILashford) : Are you prepared, and we will settle our little difference ? Alderman TINNION : Siturday afternoon at three. Councillor BRoADHIMST : We will kick off then. (Laughter). I should advise Councillor Lashford to think twice before he opens his mouth, because he always puts his foot in it. The members of the Council could tee that Councillor Lashford was short of word,

div.head: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB. Is the Popularity of Cycling Waning P
div.p: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB. Is the Popularity of Cycling Waning P

With the advent of numerous other summer attrac- t' ons, the pastime of cycllng, as far as the Warrington Cycling Club is concerned, seems to be waning in popularity. The secretary's report submitted by Mr C A Berry at the annual meeting of the club held at the headquarters, Patten Arms Hotel, on Thursday even- ing, showed that in order to meet the changed conditions the club has had to deviate somewhat from its primary object and cater for the social and howling interests which have come so much to the fore of late years. The large attendance over which Mr (4. g Anderton (captain) presided showed that interest in the club was as keen as over. _

-.-- - In an attractive review of the club's doings, the hon. secretary (Mr C A Barry) said the past season had, generally speaking, been a successful one and, while there have been a turther tailing away in the attend- ances at club rooms it was cause for congratulation that the social and bowling side of the club's activities had bean well supported. The club was as strong numerically as at any period of its existence, the 'membership standing at 107, which represented an increase of three on the previous season. It had with success passed through that transitional state which was at present being faced by other cycling clubs aith records in the world of sport perhaps much more brilliant than that of the Warrington club. While they were with anxiety endeavouring to solve the problem of the c eatinuance of club life activiti4s, the War- rington club had recognised the difficulty and by the loyalty to old traditions and the good fellowship of its members, bad been able to divert that falling away in cycling interest to the social sphere of club life. The club, in its social activities, was stronger than at any period during its long career, and the prospect of its ccntinuance as a valuable and useful institution were bright. During the pact season' they had the vilest sample of an English summer within their recollection. Con- sequently there was some excuse for the somewhat meagre attendances at club runs. There were 29 runs down on the card,2s of which were carried out,and four were abandoned through weather arta other causes. The average attendance worked out at eight for Saturdays and Thursdays combined, and three for Thursday alone. The prizes offered for the runs were awarded to :-1, J B Poole ; 2, C II Hoult ; 3, C A Berry and G II Anderton. Cycling es part of the club's programme was certainly on the decline, and they had to face the fact that they were moving back- wards in that department. The remedy looked for had been "new blood " and, while new members jiining were the right sort, they were not cyclists, and their appearance on the road could not be looked for. In past seasons the interest in cycling had come and gone, and returned again, but the prospects of any great enthusiasm in that direction in the future appearea to be remote. Something was expected with toe advent of the motor cycle, but club runs did not appeal to the "knights of the petrol tank," and only on occasions had they seen their motorist members during the season. While recognising the decline of cycling as put of the clue activities, cycling in the club was by no means dead, and it was pleasing to ncord that there were a few enthusiastic members who were ready to take advantage of an attractive and diversified list of runs which was care- fully compiled at the beginning of the season. The development of the social sine of the club, in which more members could take an active part, appeared to be the line left open upon which to work. Toe bowling interest which had so well developed in recent years and had undoubtedly helped attendances at club runs was even threatened. They had as an attractive com- petitor a local bowling club, in which nearly half their members were keenly interested. One did not raise that point with any feeling of rivalry, but in an endeavour to present the real position to the members who had the welfare of the club at la arr. The various events of the season were then passed under review' special reference being made to the successful Whitsitntide tour into Skropshire and to the annual visit to Beeston 'lowers, at the invitation of the worthy president, Mr John Naylor. On July 11th, 12th and 13th the members of the club were actively engaged in assisting the Infirmary Old English Fair. In the cause of the Infirmary the club had from time to time done yeoman service and this time they excelled any of their past achievements. It should be recorded that the members of the club were an important factor in the organizing and bringing to such a successful issue of the second M.P.F." Old English Fair, which resulted in the making up of the million pennies, together with a very substantial surplus. Thanks were accorded to Mr W Unsworth for allowing the club the use of the bowling green at Sankey on Wednesday evenings of the season. It %sae with sincere regret that he had to record the death, which occurred with tragic suudenness, of Mr Sam Hassell. He was a regular attender at the Sankey bowling meetings and was the holder of the Watkins Cup. On many occasions he contributed to their musical eveniags and, while being a very popular member he was an intimate friend of n lareo number of their musical friends. His loss would be 'deeply felt. Reference was also made to the death of an old friend of the club, Mrs Delmage, wife of Mr Delmage, an ex-captain.

After thanking Mr Barleigh for his courtesy towards the club, the secretary stated that the club's monetary affairs were in a satisfactory condition. The year's expenses, which were rather heavy, had been met out of revenue and the substantial balance at the bank had not been enerowhed upon. (Applause). Mr W H BELLIAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said no report was ever more comprehensive or more frank. Mr Berry rendered valuable services to the club, the report testitying to the diligent and assiduous manner in which he did his work._

Mr W LurroN seconded. The compilation of the repirt must have involved considerable time and thought. Mr. Berry improved every year and was indeed a valuable asset to the club. ,(Bear, hear.) The report was adopted. The FloN. TansutiEß (Mr F Garnett). submitted his report and balance sheet which showed that the year was commenced with a balance in hand of li7 lid. The total receipts were ±:3l 12s lld and they finished the year with a credit balance of Is id. The total balance in hand is £3B 04 Bd. On the proposition of Mr JAMES CRITCHLEY seconded by Mr W P AsirroN, the report was adopted.

div.head: OFFICIALS.
div.p: OFFICIALS.

The retiring officials were all heartily thanked for their valuable services, Mr BERRY proposing and Mr C E Hout.ifroN- seconding a vote of thanks to Mr G If Anderton (captain). The following officials were elected for the ensuing year :—President, Mr John Naylor ; Captain, Mr J B Poole ; sub-captain, Mr II Whittle ; hon secretary, Mr C A Berry ; hon treasurer, Mr F Garnett; committee, Messrs G H Anderton, A G Robertson, C E Houghton. H Smith, F Fieldhouse. T P Throssell and C H 'knit ; N C.A. Delegates, Messrs CA Berry, J Critchley and J B Poole.
A discussion took place as to whether the club should remain affiliated to the N.C.U. and it was decided to do so.

Mr H Cows, the secretary of the Infirmary Million Penny Fund Committee, thanked the members for the valuable aslistance they rendered at the Old English Fair. Votes of thanks to Mr and Mrs Burleigh for accommodation at headquarters and also to the Chairman completed the business.

COMPULSORY RETIREMENT OF CLERGYMEN. Remarkable statements were made by Rev Charles Davis, vicar of St. Thomas, Nottingham. He declared that he had applied to every Theological College in the United Kingdom for a curate, without a single reply. Curates were as rare as the dodo, he said. It may seem heresy," the vicar added, " but funds entrusted to the Church are badly and wastefully used. The highest and best offices are choked with old men, who have done their life's work but still hang on to their positions, keeping younger men away. One often reads of bishops or vicars dying at eighty or ninety. "A sweeping law is wanted compelling every man, whether bishop or curate, to retire at seventy. There are plenty cf able men ready to step into the livings of these ancient men, and do the work well. " Many clergyman," Mr Davis continued, "were in the cruel position of having to be prepared to walk straight to the workhouse if they retired. Arrange- ments, should be made for pensions of £lOO a year on reaching retiring age."

PRESENTATION FROM THE CONGREGATION. An interesting event took place in the vestry at the close of the service, when the Rev A J Brett was presented with a purse of gold subscribed by thee members of the congregation. Mr Edward Isherwood,. the people's warden, in making the presentation, said it, would show in a small v;ay the apprecia-,ion in which, Mr Brett was held by worshippers of the Perish, and, whilst he regretted his departure, it could not be expected that he would be with them always, and wished him every success in his new sphere of labour. Councillor S Taylor, Couucillor Locker, Messrs J T Whittle, G E Knott and H Taylor endorsed the remarks of Mr Isherwood. and expressed how delighted they had been with Mr Bratt's orations, and hoped if they were not able to have him permarientty ill Warrington, he would at least visit the town occasionally. Mr Brett, in accepting the purs., thanked the subscribers for their liberality, and said how touche d' he had been with the kindness of the worshippers in the perish, and his stay in Warrington would ever be remembered with pleasure. C.E.INI.S. TRIBUTE. Last Sunday after morning prayer in the Crypt vestry, the Rev T Vickers, B.A. (in the unavoidable absence of the Rector) presented to the Rev A 3 Brett, M.A.,on behalf of the members of the Warrington Parish Church, C.E.M.S., a framed enlarged photograph of the members. The rev gentlemen in replying,ivery sincerely thanked the members for their gift which would ever serve as a happy memento of his pleasant. ministry in Warrington. He assured the members that it had been a source of pleasure to him to beloug to. the society. Emmanuel (Reformed) Church. The vestry meeting was held on Thursday,March 27th in the Institute, Knutsford-road, the Incumbent-elect, (Rev W T Jaye), in the chair. The people's warden (Mr R Lees, sen.), said that the total income for the year was £272 6s 5 (including £ll6 4s lid from the sale of work) and toe total expenditure £255 16s lid leaving a balance in band of £l6 9s 6,id. He desired to express his thanks to all who had, by their loyal support and financial assistance, enabled him to report so sub- stantial a balance. The Rev W T Jaye nominated Mr .W Atherton as his warden and Mr N Lees was elected people's warden.- The following gentlemen were elected to the vestry : Messrs R H Armstrong, W Bibby, J Furnival, H Heald, A Johnson, .1 Jones, F Lloyd, T Lloyd, T Moon. Messrs W Atherton and J Bibby were elected lay repre- sentatives. The Rev W T Jaye briefly summarized the year's work, and expressed his gratitude at the loyalty the congregation had shown him, and hoped that he would still have their support and prayerful sympathy, which in all humility he tried to deserve. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. Twenty Years Work Completed. There was a good ateendance at the annual meting on Sunday. The Rev T T James presided, and con- gratulated the brotherhood upon the completion of 20 years' work. The Secretary (Mr B Farrar) read the annual report which expressed regret at a decline in membership, the year having closed aRh 278 on the books—about 30 fewer than last year. The meetings had, however, been quite as enthusiatic, and the spiritual tone was high. What good the society was doing to the members, their wives and families they would never fully realiz. and therefore it behoved them not be weary in well-doing. The report went on to refer to the retirement of the Rev John Yonge to whom they owed a debt of gratitude for ale interest in P.S,A. work extending over many years. It was during his active association with the early stages of the movement that their membership reached between 1,100 and 1,200. In welcoming the Rev T T James, the report said that under his guidance it Wa9 hoped to bring back to the brotherhood many of the old members and also to extend its influence. During the year a debt of between £l5 and £l6 had been liquidated. The prizes distributed had numbered 3227 making a total since the formation of the society at 14,689. At present they were putting forth efforts to help Wycliffe Church to raise £350 towards the new' school chapel in Padgate-lane. The scheme would cost £2,500. Cockhedge friends had done well in the directioa of helping themselves, having raised from £3OO to,£4oD by their own exertions. He urged the members to do their utmost to help the undertaking, and said the committee would call upon them during the next for weeks to receive their contributions. The report expressed indebtedness to all who had helped to make the meetings a success, and said the officers had done their work faithfully and well. Mr H OSBORNE read the financial statement, which showed that the society was in a very healthy condition' free from debt and with a small balance in hand.—Mr Himsworth presented the absentee report, and Mr Joe. Owen the benevolent fund report —Mr Harry Farrar gave a very satisfactory report of the Sick Club, and also a statement of the funds dealt with by the club ia 14 years.—Mr A Littlewood reported on the Savings Bank. The following officers were elected :—President, Rev T T James, M.A. ; vice-presidents, Messrs B Ferrer, Wm Beswick, A Healey, El Osborne, Jos Owen and Cotton ; treasurer, Mr H Osborne ; secretary, Mr 15 Farrar; asssistant secretary,Mr William Farrar; absentee secretary, Mr J Himsworth ; benevolent secretary, Mr Joseph Owen ; sick club secretary, Mr J Archer, treasurer, Mr H Farrar ; savings club secretary, Mr 3 Cotton ; treasurer, Mr A Littlewood ; registration secretary, Mr D McEachern ; markers MessrsW Farrar, H Farrar and Hackett' stewards, markers, J Palmer,_ DI McEachern, H Osborne, R Daniels and H Taker. The general committee of between 30 and 40 members WO elected. Three new members joined the society.
